articles.title: Polish unity on show in silent march to honour Krakow shooting victims
articles.summary: Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by Saturday's attack, writes Sarah Rainsford.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Thousands gathered at Krakow's historic Market Square to honour the victims of Saturday's attack
BySarah Rainsford
Southern and Eastern Europe correspondentReporting fromKrakow
Thousands of people joined a silent march through central Krakow on Monday night, in memory of those killed and injured when a gunman went on a violent rampage at the weekend.
The crowd were led by Poland's president and prime minister, the bitter political rivals putting on a rare show of unity after the country's deadliest attack in modern times.
As they reached the historic Market Square, a bugler played from the tower.
Many people were carrying flowers or candles to leave at the shrines that now dot the cobblestones, one marking each spot where someone died.
Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by this attack. It has left people struggling to make some kind of sense of what happened.
The alleged gunman has been named as 24-year-old Michal Oksinski by local media.
Critically injured in a shoot-out with police, he did not regain consciousness and died in hospital early on Monday.
Initially, the interior minister claimed that Oksinski was driven by far-right, extremist views. The national prosecutor's office now says that it's too soon to say he was "inspired" by any ideology.

"The minister wanted to win domestic political points. That's not responsible behaviour," Dr Pawel Musialek of the Jagiellonian University suggests, in a country where politics is highly - and often viciously - polarised.
"So far we've seen no clear message that this guy was strongly ideological, and that it's not more like something from the darknet."

There's been no mention of any letter or manifesto that Oksinski left. One neighbour told Polish news site Onet that the 24-year-old was a "bit of a loner" but few who knew him well have spoken publicly.
In addition to his electronic devices like his phone, investigators are examining a number of badges that Oksinski had attached to his military-style outfit.

The prosecutor's office says a yellow Gadsden flag with a coiled snake symbol was displayed in his bedroom. "It has various meanings of freedom and rebellion," a spokesman emphasised. "Not necessarily negative."
It was at Oksinski's home that the bodies of his parents and sister were discovered.
It's alleged that he shot them, before driving some 200km (125 miles) south to continue the killing in Krakow.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Candles and flowers have been placed around the square in places where someone died

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Candles and flowers have been placed around the square in places where someone died
Two days on, shops and cafes around the market square are beginning to fill up again, but the mood is subdued.
A Zara clothes shop is still boarded up, after bullets smashed the glass. A local man in his 50s died just outside.
Jo, a Scottish tourist, saw paramedics "who got there ridiculously fast", fighting to save him. "It was all pretty grim."
Like many, she initially mistook the rifle shots for fireworks.
On the opposite corner of the square, beside another cluster of flowers, people keep pausing to take pictures of the holes that were blasted into the wall by gunfire.
One of the six victims has been identified as a Polish painter in her 50s, who was a mother of four, and in town with friends for an exhibition opening.
A British citizen and an Austrian who died are yet to be named publicly.
Several drivers of the horse-drawn carriages that are usually poised to trot tourists around the square were seriously injured.

blocks.caption: Image caption, "This is supposed to be a safe place!" Olha, a Ukrainian citizen, moved to Krakow for safety when Russia launched its full-scale invasion

blocks.text: "This is supposed to be a safe place!" Olha, a Ukrainian citizen, moved to Krakow for safety when Russia launched its full-scale invasion
Olha, who works in a nearby chocolate shop says everyone is now nervous.
On Saturday, people rushed into her store to escape the gunman who was tearing around in his car, firing through the window.
Olha is Ukrainian, and moved to Krakow when Russia invaded. "We left our own country for safety. This is supposed to be a safe place!" she exclaimed.
"It's so sad, and so scary. Especially that he drove all the way here for two hours, planning this and thinking about it."
She regrets that the gunman did not survive: "So many are dead, so many lives have been ruined, and now there will be no justice."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Political differences were set aside between President Karol Nawrocki (left) and Prime Minister Donald Tusk (right) at the vigil on Monday

blocks.text: Image source, Filip Radwanski/Anadolu via Getty Images
Political differences were set aside between President Karol Nawrocki (left) and Prime Minister Donald Tusk (right) at the vigil on Monday
When Oksinski's car was searched, four firearms and "hundreds of rounds of ammunition" were found, all owned legally by the alleged killer and his father.
Both were members of the Swit Starachowice sports club, where there is a shooting range. A spokesman recalls Michal Oksinski as unremarkable: average competition results and normal behaviour.
He had been just three times this year, most recently in August with his father. The club spokesman is adamant that it does not train combat firing, only shooting from a fixed point.
Gun ownership in Poland has grown considerably since war broke out in Ukraine just across the border, but this is the first mass shooting anyone here can remember.
Inevitably, it has brought scrutiny of the checks over who qualifies to handle such weapons, including psychological tests, as Michal Oksinski passed all of them.
On Monday, the government announced an urgent review.

blocks.caption: Image caption, "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon"

blocks.text: "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon"
At the spot where Oksinski's car was intercepted and he was shot by police there is another memorial, this one in honour of the officers still in hospital.
Some have brought flowers, but a girl called Bianka has left a card that reads: "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon."
A couple of steps away, there's a series of bullet holes in the glass.
"This man was a real hero, he didn't hesitate," Ania says, referring to officer Jakub Kulik who was shot in the chest. His condition remains serious. "We're here to help him fight for his life."
"Nothing like this has never happened before, it's terrible," a young man called Wojtek tells me.
He's only glad that the gunman responsible for such horror turned out to be Polish.
"People here are already against immigration, so that would have been even worse."
Ania thinks Poles will pull through, though the country's image as a low-crime oasis has been shattered.
Most of all, she's angry that Michal Oksinski died without accounting for the devastation he allegedly wrought.
"I think we deserve to know why."

articles.title: Meycauayan suffers knee-deep floods despite billions in funds
articles.summary: BULACAN, Philippines – During the habagat season, floodwaters rose to waist level in Barangay Bayugo in Meycauayan City, Bulacan. Residents

blocks.text: BULACAN, Philippines – During the habagat season, floodwaters rose to waist level in Barangay Bayugo in Meycauayan City, Bulacan. Residents had to evacuate.

For Jhim Encabo, a resident, fleeing home this way had become ordinary in the 16 years he lived here, although floods have worsened recently. These days, a downpour that lasts an hour or so would trigger floods that take five to seven days to recede.
From June to August, the southwest wind brings heavy, persistent rain that causes rivers to swell, clogs drainage canals, and pushes floodwater into low-lying communities.
Residents in these areas often wake up to rising water inside their homes, forced to carry children, pets, and belongings to higher grounds as streets turn into knee-deep musky channels.
They remember that, in 2024, during Typhoon Carina, Barangay Bayugo and other villages in Meycauayan were placed under state of calamity after flood waters rose above head level (lagpas tao).
At the time, Meycauayan Mayor Henry Villarica recalled, 80 percent of Meycauayan was submerged in up to 3.66 meters of floodwater.

Barangay Bayugo has no pumping stations to drive flood water to rivers and other discharge points. So when the Meycauayan River overflows during habagat season, floodwater has nowhere to go but in the streets and inside homes until it recedes on its own.

It is one of the 17 barangays without a pumping station in Meycauayan. The others are: Bagbaguin, Bahay Pare, Bancal, Caingin, Camalig, Iba, Langka, Libtong, Liputan, Pajo, Pandayan, Pantoc, Perez, Saint Francis (Gasak), Tugatog, and Ubihan.

Meanwhile, pumping stations in nine barangays are slated for rehabilitation under a tender released on September 18, 2026: Banga, Calvario, Hulo, Lawa, Longos, Malhacan, Poblacion, Saluysoy, and Zamora.

Four barangay pumping stations are linked to now-in-hiding congressman contractor Zaldy Co: in Banga, Calvario, Lawa, and Saluysoy. The contracts for these four villages was around P19 million each or roughly P77.34 million combined.
Last July 16, the chairman of Barangay Bayugo sent a letter to Mayor Villarica, requesting the construction of a pumping station in the barangay.

“We believe that having our own pumping station will help speed up the drainage of accumulated floodwater, reduce the extent and duration of flooding, and protect the welfare and livelihoods of our residents,” the letter read.
Flood control projects in Meycauayan have reached up to approximately P3.15 billion, according to available data in the Sumbong sa Pangulo website.

Bulacan State University’s Student Government claimed in 2025 that Bulacan’s 4th District, represented by the mayor’s wife, Linabelle Villarica, received a total of ₱5.16 billion for flood control projects.

The Villarica couple has ruled Meycauayan for more than a decade. Henry Villarica served as mayor from 2016 to 2019, followed by his wife Linabelle in 2019. They swapped posts from 2019 to 2022 after they reached their term limits. Henry returned to the mayor’s office in 2022, while Linabelle resumed her seat in the House of Representatives.
The Transparency Portal of the Department of Public Works and Highways listed ID 23CD0021 as a flood control project in 2023 for Meycauayan’s tributaries within the Bayugo-Bancal section.
The project cost P49 million, and is now marked as completed. Although the project was incomplete when this writer visited the site recently.

Excavators, including long reach and amphibious units, were digging along the channel. Open pits, piles of soil and rubble, exposed rebar and trash-filled excavations were visible, and no finished structure could be seen along the stretch we photographed.
“Mike” (not his real name), who lives near the site, told Rappler that the structure was supposed to be a dike but was left unfinished after the contractors abandoned the project.
According to the DPWH Transparency Portal, the project began on February 22, 2023, and was set to be completed by August 12, 2023, giving contractors nearly six months to finish it.
The contract bid was acquired by JB Construction and Supply Inc., which had bagged at least 26 other projects in Bulacan worth an estimated P1.5 billion in total.
There are also other projects along the tributaries from the same contractor in the Meycuayan River, including Contract ID’s 23CD0022, 24CD0004, 25CD0087, and many more.
The projects are marked as completed on the DPWH Transparency Portal. – Rappler.com

Paolo Emmanuel DC Blanco is a Mover based in Bulacan. A student taking AB Communication at the University of Santo Tomas, he is also a news writer for its official student publication, The Varsitarian.

articles.title: Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
articles.summary: AI safety regulator will also be created after a rogue OpenAI agent hacked government websites.

blocks.text: Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.

In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.
On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.
AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".
"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.
One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .
This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".
The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.
This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.
In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.
OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.
It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.
Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident" and with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.
Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

articles.title: Pax Silica signing eyed by year-end, not during ASEAN Summit – DTI
articles.summary: 'We would like to give the project its own dedicated moment, so if there will be a signing, it would be on its own,' DTI Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolo says

blocks.text: 'We would like to give the project its own dedicated moment, so if there will be a signing, it would be on its own,' DTI Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolo says

items: The Philippines will not sign the US-backed Pax Silica project agreement during the upcoming ASEAN Summit, prioritizing regional initiatives instead.
US Ambassador clarified that no announcement regarding Pax Silica is planned for the summit, emphasizing the need for a dedicated moment for the project.
Despite the delay, the Philippine government remains optimistic about signing the agreement before the end of 2026, with ongoing consultations with stakeholders.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines will not sign the agreement for the US-backed Pax Silica project during the upcoming 49th ASEAN Summit, with the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) saying the ambitious development deserves a moment of its own.

DTI Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo confirmed on Tuesday, November 10, that the government would instead give priority to regional initiatives during the summit, which the Philippines will host from November 15 to 18.

“We do not want to distract attention or take away attention from the regional initiatives that ASEAN and the Philippines are proposing,” Rodolfo told reporters. “Equally important also is we would like to give the project its own dedicated moment. So if there will be a signing, there will be some finalization, conclusion, it would be on its own.”
The signing had reportedly been targeted for November, coinciding with US President Donald Trump’s visit to the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit next week.

However, US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton clarified on November 7 that no announcement on Pax Silica had been planned during the summit. He also stressed that decisions would be made in consultation with the Philippine government and affected stakeholders.
“Precisely because it’s a significant, transformative project, […] we do not need to piggyback it with another important event,” Rodolfo said at the sidelines of the Fourth ASEAN Investment Forum.
Despite the delayed timeline, Rodolfo said the government remains optimistic that an agreement for Pax Silica could be signed before the end of 2026.

“I think we’re still on track towards having an agreement by the end of this year,” he said. “And if we’re able to do that, then the timeline for the two-year development period, master planning, everything, is still on track.”

The trade undersecretary said he was “hopeful” given that there’s “no significant substantive issue that would prevent us from signing,” and that there was a “clear convergence of what we would like to happen, what we envision for the advanced manufacturing hub.”

Pax Silica is eyed to be a roughly 1,600-hectare development in New Clark City, Tarlac. The initiative seeks to strengthen supply chains for semiconductors, critical minerals, and other advanced technologies.
The project has, however, faced opposition from environmental groups, farmers, and indigenous communities over concerns about displacement and its potential energy and water costs.

Rodolfo denied that the delay in the signing was related to pushback on the project, adding that consultations with affected stakeholders have been ongoing and were always part of the process. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Mortgage holders’ confidence crashes to lowest level since 1994 as year that ‘feels like a recession’ looms
articles.summary:
Westpac survey results signal growing sense of ‘helplessness’ while Jim Chalmers faces growing pressure to rein in spending

Confidence among mortgaged households has crashed to its lowest…

blocks.text: Confidence among mortgaged households has crashed to its lowest level in more than three decades amid a growing sense of “helplessness” about the economy, even as a dramatic shift in financial markets suggests there is now a strong chance of a Reserve Bank rate cut by this time next year.
The latest Westpac survey showed its consumer sentiment index sinking again in November to reach a four-year low, amid deepening pessimism about the near-term prospects for the economy.
As Labor comes under increasing pressure over persistent cost-of-living pressures, the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, played down tensions with the treasurer, Jim Chalmers.
A day after the frontbencher Murray Watt called for colleagues to stop undermining Chalmers, Albanese said: “The treasurer is doing a great job”.
The PM said he was working closely with Chalmers in the lead-up to next month’s mid-year budget update, which will include cuts to government spending as pressure mounts to contain inflation.
“This is a treasurer who’s produced a couple of budget surpluses, lower deficits, [who is] producing economic reform,” Albanese said.

Matthew Hassan, Westpac’s head of economic forecasting, said the mood among households was last this bad in 2022, when inflation was running close to 8% and after the RBA had lifted borrowing costs by 4 percentage points over the previous year.

“Prior to that, readings this weak had only ever been seen in the economy’s darkest moments: at the onset of the Covid pandemic; the height of the GFC; and during the recessions in the early 1990s and early 1980s,” Hassan said.
Hassan said while the economic backdrop was not as extreme now as it was during the pandemic and its immediate aftermath, there were “shades of Covid in the responses” from households.
Confidence in the economic outlook over the coming year reached its weakest since August 2020, the survey showed, matching a low point last recorded during the pandemic.
“The comparison with August 2020 is quite useful as that was when Melbourne went into its second lockdown and just before the government massively scaled up income support,” Hassan said.

“There was a sense of helplessness at that stage; there was nothing we could do to avoid the pandemic, and there was nothing the government could do [to avoid the pandemic]. Obviously when the jobkeeper measures were put in place that comforted a lot of people.

“There is a similar feeling of helplessness now. You can argue a substantial portion of what is happening is out of our control, such as rising fuel prices, and there’s only so much the authorities can do to cushion Australians from that impact.”
Indebted households were gloomier still, the survey showed, with pessimism among this group at its worst in records stretching back to 1994.

The latest survey comes a week after Michele Bullock, the RBA governor, warned that the year ahead would “feel like it’s a recession” thanks to persistent cost-of-living pressures alongside weak economic growth.
After five rate increases this year, nearly three in four respondents said they expected another rate hike over the coming 12 months.
Even as the mood in the community darkens, financial markets have begun factoring in the chance of lower interest rates from the middle of next year.
The implied probability of an RBA rate cut was more than 50% by August next year, according to ANZ data, and a decrease to 4.6% was fully priced in by December 2027.
Investors have been rethinking their forecasts for central bank moves alongside a rapid retreat in the global oil price.
After testing a post-Iran war high of nearly US$118 a barrel at the end of October, the global benchmark, Brent crude, has plunged by 20% to below US$94.
“Our base case is that rates do start to come down from August next year, and we don’t see any further hikes,” Hassan said.
– Additional reporting by Tom McIlroy

articles.title: US officials seek ‘final end’ to Russia-Ukraine war as Abu Dhabi talks begin
articles.summary:
First substantive peace talks since February to include US proposal for ‘long-term security architecture’ between Moscow and Europe

US officials said they would seek a “final end” to the war…

blocks.text: US officials said they would seek a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine, beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday in the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February.
The talks are also the first since the US launched joint strikes with Israel against Iran, and they follow bruising midterm elections that have weakened Donald Trump at home.
Part of the Trump administration’s proposal involves drawing a new “long-term security architecture” between Russia and Europe, administration officials have said.

European officials are concerned that Russia may stick to its hardline demands that Nato should roll back its military footprint across eastern Europe, which would threaten to leave allies vulnerable to Moscow’s influence at a time of historic tensions with the west.

Since his first decade in power, Vladimir Putin has complained about Nato’s eastward expansion and sought to renegotiate the balance of power between Nato and Russia – but never before have those demands been embraced by a sitting US administration, which has made it clear that it is desperate to get to a deal.

Previewing the discussions, a US administration official said the US would “need Europe at the table” to end the war. He said negotiators could also revive the Nato-Russian council that was suspended after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and potentially lift sanctions against Russia to get to a deal.

The US officials also claimed that they had discussed with Russia potential security guarantees to Ukraine similar to Nato’s article 5, which protect member states in case of an attack. Russia has strongly opposed Nato admitting Ukraine or western countries placing troops in Ukraine.
“What they would be getting would be effectively very similar to Nato,” an administration official said.

“Getting a US security guarantee is a really, really big deal,” the official added, saying it would be up to Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy to discuss. “And if he wants to do that, that’s that’s a very, very big deal in terms of resources and funding and military support.”

Critics have expressed skepticism about what may trigger those security guarantees, however, noting that article 5 does not oblige Nato member states to defend others, and that cyber-attacks and other forms of hybrid warfare have blurred the line for what would require a military response.

Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a lead negotiator for the United States, described a potential new framework for European in general terms on Monday, saying the US would seek “stronger consultation, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, and reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, while fully respecting the sovereignty and independent decision-making of every nation”.

European delegations from Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy and the European Union will meet US negotiators in Abu Dhabi to discuss the “long-term security architecture between Russia and Europe in order to figure out how to reduce future conflicts”.

A European security official from a country attending the talks said that the US proposal was not yet clear and that they were bracing themselves for the US to pose serious concessions to Russia during the Abu Dhabi consultations.

“We already have a European security architecture in place,” said Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s top diplomat, at a G7 foreign ministers meeting on Monday. “This includes international agreements under which Russia has undertaken obligations, including with regard to sovereignty and territorial integrity. The problem is that Russia is not respecting these agreements.”
Donald Trump has also said that Ukraine would like be expected to give up territory in a final deal, and would end with a “little bit different shape“.

Trump last week after meeting with Kremlin advisor Kirill Dmitriev said he would seek a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”. Critics are concerned that Trump and Putin could try to go over the heads of European leaders in order to negotiate a peace that gives serious concessions to Russia.

“There’s a lot of baggage that people in Europe have about this idea,” said a US administration official, pointing specifically to Russia’s 2021 proposal that was viewed as an ultimatum to Nato to get out of eastern Europe.

In 2021, Russia issued a list of demands to Nato that included a ban on expansion to new countries including Ukraine, a rollback of troops to its pre-1997 borders, and limits on where it could place missiles. Nato rejected that proposal and Russia invaded Ukraine less than a month later.

“We have to build something new that works today… Because if all the old architecture was working well, then we wouldn’t be in this long war. And so obviously something’s not working, and we need to come up with a way that when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war,” said the US administration official.
The content of those proposals are not clear yet, although the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, claimed on Monday “there’s been some advances made in what that architecture should look”.
“We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point,” he added.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Marcos quote on P21 food threshold is fake
articles.summary: Marcos never said P21 per meal is sufficient for a family, contrary to the claim

blocks.text: Claim: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. asserted that P21 per meal is already sufficient for one family, citing research.
Why we fact-checked this: Multiple Facebook users posted an alleged quote card from PTV News containing Marcos’ supposed statement.
The quote read: “Base sa aming research. Sapat na ang 21 pesos kada meal ng isang pamilya.”
(Based on our research, P21 per meal is sufficient for a family.)

One Facebook user wrote in her caption, “Ganyan kaliit ang tingin sa mga mamamayan. Pwede na 21 pesos para sa isang pamilya. Wala halong lungkot, pag-aalala. Sapat na. The complacency and indifference of this government…”

(This shows how little they think of the people. They think P21 is enough for an entire family. Not a shred of sadness or concern — ‘it’s enough.’ The complacency and indifference of this government.)
Another Facebook user said in their caption, “Grabe naman yan BBM, 21 pesos kada meal?”
(That’s unbelievable, BBM — P21 per meal?)
Combined, their posts had 8,800 reactions, 4,100 comments, and 5,500 shares as of writing.
The facts: The quote is falsely attributed to Marcos. There are no credible reports or announcements where he or the Palace made this statement.

The P21-per-meal figure made rounds online in 2024. The figure is based on the Philippine Statistics Authority’s (PSA) 2023 poverty statistics, which pegged the food threshold — the minimum amount for a family to meet their basic food needs — at P9,581 a month for a family of five. That comes out to around P63 per person per day, or P21 per meal.
At the time, the National Economic and Development Authority (NEDA) said that individuals spending this amount and below for three meals a day are considered “food poor.”
Contrary to the claim, neither the Presidential Communications Office nor Marcos made any direct statement addressing the matter.
Rappler recently debunked a similar false claim that Marcos supposedly commented on the PSA’s 2025 poverty statistics, showing the poverty threshold at P96 per day.

Living standards: NEDA (now the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development) faced backlash in 2024 about the P21 per meal figure, with critics pointing out its unrealistic portrayal of how much Filipinos spend on food and the full picture of poverty in the Philippines.

The agency clarified that the P21 per meal metric does not reflect the cost of meals for a “decent standard of living” and is meant to serve as a measurement tool for the government’s poverty policies. (WATCH: Newsbreak Chats: The controversy over the so-called NEDA P21 meal)

In a statement in 2024, the agency’s secretary Arsenio Balisacan said, “They are not, and were never intended to be, prescribed budgets for a decent standard of living. They do not dictate how much a family should spend on food, nor do they provide an idea of a desirable household budget.”

Meanwhile, the PSA said it would review the methodology for calculating the food poverty threshold, acknowledging that the P64 food budget per day is not reflective of actual food spending. – Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Duterte's SALNs list property in nonexistent Davao del Norte barangay
articles.summary: Second defense witness confirmed a mismatch between SALN and tax records on a lot in Samal, Davao del Norte.

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:56pm
Island Garden City of Samal Assessor John Kenneth Enumerables during the 41st day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Nov. 10, 2026.
Senate PRIB
MANILA, Philippines — A property declared by Vice President Sara Duterte in her asset disclosures is listed under a barangay that does not exist in Samal, Davao del Norte.

Samal Assessor John Kenneth Enumerables, the second defense witness, testified on Tuesday, November 10 that the property, covered by a transfer certificate of title ending in 3134, was listed under "Barangay Matanos" in Duterte's Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth.
But the city's tax records place the property in Barangay San Isidro. Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero questioned the witness about the conflicting locations.
"May barangay po ba na Matanos sa Samal?" Escudero asked. ("Is there a barangay called Matanos in Samal?")
"Wala po," Enumerables replied. ("There is none.")
Escudero also asked whether the two locations were the same, which Enumerables denied.
The assessor explained that he had identified the property based on its assessed and market values.
Discrepancy traced to older title
Escudero then referred to the October 1 testimony of Marco Pineda, deputy Register of Deeds of Samal, who had previously addressed the property's location.
According to Escudero, Pineda testified that the Barangay Matanos address had been carried over from the property's mother title, the original land title from which subsequent titles were derived.
Escudero explained that under Presidential Decree 1529, the Register of Deeds cannot alter the original location details and must instead carry them over to subsequent titles.
Duterte's 2019 SALN listed a residential lot in Barangay Matanos, Kaputian District, Samal, with a reported acquisition cost of P4.04 million.
The property had an assessed value of P52,500 and was declared as acquired in 2013.
Prosecution counsel Benjamin Tolosa noted the property also appeared in Duterte's SALNs for 2020, 2021 and 2022.

articles.title: Australia to introduce mandatory AI safeguards
articles.summary: The Australian government's decision to establish an AI safety regulator comes after an OpenAI agent accessed a government medical statistics portal without authorization.

image.caption: OpenAI and rival Anthropic have agreed to meet the reporting requirements for data breaches that involve AI agentsImage: Jonathan Raa/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Australia will introduce mandatory safeguards for artificial intelligence companies, including compulsory reporting of security breaches and independent oversight of AI systems, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday.
The decision comes after an incident in which an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to a government medical statistics portal while researching public medical spending.

Albanese said his center-left Labor government had accepted all the review's recommendations, which include requiring AI companies to report misaligned behavior and cyber incidents. The government will also consider reforms to criminal law to address cases of serious misconduct.

The government plans to establish an AI safety regulator to oversee security controls during the development and deployment of AI systems, identify serious risks and conduct independent evaluations of models.
My AI therapist: A chatbot experiment
"The AI ⁠safety regulator will be ​able to enforce significant penalties for AI companies doing the wrong thing," Albanese said.
"The law needs to get ahead of, and in some cases, make sure that it catches up with what is a very fast-changing world," he told reporters.
AI breach stirred tension between Australia and US tech companies
OpenAI has said it learned of the breach in August and that the incident was unintentional. Its review found no evidence that the AI agent had accessed patient records.

Canberra declined to exempt ChatGPTmaker OpenAI and rival Anthropic from copyright laws for model ⁠training which would require them instead to negotiate licensing agreements with Australian rights ​holders.
Both companies told an Australian parliamentary committee last month that they would welcome mandatory reporting requirements for data breaches involving their AI agents.

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Justice (DOJ) has ordered the filing of a cyber libel case against several pro-Duterte personalities, including lawyer Ferdinand Topacio, over a complaint filed by Senator Risa Hontiveros.

“The Office of the Secretary of Justice-Prosecution Staff is hereby directed to FILE an Information for Cyberlibel under Article 355 of the RPC in relation to Section 4(c)(4) of RA No. 10175 against Respondent-Appellees Atty. Ferdinand Topacio, Byron Cristobal aka ‘Banat By,’ Jeffrey Celiz aka ‘Ka Eric,’ Krizette Chu aka ‘Kiffy,’ Jose Sonza aka ‘Jay Sonza,’ and Alex Destor aka ‘Tio Moreno’,” said the DOJ resolution made public on Tuesday, November 10.

The complaint stemmed from the Senate’s hearings on the reported crimes of Kingdom of Jesus Christ founder and doomsday preacher Apollo Quiboloy (Quiboloy). Hontiveros presented as a witness Michael Maurillo, a supposed KOJC full-time worker who allegedly suffered abuse and exploitation under Quiboloy.
Maurillo had sought Hontiveros’ help in rescuing him, “after he claimed that he was kidnapped following his earlier claim that he was being pressured by Quiboloy’s camp to recant his testimony.”

On June 24, 2025, a video was uploaded on YouTube where Maurillo alleged that he was induced by Hontiveros to give fabricated testimony against Quiboloy, former president Rodrigo Duterte, and Vice President Sara Duterte in exchange for P1 million, and even more money to implicate senators Bong Go and Bato dela Rosa.

In July of the same year, Hontiveros filed a cyber libel complaint against Maurillo as well as the six personalities who posted content echoing Maurillo’s claims — Topacio, Celiz, and the four vloggers.

While the DOJ indicted Maurillo in December 2025, DOJ prosecutors dismissed Hontiveros complaint against the six other personalities, citing lack of evidence. She filed a motion for reconsideration, but was denied in a resolution dated March 16, 2026.
This pushed Hontiveros to file a petition for review before the DOJ, which was granted.

“Wherefore, premises considered, the instant Petition for Review is hereby granted. The assailed Resolutions of the Office of the Secretary of Justice-Prosecution Staff dated 22 December 2025 and 16 March 2026 are reversed and set aside,” said the DOJ resolution.
The DOJ said it found the elements of cyber libel present in the allegations.

It explained that the respondents’ accusations were not presented as mere suspicions or opinions, but rather as statements “stating that she had in fact bribed or coached witnesses, fabricated testimony and evidence, manipulated affidavits, orchestrated witnesses to falsely implicate other persons, and participated in organized political schemes against her perceived opponents.”

“The additional assertion that she had a ‘pattern’ of paying witnesses in exchange for favorable testimony further transforms the accusation into a claim of an established course of wrongful and criminally punishable conduct,” the DOJ added.

In a statement following the release of the DOJ resolution, Hontiveros said: “We welcome the latest resolution of the Department of Justice which recommended the criminal indictment of 6 persons — Atty Ferdinand Topacio, Banat By, Jeffrey Celiz, Jay Sonza, Krizette Chu and Tio Moreno. This follows the earlier indictment of Michael Maurillo.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sydney private school accused of sexual abuse should be banned from enrolling new students, inquiry says
articles.summary:
Inquiry recommends police investigate allegations of sexual assault and other abuse at Redeemer Baptist school

  • Get our

blocks.text: An investigation into a private religious school accused of sexual, physical, psychological, spiritual and financial abuse has recommended it be barred from enrolling new students.
Former students and teachers of western Sydney’s Redeemer Baptist school told a New South Wales parliamentary inquiry about a string of disturbing allegations.
They included students being made to share beds with teachers and its principal once wandering naked through a common area.
In a report tabled in state parliament on Tuesday, a committee found the school – run by the Redeemer Baptist Church – breached basic child safeguarding standards.
Sexual assault allegations were not handled appropriately and the school put children at significant risk of harm, the committee found.
It also found staff at the school lacked essential workplace rights and failed to satisfy basic standards of good governance.
The committee recommended the school be prevented from enrolling new students while it was under investigation by the NSW Education Standards Authority.
It also recommended the allegations raised in the inquiry be investigated by NSW police and the office of the children’s guardian.

The committee chair and Greens MP, Abigail Boyd, noted the school was subjected to parliamentary scrutiny in 2006, but no procedures had been put in place to monitor what was clearly a “high-risk situation”.

blocks.caption: Redeemer Baptist school in Parramatta. Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAP

blocks.text: She said it was thanks to the bravery of those who had spoken out that the committee had enough evidence to make its strong findings and recommendations.
The school received about $6m a year in government funding, Boyd said, and had enough cash to launch legal challenges against those who raised their voices against the religious group.
“They also have deep political ties with both state and federal politicians,” she told parliament.
People who had escaped the school appeared to be absolutely terrified of its leaders, Boyd said.
after newsletter promotion
“When you know that leaving means leaving with no financial assets, and when you have finally managed to escape, it’s no wonder that you would be terrified of your abuser,” she said in parliament.
The committee lashed a lack of regulatory oversight, including from the education authority, suggesting a number of alarming matters needed proper investigation.
They included allegations of persistent Centrelink fraud and dodgy tax practices.

“It is, at the very least, troubling that an asset-rich, seemingly prosperous school operates by withholding wages from its workforce, who claim benefits, while the school receives millions of dollars in public funding,” the report said.
A Redeemer Baptist school spokesperson previously said the school had fully cooperated with the relevant regulators.
“Redeemer Baptist School takes its child safety obligations extremely seriously and has an unblemished record of compliance with state and federal regulators for 45 years,” they said.
The school did not immediately respond to a request for comment following the report’s release.

articles.title: NAMFREL urges no more delays after SC ruling on BSKE
articles.summary: “Our concern is not the length of the term. It is how the term was lengthened. Congress may set a term, but only voters can grant a mandate,” the poll watchdog said in a statement.

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:43pm
Women cast their vote at Pasong Tamo Elementary School in Quezon City during the automated mock barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) elections on August 8, 2023.
STAR / Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — Election watchdog National Citizens’ Movement for Free Elections is warning against further delays to the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections after the Supreme Court declared constitutional a law extending barangay officials' terms and moving polls to 2028.
In a statement on Monday, November 9, the organization said that while it respected the High Court's decision, it has not "exhausted the ways the right to suffrage can be protected."
The group cited objections raised by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen and Associate Justice Antonio Kho on the law’s potential to impede the right to vote.

Leonen, joined by Associate Justices Ramon Paul Hernando and Ricardo Rosario, reasoned that successive extensions may "defer the vote unconstitutionally," and that the law prevented Filipinos ageing out of SK eligibility before 2028 from exercising their right to vote.
Kho, meanwhile, was joined by Associate Justice Alfredo Caguioa in saying that Congress could have adopted the new term while holding the elections as scheduled.
The 2028 cycle, Kho argued, created the overlap with the 2028 elections that the law claimed to avoid.
“Our concern is not the length of the term. It is how the term was lengthened. Congress may set a term, but only voters can grant a mandate,” the poll watchdog said in a statement.
The organization also emphasized the need for Congress to be proactive in future scenarios, saying it need not wait for another court case to reform election laws.
Passed in September 2026, Republic Act 12326 moved the next BSK elections from Nov. 2, 2026 to November 2028.
The law also fixes the terms of such officials at five years, effectively granting term extensions to officials voted in during the 2023 elections.

Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal challenged the constitutionality of the law, arguing that it failed to meet the guidelines of a 2023 ruling that allowed the postponement of elections “only for important, substantial or compelling reasons.”
Macalintal also argued that the law violated the people’s right to vote, as voters in 2023 elected the incumbent officials with the belief they would serve three-year terms.

articles.title: After witness' 'China' flip-flop, senator-judges warn vs lying under oath
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court warned witnesses that false testimony could lead to contempt and possible perjury cases.

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:32pm
MANILA, Philippines — Senator-judges warned witnesses in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial that false testimony could lead to contempt and perjury proceedings.

On Tuesday, November 10, Senator-judge Tito Sotto sought clarification from Presiding Officer Chiz Escudero on the penalties that could be imposed on witnesses caught lying before the impeachment court.

"We have penalties and sanctions against those who lie before the impeachment court. Will you please refresh my memory on this matter so that the witnesses and the prosecution and the defense will be reminded as well?" Sotto asked.
Escudero then said witnesses who lie under oath may be cited for contempt and could also face perjury complaints.

"They may be subject to contempt by the court, Your Honor, and in addition to that, may be subjected to cases of perjury should one be filed against him before the proper prosecutor's office and or courts of law, because the statements given by any witness is under oath and is therefore covered by our laws on perjury as well," Escudero said.
Senator-Judge Ping Lacson also stressed that the impeachment court's power to punish contempt is expressly provided under its rules and is not merely implied.
The reminder came a day after the testimony of Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin, the first witness presented by Duterte's defense, drew questions from senator-judges over his answers.

During Monday's hearing, senator-judges pressed Adalin after he initially said he could not recall details of a trip he supposedly made to China. He later acknowledged that he traveled there in January 2026 with Davao City officials.
Questions were also raised over his testimony concerning properties listed in Duterte's Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth.
The properties are being examined under Article II of the impeachment complaint, which covers allegations of unexplained wealth and discrepancies in Duterte's asset declarations.

articles.title: DOJ seeks cyberlibel charges vs Topacio, 5 others
articles.summary: The Department of Justive has filed a resolution reversing its decision to junk a cyberlibel complaint filed by Sen. Risa Hontiveros against six social media personalities who accused the lawmaker of…

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:30pm

MANILA, Philippines — Cyberlibel charges have been recommended against lawyer Ferdinand Topacio and five other social media personalities following a Department of Justice resolution granting the review of a complaint filed by Sen. Risa Hontiveros that was dismissed in December 2025.

Though Hontiveros must tolerate criticism as a public official, the respondents “crossed the line separating protected criticism and opinion from the public and malicious imputation of specific, discreditable acts,” the resolution said.
Hontiveros welcomed the indictment of Topacio, Byron “Banat By” Cristobal, Jeffrey “Ka Eric” Celiz, Jose “Jay” Sonza, Krizette “Kiffy” Chu and Alex “Tio Moreno” Destor.
“Sinabi natin dati pa: hindi dapat palampasin ang mapanganib na kasinungalingan laban sa mga tumestigong biktima ng pang-aabuso ni Apollo Quiboloy,” the senator said.
(“We’ve said it before: lies directed at the victims who testified to the abuse committed by Apollo Quiboloy must not go unaddressed.”)

Hontiveros' complaint, filed in July 2025, stemmed from social media posts published by the personalities that accused her of bribing and coaching witnesses during the Senate investigation into sex trafficking allegations against Quiboloy.
The posts also alleged that Hontiveros launched “organized propaganda efforts” to discredit various public officials, including Vice President Sara Duterte and former President Rodrigo Duterte.

Hontiveros filed a similar complaint against Michael Maurillo, a former Kingdom of Jesus Christ member who claimed he was coerced by Hontiveros to give false testimony against Quiboloy and the Dutertes.
Murillo was indicted early 2026, with an arrest warrant issued against him by the Pasay Regional Trial Court Branch 111 in February.

Quiboloy, meanwhile, is detained at the Pasig City Jail for sexual abuse charges and qualified human trafficking. The DOJ is preparing to file a court petition to extradite the church leader as he also faces child sex trafficking and fraud charges in the US.

Criminal and libel complaints were filed by his camp against Hontiveros, Rep. Leila de Lima (Mamamayang Liberal) and Rep. Perci Cendaña (Akbayan) in September, over statements referring to him as a “sex offender."

articles.title: This is the estimated amount PH needs to implement its climate commitments
articles.summary: According to the Climate Change Commission, we'll need an estimated amount of at least $250B in investments to implement our climate commitments

blocks.text: Published November 10, 2026 12:19pm

COP31 is underway in Antalya, Türkiye and in the sidelines of the biggest United Nations conference, the Climate Change Commission formally opened the Philippine Hub, where the country's updated Nationally Determined Contribution or NDC was also presented.
NDCs are climate action plans that each of the 195 signatories of the Paris Agreement is required to submit to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) every five years.

In the Philippines' NDC 2026, we maintained the total 75% emissions reduction target, as we increased our unconditional commitment to 7% or reductions we plan to do on our own through domestic resources. The remaining 68% conditional target will depend on international support.

At the Philippine Hub opening on Monday in Antalya, CCC Vice Chairperson and Executive Director Robert Borje said the country will need an estimated amount of at least $250B in investments to implement our climate commitments.

"'Development partners have now been formally apprised of the NDC 2026, and we are in ongoing negotiations and discussions with them on the NDC needs of the Philippines,' Borje said, adding that partners including the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, and civil society organizations have already provided resources and expertise during the NDC's formulation," the CCC said on Facebook Tuesday morning.
The Philippines has contributed less than half of 1% to global greenhouse gas emissions but we continue to bear the brunt of climate change impacts.
So "this is really a question of climate justice and equity," Borje said.
According to CCC, the estimated amount is based on national documents and data, which became part of the assessment for the 2026 NDC.
"Specifics will be addressed through the updating of the NDC Implementation plan," CCC told GMA News on Viber.

At the Philippine Hub opening, Borje was accompanied by the Department of Energy Undersecretary Undersecretary Felix William B. Fuentebella, Department of Agriculture Assistant Secretary U-Nichols A. Manalo, and Department of Transportation Director Crinezza Veil L. Mendoza who each provided detailed responses on financing requirements and sectoral initiatives.
Stressing the need for accessible climate finance, Manalo expressed the importance of scaling up climate-resilient agricultural technologies that will help farmers adapt to climate change.
Said Fuentabella, among those technologies that will benefit farmers and fisherfolk include solar-powered irrigation facilities and floating solar for watershed management.

Meanwhile, Mendoza highlighted short-term initiatives on sustainable mobility including sidewalk and bicycle lanes improvement, mass transit expansions and the targeted partial operations of the Metro Manila Subway Project in 2033.
— GMA News

articles.title: Duterte defense asks ICC to drop two witnesses, calls their accounts hearsay
articles.summary: Lawyers for former president Rodrigo Duterte have asked the International Criminal Court to remove two prosecution witnesses from his case, arguing that what they claim to know about his drug war…

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 12:16pm
Peter Haynes, president of the International Criminal Court Bar Association, speaks at the opening of the International Criminal Court's judicial year in February 2020.
ICCBA

MANILA, Philippines — Lawyers for former president Rodrigo Duterte have asked the International Criminal Court to remove two prosecution witnesses from his case, arguing that what they claim to know about his drug war comes mostly from rumor and hearsay.

In a filing dated November 9 and released in redacted form, lead defense counsel Peter Haynes said the witnesses, identified only as P-1334 and P-1348, were absent for nearly the entire period covered by the two counts under Duterte’s presidency.
As a result, the defense said, they could have “almost no direct knowledge” of how decisions were made or how operations were carried out.
The filing responds to an October 21 prosecution request to admit the witnesses’ earlier recorded statements without calling them to testify.
Prosecutors are arguing the two witnesses' statements will help prove the broader elements of crimes against humanity, particularly Duterte's alleged policy of “neutralizing” criminals.
Prosecutors are relying on Rule 68(2)(b) of the court’s rules, which lets judges admit prior recorded testimony from absent witnesses.
According to the defense's November 9 filing, P-1334 confirmed she had no personal knowledge of how Duterte allegedly passed instructions through former national police chief Bato dela Rosa.
"She never saw Dela Rosa do anything of the sort, and recognized that her account is based on stories she had heard," the filing read.
The defense also argues that "the little she claims to know about Incident 13 comes entirely from newspapers or 'people talking,'" the redacted filing read.
If the court decides to keep the two witnesses, the defense said it would not cross-examine them and would leave their admission to the judges’ discretion.
It asked, however, that the chamber disregard passages on Duterte’s own conduct, including allegations that specific orders to kill were issued and claims attributing certain funds to him.

Government figures put the number of people killed in police anti-drug operations under Duterte at more than 6,000, while human rights groups estimate the toll is several times higher. Duterte has consistently defended the campaign.
Duterte's trial opens November 30.

articles.title: DOLE to employers: Release 13th month pay by Christmas Eve 2026
articles.summary: The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) reminded private sector employers to release the 13th month pay of their workers by December 24, 2026.

blocks.text: Published November 10, 2026 12:06pm
The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) reminded private sector employers to release the 13th month pay of their workers by December 24, 2026.

"The 13th month pay must be released on or before December 24, 2026. Compliance with the payment requirements shall be monitored by the appropriate DOLE Regional, Field, or Provincial Office having jurisdiction over the workplace," DOLE said in a statement.

In Labor Advisory No. 21, Series of 2026, DOLE set guidelines for the payment for the 13th month pay, saying that employees, regardless of their position, designation, or employment status, are entitled to the additional payment.

According to the advisory, the 13th month pay must also be given to rank-and-file employees who are paid on a piece-rate basis, fixed or guaranteed wage plus commission, workers with multiple employers, workers who resigned or terminated, or those who went on maternity leave and received a salary differential.
DOLE said the minimum 13th month pay must not be less than 1/12 of the total basic salary earned by an employee within a calendar year.
For the purpose of computing the 13th month pay, DOLE said an employee's basic salary included remunerations for earnings paid by the employer for services rendered.

Allowances and monetary benefits are not included as part of the basic salary, including unused leave credits, night differentials, overtime, and more. However, DOLE said these benefits could be included if there is an agreeable collective agreement, company practice or policy.
An employee's 13th month pay is their entire year's basic salary earned during the year divided by 12, DOLE said.

"For example, an employee earning P228,010.04 in annual basic salary is entitled to P19,000.84 in 13th month pay. A piece-rate worker earning P120,000.00 receives P10,000.00, while an employee receiving P235,560.04 in fixed wages and P30,000.00 in commissions is entitled to P19,630.00, based on basic salary alone," DOLE said.

Even employees who resign before the end of the calendar year are entitled to a proportionate 13th month pay, DOLE said. For example, an employee who earned P177,236.28 in basic salary is entitled to P14,769.69 if they resigned in September.
"The Department urges all employers to comply with the prescribed payment guidelines and ensure that qualified workers receive their rightful 13th month pay," the agency said. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: [Vantage Point] Can BPI earn back its premium?
articles.summary: For shareholders, true confidence will come from dependable, cash-backed profits after all credit costs are absorbed, not from the fleeting euphoria of a one-day market rally

blocks.text: (In case you missed, read the first part of this series here.)
The loan book that Maria Cristina “Ginbee” Go is preparing to inherit will ultimately determine what Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) shareholders truly own.
Investors now face the critical task of pricing a franchise whose aggressive balance sheet expansion is still revealing its full credit costs.

A sharp rally on November 4 lifted BPI shares by 7.93% to P100 on 3.04 million shares traded. While the stock remains 13.87% below its end-2025 level, excluding dividends, it now sits 6.38% above the P94 mark recorded when this analysis was first drafted.

Yet a climbing quotation makes the valuation question considerably more demanding, not less. The one-day surge visibly outpaced the Philippine Stock Exchange index’s 1.26% gain, as well as peer advances of 4.39% in Metrobank and 2.27% in BDO.
These comparisons establish clear outperformance on the trading board, but they tell us little about its fundamental catalyst.
Without concrete evidence linking the buying wave to executive moves, fresh credit disclosures, or a definitive corporate transaction, investors should resist adopting convenient narratives.
A rising share price can anticipate operational improvement, but it cannot substitute for verifiable cash collections, durable earnings, and transparent capital disclosures.

At P100, BPI’s 5.296 billion outstanding shares command a market capitalization of approximately P529.64 billion. That valuation translates to 1.10 times the bank’s June book value of P91.11 per share, compared to 1.29 times book value at the close of 2025.

September’s P488.6 billion headline equity still requires detailed reconciliation against common-shareholder equity, and June book value represents neither tangible book value — after deducting goodwill and other intangibles — nor a current liquidation estimate.
Annualizing nine-month headline net profit of P48.9 billion yields P65.2 billion, pointing to an apparent screening price-to-earnings multiple of 8.12 times.
Yet this metric is neither a trailing nor a forward forecast P/E.

Fourth-quarter credit provisions, seasonal adjustments, and earnings attributable specifically to common shareholders must all be rigorously reconciled before an apparently modest multiple can be declared a defensible bargain.
To be sure, the underlying franchise continues to expand. Gross revenue grew 9.8% over the first nine months, supported by a 13.6% expansion in loan portfolios and a 15.5% increase in fee income.
But credit provisions surged 69.2% to P19.88 billion, operating expenses outpaced top-line revenue, and net profit slipped 3.1%.
The bank is generating substantially more business, but that volume has not translated into higher bottom-line earnings.

There are qualified signs of relief. Quarterly provisions eased to P6.54 billion from P7.84 billion, helping third-quarter net income reach P16.07 billion. Pre-provision operating profit, however, slipped from P27.96 billion to P27.23 billion. Lower credit charges provided bottom-line support without demonstrating that troubled lending vintages had definitively rounded the corner.
September’s non-performing loan ratio for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) climbed to 15.62%, though the SME segment accounts for only 2.7% of the total loan portfolio.
Credit cards edged up to 5.44%, while personal lending and microfinance showed relative improvement at 6.99% and 13.95%, respectively.

Across the entire bank, the gross NPL (non performing loans) balance rose 6.1% from June to P68.05 billion. Neither blanket pessimism nor an uncomplicated narrative of recovery fits these divergent figures.

An accounting NPL coverage ratio of 89.57%, compared to 113.05% under broader regulatory guidelines, does not by itself prove inadequate reserves. Underlying collateral values, expected recoveries, and precise reserve definitions matter tremendously.

To know if this growth is turning into bad debt, investors need the real numbers behind it: which loan batches are defaulting, which debts are being rewritten, how much is being written off, and how much cash is actually being collected.

Management attributes recent staging recalibrations to Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas findings and notes a P2.7 billion year-to-date expected credit loss impact from macroeconomic assumptions carried over from June.

The underlying regulatory documents and an independent allowance reconciliation are still essential to test those explanations. Forward-looking provisioning and deteriorating borrower repayment capacity frequently coexist; the presence of one does not negate the other.

BPI generated an annualized nine-month return on equity of 13.6%. Reclaiming a sustained market premium requires conviction that long-term returns will exceed the cost of equity that shareholders demand for risk.
Lending growth that consumes capital without earning adequate compensating spreads can enlarge an institution while quietly weakening its investment thesis.
Consider a valuation model assuming an illustrative 14% required shareholder return and 5% perpetual growth funded through retained earnings.

Dividing sustainable Return on Equity (ROE) minus growth by the required return minus growth yields a simplified justified price-to-book ratio: 0.78 times at a 12% ROE, and 1.22 times at a 16% ROE. At BPI’s current multiple of 1.10 times book, this framework implies an expected sustainable ROE of roughly 14.9%.
Any shift in underlying risk assumptions alters that equation, and dated equity numbers cannot replace forward-looking estimates.

Our stress test illustrates the earnings sensitivity. Adding P27 billion in incremental credit provisions — equivalent to roughly 1% of the bank’s rounded loan base — would reduce net income and equity by P20.25 billion after a usable 25% tax shield, or approximately P3.82 per share.

That adjustment would absorb about 41% of nine-month earnings. This exercise represents a disciplined balance-sheet sensitivity test, not a definitive prediction of default or an explicit share-price target.

Margin dynamics also warrant scrutiny. Quarterly net interest margin narrowed from 4.70% to 4.56%. While management expects loan yields to gradually catch up with rising deposit costs, borrowers must have the financial stamina to service higher debt loads.
Preliminary 2027 planning points to credit costs near 100 basis points and loan growth around 10%, though corporate budgets remain unfinished.

Balance sheet buffers offer mixed signals. June’s P13.44 billion net-of-tax fair-value reserve loss on debt securities was already charged against equity; deducting it again would double-count the impact.
However, amortized-cost paper carried a separate P5.53 billion unbooked fair-value shortfall. Updated September marks and interest-rate sensitivity schedules remain essential checks.

An indicative Common Equity Tier 1 ratio of 13.9% and a total capital adequacy ratio of 14.7% temper claims of an immediate capital crisis. Still, the proposed P5 billion SIBOL bond issue will raise debt rather than common equity.

Furthermore, LandBank has clarified that Citicore’s P35.014 billion solar syndication is shared equally with BPI and the Development Bank of the Philippines, implying an exposure of P11.67 billion each before verifying actual funding drawdowns and retained risk.
Meanwhile, BPI’s November 3 clarification stated that no definitive agreement or binding commitment currently exists regarding the reported CIMB opportunity.
Buying expansion abroad or domestically demands rigorous inspection of acquired asset quality, goodwill, and post-merger integration costs, not automatic applause.
Go is scheduled to succeed Jose Teodoro “TG” Limcaoco on April 26, 2027, subject to customary regulatory approvals.
Limcaoco still has five months to solidify the balance sheet his successor will inherit.
For shareholders, true confidence will come from dependable, cash-backed profits after all credit costs are absorbed, not from the fleeting euphoria of a one-day market rally.
BPI must earn back its premium the hard way: by proving the durability of its cash collections.
I welcome your views on these and other issues where decisions made in power shape the country’s economic future. – Rappler.com

(This analysis draws from BPI’s October 21 leadership transition announcement and nine-month financial results; the October 27 investor presentation and earnings briefing transcript; BPI’s June 30 SEC Form 17-Q and historical stock valuations; the November 3 PSE clarification on CIMB; LandBank’s October 26 Citicore syndication release; and November 4 closing records and PSE trading data. Management statements remain attributed disclosures. Valuation multiples and stress-test calculations are the author’s independent analytical illustrations, not bank forecasts or formal price targets.)

articles.title: Iran war oil shock drives dip in global emissions, study shows
articles.summary: Global carbon emissions are expected to fall slightly in 2026, but not because of major progress on climate action. Instead, it's high energy prices following the US attack on Iran that's driving the…

image.caption: Carbon emissions are the main drivers of climate changeImage: Jason Whitman/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a new study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.
Emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change. While over the past decade, these emissions have risen by 0.9% per year, they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026.

"It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.
"So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons."
The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the United Nations' COP31 climate conference.
No structural change yet

The study published by international research group the Global Carbon Project found that oil emissions dropped by 1.9% in 2026, while natural gas fell by 0.3%. Coal emissions however continued to rise, by around 0.6%.
"A drop in emissions in ‌one year is not a peak unless it ‌is driven ​by structural change," Peters cautioned.
Turkey on the climate frontline

A structural change would mean that emissions would slowly rise to a peak and then slowly decline afterwards, indicating a long term trend. That's not what happened though, Peters said. "What we see this year is oil emissions are going up and then suddenly, bang, down 2%."
Emissions expected to rebound

It is the third time in recent years that global carbon pollution has dropped. The previous declines were during the global economic crisis in 2009 and during the COVID pandemic in 2020. In each of those cases, emissions went back up once global economies recovered.

While the geopolitical shocks of the past year have been the driving factors behind, the temporary emissions reversal, there's also been a rise in renewable energy contributing to the data. So while solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles did make a difference, they were just not enough to cut emissions by themselves.
"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies," according to co-author of the study, Pierre Friedlingstein, of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University.

And even though emissions from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions still went up by about 1%, the study warns. The overall rise is because of land use changes like deforestation and peat fires, which increased too fast to be offset by the slight decrease in fossil fuel burning.

blocks.text: Published November 10, 2026 11:54am
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero expressed hope Tuesday that the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte will be finished before Christmas or New Year.

Escudero, however, clarified that the impeachment court is not following any timeline and could not say exactly when the trial would end as it would depend on the evidence presented by the defense and the flow of the hearings.

“Sa akin mismo, kung ako ang tatanungin syempre in a perfect world, sana matapos ang impeachment sinuman ang matalo o manalo bago mag-Pasko, bago mag-New Year para may bago tayong yugto na namang haharapin sa bagong taon, hindi ‘yung babalikan na naman natin ito sa darating na bagong taon ng 2027,” he said in an ambush interview.

(Personally, if you ask me, in a perfect world, I would hope that the impeachment concludes before Christmas or the New Year, regardless of who wins or loses. This way, we can face a new chapter in the coming year, rather than having to revisit this same issue when 2027 comes.)
“Whichever side prevails, sana ito ay malampasan at matapos natin ngayong taong ito para may bagong mga hamon at problema na naman tayong haharapin sa darating na taon,” he added.
(Whichever side prevails, I hope we can move past this and bring it to a close within this year, so that we may face new challenges and problems in the year ahead.)

The defense is currently presenting evidence and witnesses for Article II of the impeachment case against Duterte alleging her unexplained wealth due to supposed failure to truthfully disclose assets in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) and failure to divest in businesses as required for the President and Vice President under a Constitutional provision.
The prosecution previously dropped three out of the four Articles of Impeachment leveled against the Vice President, saying its case would stand on Article II alone.

The withdrawn impeachment articles were: Article I on confidential funds; Article III on bribery; and Article IV on assassination plot, grave threats, and inciting to sedition against President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former Speaker and incumbent Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: California voters reject proposed billionaire tax
articles.summary: California voters have rejected a proposed one-time tax on the net worth of billionaires in the state following a contentious ballot fight that generated huge spending by some prominent tech leaders…

image.caption: A sign is displayed at the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco in February 2026. California voters have since rejected a tax on the net worth of billionaires. (Jeff Chiu/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

California voters have rejected a proposed one-time tax on the net worth of billionaires in the state following a contentious ballot fight that generated huge spending by some prominent tech leaders eager to stop their taxes from going up. one-time tax on state billionaires' fortunes
Critics said one-time tax on state billionaires' fortunes would prompt ultrawealthy taxpayers to leave state

California voters have rejected a proposed tax on the net worth of billionaires following a contentious ballot fight that generated huge spending by some prominent tech leaders eager to stop their taxes from going up.

The measure's failure is a win for Democratic leaders who opposed it, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, who's deciding whether to run for president in 2028. Critics of the tax, known as Proposition 40, said it would have prompted ultrawealthy taxpayers to leave the state.
The "no" side raised roughly 10 times as much as the "yes" side. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone dumped more than $100 million US into a political action committee working to defeat the measure.
The measure would have imposed a one-time five per cent tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion US. It would have been the first of its kind in the U.S.

Most of the money would have been used to backfill federal funding cuts to health care, and 10 per cent would have gone toward education and food-assistance programs. SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, California's health-care union, said the tax was necessary to replace an estimated $100 billion US the state will lose in federal health-care funding over five years.
Long championed by progressives

Proposition 40 was the nation's biggest test yet on an idea progressives have long championed: raising taxes on the ultra-rich by targeting the main way they make their money — through their investments as opposed to their work paycheques.

The measure attracted support from liberal leaders beyond the state, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who rallied in cities across California in the race's closing weeks to urge voters to pass it.

The measure attracted support from liberal leaders beyond the state, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders — seen speaking at a Ballots Over Billionaires rally in Los Angeles last month. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Billionaires donated millions of dollars to a political action committee, Building a Better California, working to defeat the measure. The committee, which backed other measures on the ballot designed to nullify the tax, raised more than $333 million US, nearly a third of which came from Brin.

Brin, along with his fellow Google co-founder Larry Page, was among the billionaires who started cutting ties with the state in anticipation of the possible tax. Another tech mogul, Facebook co-founder Mark Zuckerberg, said he would remain in the state for eight years and made a deal with Meta to help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company.
Opposed by some Democratic allies

Some traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Medical Association, were part of a coalition opposing the measure. They were concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state's budget if there was a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers.
California's budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state's richest residents.
"Proposition 40 was a reckless experiment conducted on our state's economy with little regard for the harms it would cause," the coalition said in a statement.
Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who is politically independent, said before voting concluded on Nov. 3 that he planned to vote against it.
"Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do," he said. "But I don't believe taxing them out of existence is going to work."

California Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed Proposition 40. He says a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million US. (Jill Connelly/The Associated Press)
Tax would disadvantage state: Newsom

Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom says a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million US.

Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month, Newsom told reporters that the senator's focus on wealth inequality was "spot-on." But he said that "on this issue, we fundamentally disagree."

Supporters of the California tax started running ads recently in New Hampshire, New Mexico and Virginia, states that will vote early in the Democratic presidential primary in 2028, that criticize Newsom for his opposition to the measure.

articles.title: Marcos to newly appointed AFP officials: Never lose trust, confidence of Filipinos
articles.summary: President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. on Tuesday urged newly promoted generals and flag officers of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) to never lose the "trust and confidence" of Filipinos…
