President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. on Tuesday urged newly promoted generals and flag officers of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) to never lose the "trust and confidence" of Filipinos as they take their oaths of office.
"No matter how advanced our capabilities may become, we must never lose sight of the trust and confidence of the Filipino people," Marcos said during his speech.
"Sustaining that trust is a responsibility that all of us share, government, our institutions, and our communities," he added.
Marcos made the statement as he said, "a modern military requires leaders who serve with competence, integrity, and accountability."
He also committed that the government will provide the support needed by the AFP to perform its mandate.
General Antonio Nafarrete took his oath as AFP chief of staff along with 33 other newly promoted generals and flag officers of the AFP.
In August, the Commission on Appointments confirmed the appointments and nomination of Nafarrete and 37 other generals, flag and senior officers.

Suceeding General Romeo Brawner Jr., Nafarrete previously headed the Western Mindanao Command (WestMinCom), where he oversaw joint military operations against communist insurgents and local terrorist groups.

He also commanded the 1st Infantry Division, Joint Task Force Zampelan, and held leadership posts in the 11th Infantry Division, the 1101st Infantry Brigade, and the AFP's operations staff (J3). — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Who gave barangay execs 5 years? Supreme Court dissenters say not voters
articles.summary: The dissenters raised different arguments, from the lack of a compelling reason for the delay to the application of the longer term to officials already in office.

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 11:41am

MANILA, Philippines — Five Supreme Court justices warned that extending the terms of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) officials to five years and moving the elections to November 2028 improperly curtails the people's right to vote.

Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen and Associate Justices Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa, Ramon Paul Hernando, Ricardo Rosario and Antonio Kho Jr. dissented from the majority decision upholding the constitutionality of Republic Act 12326. Leonen, Caguioa and Kho issued separate opinions, with Hernando and Rosario joining Leonen's dissent.

The majority held that RA 12326 is primarily a term-setting law rather than an election-postponement measure and that Congress has the authority to determine the terms of barangay officials. It also found the November 2028 election schedule reasonable.
The decision, penned by then Associate Justice and now Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda, was promulgated on October 14 and released to the public on November 6.
Caguioa: No compelling reason for extension
Caguioa cautioned that allowing the law to stand would permit Congress to evade judicial review by packaging constitutionally questionable election postponements as term-setting measures.

"I register anew my strong dissent. The Court should not countenance, for a second time, a legislative maneuver that unduly curtails the people's right of suffrage. Republic Act No. 12326 must be declared unconstitutional," Caguioa said.
He also argued that no compelling government interest was shown to justify extending the terms of barangay and SK officials from four to five years so soon after the previous extension.

"If 'effective local governance' is the objective, what has changed in the past year to warrant yet another term extension? Without any study or evidence showing that the four-year term is inadequate or ineffective, the further extension to five years can only be described as whimsical and arbitrary and unduly lengthens the intervals between elections without any demonstrated necessity," Caguioa said.
Kho: Law also postpones elections

Kho argued that RA 12326 is not merely a term-setting law but also an election-postponement measure and should therefore have been subjected to the standards laid down by the Supreme Court in its 2023 Macalintal v. Comelec ruling.
Under that ruling, the postponement of elections must be supported by an important, substantial or compelling reason.
Kho said RA 12326 failed to present a sufficiently important or compelling justification for moving the elections to 2028.

"The postponement of the BSK elections to November 2028 is unreasonably long that the authority of the incumbents to discharge the functions of the office no longer continue to be based on the free expression of the will of the electorate," Kho said.
He also criticized the majority for declining to strike down the law.
"Verily, the Court must not remain passive. The Court should not shirk from its duty in declaring unconstitutional a law that evidently violates the Constitution," Kho said.

"In doing so, the Court will not claim to exercise authority over Congress. Far from it. It would be merely fulfilling its solemn duty to uphold the supremacy of the Constitution. This, the ponencia unfortunately blatantly fails to perform."
Leonen: New term should not apply to incumbents
Leonen, meanwhile, agreed that Congress has the authority to change the terms of barangay officials but said it cannot apply the new five-year term to incumbents elected under a shorter term.

"I regret that I cannot fully join the majority. Postponing the barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections abuses the inherent sovereign right to suffrage. This undermines our democracy and the concept of a republican government," Leonen said.

"While the Constitution allows Congress to modify the terms of office of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials, it cannot, however, apply that change to incumbents. Otherwise, our right to suffrage will be infringed," he added.
Leonen likened the vote to a sacred covenant and a public act through which "sovereign" people, the voters, confer authority on officials for a defined period.

"Unlike a contract, which ordinarily arises from private agreement between parties, an election is a public act through which the sovereign people confer authority upon their chosen representatives," he said.

"Through this act, the electorate entrusts the exercise of governmental authority to particular officials for a period prescribed by law. In turn, the candidate elected assume office pursuant to the same legal framework," he added.

Leonen also raised concerns about the effect of the postponement on young voters and prospective SK candidates. Because SK membership and candidacy are subject to age limits, some who would have been eligible to participate in the November 2026 elections may no longer qualify by 2028.
He closed his opinion by urging the court to "do better and protect the sacred fundamental covenant of suffrage."
"We owe the people that much," Leonen said.

articles.title: One Nation dumps Victorian election candidate who praised Adolf Hitler as ‘GOAT’
articles.summary:
Party disendorses Preston candidate Franco Guardiani after social media posts emerge

One Nation Victoria has disendorsed a candidate whose private social media account described Adolf Hitler…

blocks.text: One Nation Victoria has disendorsed a candidate whose private social media account described Adolf Hitler as the “GOAT” and claimed that “importing Islam is making pedophilia legal”.
In a now deleted social media post, the party’s candidate for Preston, Franco Guardiani, commented on a social media post on X asking people to: “Describe Hitler in one word? Be brutally honest”.
Guardiani then replied with the acronym GOAT, which stands for greatest of all time.
The party was made aware of Guardiani’s social media posts on Tuesday morning and disendorsed him a short time later. A party official discussed the posts with Guardiani and confirmed they were real.
“At a time when Jewish Australians are experiencing unprecedented persecution, we are appalled that these comments have been made,” said the party’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering.
“As soon as we became aware, we acted. Preston candidate Franco Guardiani is no longer part of our party.
“Anyone who holds such views is on notice: they do not have a place in One Nation.”
The former candidate’s X account contains several Islamophobic comments including references to bulldozing or setting fire to mosques.
The account has also engaged with posts by the anti-immigrant group Kights Templar International.

It is unclear how the candidate’s social media history was not detected during candidate selection and vetting processes. The party has claimed to have invested time and money into improving this process.
Guardiani is no longer listed as a One Nation candidate on the party’s official website.
Guardiani has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Lula, a staunch Trump critic, to make first state visit during ASEAN
articles.summary: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will make a state visit to the Philippines on November 14 and 15, the first by a sitting Brazilian head of state, Malacañang said on…

blocks.text: November 10, 2026 | 11:30am

Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva speaks during a meeting of the National Council for the Industrialisation of Critical and Strategic Minerals at the Planalto Palace in Brasília on November 5, 2026.
AFP / Evaristo Sa

MANILA, Philippines — Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will make a state visit to the Philippines on November 14 and 15, the first by a sitting Brazilian head of state, Malacañang said on Tuesday, November 10.

Lula, who won a fourth term in Brazil's presidential runoff last month, will join the November 15 session of the 49th ASEAN Summit as "Guest of the Chair" at the invitation of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) said in a statement.
The Philippines, which holds the ASEAN chairship this year, will host leaders from the bloc and its partner countries in Metro Manila through November 18.

Marcos will receive Lula at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City, where the two leaders will hold bilateral talks on trade and investment, agriculture, energy, science and technology, defense and technical cooperation.
The agenda also includes closer coordination in multilateral forums and among developing economies of the so-called Global South.
The trip is one of Lula's first major foreign trips since the October runoff in which he defeated Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.

Brazil became ASEAN's first Latin American "sectoral dialogue partner" in August 2022, a tier lower than the full dialogue partnerships the bloc holds with powers such as the United States, China and Japan

Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro in August paid a courtesy call to Lula and Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira, in which both sides discussed bilateral agreements covering cooperation in energy and tourism, among others.
There is no official confirmation yet that Lula's visit will overlap with Trump, whose attendance at the main summit from November 16 to 18 was confirmed by Malacañang in October.
Trump has called Brazil's vote a disgrace and has questioned the result without offering evidence.

blocks.text: Tensions in the South China Sea persist as Beijing claims almost the entire strategic waterway, through which more than $3 trillion worth of goods are shipped annually.
The area is also subject to overlapping territorial and maritime claims by the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia.

The Philippine government uses the name West Philippine Sea to refer to maritime areas on the western side of the Philippine archipelago, including the Luzon Sea and the waters around, within and adjacent to the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.

In 2016, an arbitral tribunal constituted under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea ruled in favor of the Philippines in its case against China, finding that China's claims to historic rights within the so-called nine-dash line had no legal basis under the convention.
China has refused to recognize the ruling. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Impeachment court warns contempt, perjury cases vs lying witnesses
articles.summary: Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero reminded Tuesday that witnesses who lie under oath may be cited in contempt and face perjury charges.

blocks.text: Published November 10, 2026 11:14am
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero reminded Tuesday that witnesses who lie under oath may be cited in contempt and face perjury charges.

Escudero said this on Day 41 of the impeachment trial after Senator-Judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III asked to be reminded of the penalties and sanctions against those who lie before the impeachment court.
“They may be subject to contempt by the court, your Honor,” the presiding officer said.

“In addition to that, may be subjected to cases of perjury, should one be filed against him before the proper prosecutor’s office and/or courts of law because the statements given by any witness is under oath and is therefore covered by our laws on perjury as well,” he added.
This was echoed by Senator-Judge Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, citing Rule V of Resolution No. 39 on containing the rules of procedure on impeachment trials, which states that:

The Senate shall have power to compel the attendance of witnesses, to enforce obedience to its orders, mandates, writs, and judgments, to preserve order, and to punish in a summary way contempts of, and disobedience to, its authority, orders, mandates, writs, or judgments, and to make all lawful orders, rules, and regulations which it may deem essential or conducive to the ends of justice.

“Yesterday was not a good day for the impeachment court simply because we had a witness who smirked, who laughed, and almost made a mockery of the impeachment trial. And we don’t want to have a repeat of that kind of testimony,” Lacson said.
“Just a reminder to everyone that this is not an implied power of the impeachment court but an expressed power granted by such resolution,” he added.
On Monday, Davao City assessor Engineer Jaime Adalin, the first witness presented by the defense, was grilled by the prosecution and some senator-judges about his travel to China.

During his cross-examination, Adalin said he could not remember details of the trip, but he later admitted traveling to China in January 2026 for “personal” purposes, when he was being questioned by senator-judges.
The witness also said he would submit official documents regarding the trip.
No submission
But Escudero announced Tuesday that Adalin has yet to submit relevant details regarding his trip to China, as requested by Senator-Judge Raffy Tulfo.

The impeachment court presiding officer thus directed the clerk of court to follow up with Adalin regarding the matter, and also remind him to provide the list of properties owned or are in the name of the Vice President and her husband, Atty. Manases Carpio.
“If by tomorrow the same is not yet complied with, unless sufficient cause or reason is given, the court will be forced to issue compulsory process on the same,” Escudero said. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Who is defense witness Engineer John Kenneth Enumerables?
articles.summary: The second witness for the defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte for her impeachment trial is Engineer John Kenneth Enumerables, the assessor of the Island Garden City of Samal.

blocks.text: Filtered By: Topstories
News
IMPEACHMENT TRIAL
Published November 10, 2026 11:03am
The second witness for the defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte for her impeachment trial is Engineer John Kenneth Enumerables, the assessor of the Island Garden City of Samal.
Enumerables is a civil engineer who passed the licensure exam in year 2000.
Likewise, he is also a licensed real estate appraiser. He passed the board exam for real estate appraiser in 2011.

His testimony is being offered by the defense team to prove that the land under Transfer Certificate of Title 142-2019013134 in Samal Island is a declared asset of the Vice President under her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) she jointly filed with her husband, Atty. Manases Carpio.

Prosecution witness and Acting Samal Register of Deeds Atty. Marco Pineda earlier told the Senate court testified that a P3.4 million property in the Island Garden City of Samal purchased in 2018 as reflected in the 2018 Deed of Absolute Sale is owned by the Vice President’s husband.
Pineda also testified that the said P3.4 million property is not listed as an asset of the Vice President in her joint SALN filing with her husband. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: California voters fail to pass proposed one-time tax on billionaires’ wealth
articles.summary:
Campaign over Prop 40, as measure was known, was most expensive in state history, flush with Silicon Valley dollars

California billionaires won a contentious ballot measure campaign,…

blocks.text: California billionaires won a contentious ballot measure campaign, defeating a proposed one-time tax on their wealth.

The bruising campaign over Proposition 40 was the most expensive in state history and witness to back-and-forth dealing from tech billionaires and democratic leaders, including Gavin Newsom, the governor, who steadfastly opposed the measure. While supporters of Prop 40 cast it as a solution to drastic healthcare cuts from Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, opponents led by prosperous billionaires mounted an influential campaign saying the billionaire tax was instead “an everyone tax”.
This result could hamper nationwide momentum on demands that billionaires pay their fair share and states enacting new laws to tax the ultra-wealthy.

Prop 40 proposed a one-time 5% tax on all individuals in California with a net worth of more than $1bn as of 1 January 2026. It was sponsored by the healthcare union SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, and dictated that the proceeds from the tax would fund healthcare programs, along with some education and food assistance.

The state’s major unions, and progressive politicians such as Bernie Sanders, the Vermont senator, and Ro Khanna, a California congressman, backed Prop 40. But both the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor, as well as organizations such as Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, a lobbying branch of the healthcare group, opposed it – pointing to its structure as a one-off tax that would only fund certain healthcare programs. Prop 40’s most vocal critics, however, were the state’s billionaires.

Donors to the opposition campaign were a who’s who of Silicon Valley, including executives from Google, Palantir, DoorDash, Stripe and Reddit, along with several prominent venture capitalists. The biggest donor, by far, was Sergey Brin, a Google co-founder, who contributed at least $132m to fight the tax, according to campaign finance filings.

All told, the billionaires mounted a nearly $425m battle against Prop 40, making it the most expensive opposition campaign in state history. In the first two weeks of October, spending surpassed $2.5m a day, according to the most recent campaign finance filings.

Part of the opposition campaign’s strategy was mounting two separate counter-measures on the ballot, Proposition 41 and 42. Prop 41 directly targeted the billionaire tax, while Prop 42 was a general proposal on limiting certain new taxes and would ban any taxation on billionaire wealth. If either measure received more yes votes than Prop 40, they would stop the billionaire tax from taking effect – even if it passed.
Supporters of the billionaire tax called Props 41 and 42 “poison pills”.

articles.summary: The defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte opened their presentation of evidence by presenting Davao City assessor and Engr. Jaime Adalin, who has maintained that the P6 million property…

blocks.text: Published November 10, 2026 10:42am

The prosecution, however, argued that Adalin’s basis for his conclusion is erroneous because the details of the property provided under the TCT and the Electronic Certificate Authorizing Registration (E-CAR) differ from or are absent in the details stated in the Vice President’s 2024 and 2025 SALN, which she jointly filed with her husband.
Adalin said his conclusion is based on tax declaration for the property’s land title under Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT) 146-2024-010775 as well as local maps and Comprehensive Land Use Plan.

The prosecution, however, argued that Adalin’s basis for his conclusion is erroneous because the details of the property provided under the TCT and the Electronic Certificate Authorizing Registration (E-CAR) differs from or are absent in the details stated in the Vice President’s 2024 and 2025 SALN which she jointly filed with her husband.
The discrepancies raised by the prosecution include:

items: P6 million acquisition cost in the E-CAR and Deed of Sale as against the P10 million acquisition cost in SALN
SALN entry showing the property is a lot, while E-CAR shows it is a lot with improvement
SALN entry showing the property is a residential lot when present site features a commercial establishment

blocks.text: Senator-judge Sherwin Gatchalian likewise questioned Adalin’s testimony that the P6 million and P10 million property are one and the same by citing that the SALN entries on the P10 million property do not include the TCT number and corresponding tax declaration number.
The prosecution and Senator-judges also repeatedly quizzed Adalin about his trips to China in November 2025 and January 2026.
It took repeated questions and being confronted with immigration records before Adalin admitted that he indeed travelled to China, as well as Hong Kong, Thailand, and Australia.
Adalin, however, maintained that he is not keen on traveling.

Ahead of the Day 40 of the impeachment trial, defense team spokesperson Michael Poa said that it is too early to tell if the Vice President will take the witness stand to defend herself from impeachment allegations of accumulating unexplained wealth. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Trump says Iran war is 'effectively over' militarily with further strikes unlikely
articles.summary: The president says the US is keeping "status quo" with Iran but remains “locked and loaded” should the situation in the Middle East change.

blocks.text: Donald Trump says the Iran war "militarily is effectively over" declaring that there is "positive momentum" behind negotiations to end the Middle East conflict.
"We're just keeping it the status quo," the US president said on Monday. "And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours."

Addressing reporters from the White House press briefing room, Trump said that renewed US attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" but that the US was "locked and loaded" should the circumstances change.
Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed doubts about the US president's prior comments about resolving the conflict.
Responding to a question over why he would not officially declare an end to the conflict, Trump said that some of the Gulf allies could still face Iranian aggression.
"We have some great allies there and we have to make sure they're not hurt," Trump said, suggesting that the US naval blockade on Iranian ports was helping to make the region more secure.
Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani in the Oval Office earlier on Monday, saying they had an "excellent conversation" about negotiations to end the war.
In a post on X, the Qatari prime minister said he held "positive discussions" with Trump and Vice-President JD Vance on "reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region".
Efforts to broker a peace between Washington and Tehran have largely been held indirectly through mediators since the war first broke out following joint US-Israeli strikes in February.

Saudi Arabia, Qatar and United Arab Emirates are among the US's Gulf allies that have been hit by Iranian strikes over the course of the war, in addition to threat of strikes that have led to major air travel disruptions in the region.
This is not the first time that Trump has said Iran war is "militarily" over, but the circumstances for him are different now.
Trump has hinted at de-escalation in Iran after a bruising set of midterm election results for the Republicans last week, which senior figures including Vice-President Vance blamed on the Iran War.
In an interview with 60 minutes that aired on Sunday, the president said he did not currently see "any reason" to escalate the war.
Ahead of the midterms, Trump said US forces conducted what he described as "minor strikes" on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz.
Post-election recriminations over the US war in Iran are already placing pressure on members of the Trump administration.

Republican congressman Thomas Massie launched a strong attack against Trump's Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday over the war in Iran, requesting a vote in the House of Representatives to impeach him.
Trump has backed Hegseth, who says he is "not worried" about the looming impeachment threats, calling Massie's effort a "sham".

While the move is unlikely to succeed with Republicans still in control of Congress until January, Democrats have expressed willingness to impeach Hegseth once the new session begins and they have control of both the House and the Senate.

articles.title: Police investigate as nearly 30 Santa Barbara half-marathon runners fall ill with ‘unusual symptoms’
articles.summary:
Runners seek medical treatment as 13-mile race held amid unusually high November temperatures

Police in southern California are investigating the circumstances that led to the…

blocks.text: Police in southern California are investigating the circumstances that led to the hospitalization of nearly 30 runners who participated in the Santa Barbara Half on Sunday.

Santa Barbara police said in a statement to the Associated Press that they had opened an investigation after receiving reports from Santa Barbara Cottage Hospital about multiple half-marathon participants seeking medical treatment for “unusual symptoms”.
Cottage Health said in a statement it had a “larger than expected number of emergency visits … a number of them with similar symptoms of undetermined cause”.
Race organizers say they believe any illness is attributable to heat or dehydration. The high on the day of the race was 88F (31.1C), an unusually high temperature for this time of year.

Neither the hospital nor police have detailed the symptoms beyond calling them unusual. Cottage Health said on Monday that 27 participants came to emergency rooms in Santa Barbara and Goleta, a small city about 10 miles west.
More than 4,640 people competed in the half-marathon, which spanned about 13 miles, according to the Santa Barbara Half Marathon website.

Of those who were either taken to the hospital or arrived there on their own, 24 patients had been treated and discharged as of Monday morning. The three others were in stable condition, the company told the Associated Press.

Event director David Monico said organizers transported 15 people from the medical tent to local hospitals. He said the event’s medical team treated numerous runners for dehydration and overheating both on the course and at the finish line.

The half-marathon’s event director, David Monico told the Guardian that they have “no additional information to suggest that the issues some of the participants experienced were caused by anything other than endurance event exertion-related symptoms”.

articles.title: Senators urge state of calamity declaration in El Niño-hit areas
articles.summary: Twenty senators have signed a resolution calling on President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. to declare a state of calamity in areas affected by the strong El Niño phenomenon.

blocks.text: Published November 10, 2026 10:15am
Twenty senators have signed a resolution calling on President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. to declare a state of calamity in areas affected by the strong El Niño phenomenon.

Under proposed Senate Resolution 765, the President is urged, upon the recommendation of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC), to declare a state of calamity under Republic Act (RA) 10121, or the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act, in areas experiencing drought-related disaster impacts.

The President may also declare a state of imminent disaster as warranted under RA 12287, or the Declaration of State of Imminent Disaster Act, in areas facing “highly probable disasters with projected catastrophic impacts,” as determined through appropriate disaster risk assessment.

The resolution was signed by Senate Agriculture, Food and Agrarian Reform committee chairperson Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan, as well as Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and Senators Vicente Sotto III, Juan Miguel Zubiri, Alan Peter Cayetano, Imee Marcos, Robin Padilla, Bam Aquino, Risa Hontiveros, JV Ejercito, Lito Lapid, Joel Villanueva, Erwin Tulfo, Raffy Tulfo, Ping Lacson, Chiz Escudero, Pia Cayetano, Bong Go, Camille Villar, and Mark Villar.

The senators also urged the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) and concerned agencies to mobilize available and eligible funds under the 2026 national budget, including the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund and agency Quick Response Funds.

They also called on concerned agencies and local price coordination councils to monitor the prices of basic necessities and prime commodities, and to take action against overpricing, profiteering, and hoarding in affected areas.
As of October 21, the agricultural sector incurred P8.57 billion in damage and losses due to El Niño, according to the Department of Agriculture (DA).

The agricultural damage was reportedly recorded in Cordillera Administrative Region, Cagayan Valley, Central Luzon, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, Bicol Region, Western Visayas, Negros Island Region, Central Visayas, Eastern Visayas, Zamboanga Peninsula, Davao Region, SOCCSKSARGEN, and Caraga.
The DA earlier proposed a P61.99-billion action plan to mitigate the impact of El Niño on the country’s food supply and livelihoods.
The proposed spending package includes P6.2 billion already released under the government’s Unified Package for Livelihoods, Industry, Food, and Transport (UPLIFT) Program. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Qantas to outsource 850 local jobs with most roles moving to India
articles.summary: The Australian airline said the move was aimed at modernising its IT systems and noted the impact of AI.

blocks.text: Qantas will outsource 850 local corporate jobs to consulting giant Accenture with most roles moving to India as the airline fast-tracks AI investment.
In an internal email to staff on Tuesday, the Australian company's CEO Vanessa Hudson said "this is hard news for some and I'm sorry for the uncertainty it brings".

The job cuts will begin mid-2027, she said, and start with finance, procurement, people and marketing roles shifting "mostly" to teams in India and "some in Australia" as the firm seeks to modernise its IT systems.
Hudson said the "scale and speed of change in technology and AI is something none of us has seen in our lifetime", and it was in talks with unions and staff on the plans.
The move comes days after the airline provided a market update, flagging fare increases and flight cuts amid higher fuel costs.
On its new multi-year deal with Accenture, Hudson said it was about "modernising" the airline's IT systems to become "more efficient".
Qantas spends more than AU$1bn (US$691m; £514m) a year on technology, she said, and the company's back-end systems needed to be upgraded.
"Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," she said.

The deal with Accenture means "we will redesign and simplify parts of how our corporate functions work and reduce duplication", Hudson said, so staff can "spend more time on work that creates value for our customers and the business".
The company said that "in time", the work that Accenture takes over will be "transformed further with automation and AI".
Staff affected by the job cuts will be redeployed "where possible", the firm added, including new roles in Australia.
Qantas - which employs about 28,000 staff in Australia and another 4,000 globally - said thousands of its staff already use AI in their daily work.
The BBC has contacted the Australian Services Union for comment.

articles.title: 'Cruise for life' ship seized in Singapore
articles.summary: The ship was meant to take guests around the world, but the trip was cut short after its operator ran out of money.

blocks.text: A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore.
The Odyssey, which set off from Belfast in October 2024 and was meant to take guests on a years-long voyage around the world, is now anchored in Singapore port waters, local authorities say.

Around 200 guests were forced to leave the ship last month in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, after its owner Villa Vie Residences abruptly suspended operations citing "extraordinary increases in fuel costs".
The crew onboard are reported to be well, Singapore's port authority said.
"Arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors," the authority said, adding that the vessel had been "placed under arrest pursuant to a court order".
Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC has been named the "arresting solicitor", but it is not clear which party it represents.
The Odyssey was meant to go on a three-and-a-half-years voyage covering 150 countries.

Passengers were given the options of buying their cabin outright, which allows them to stay onboard beyond its initial voyage, paying for a five-year residency, or renting a cabin for days-long tours.
Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 (£89,272) to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month, according to its website.
"For roughly the price of a car, you can own your home on a ship that travels the world," its founder Mikael Petterson had earlier said.
However the cruise was beset with problems from the start, with its departure delayed for four months because of repairs and paperwork.

While in Vietnam, crew members reportedly bought food from local grocery stores because the company owed money to a vendor who refused to deliver food, according to CBS News, the BBC's partner in the US.

CBS also reported that the operator warned passengers of its financial troubles in August, when it had sailed on a separate occasion into Singapore, and had to raise money from guests to keep the cruise going.
It had also mentioned the risk of being detained then.
Holly Hennessey, one of the ship's passengers, had earlier told the BBC guests were asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".
The vessel sailed again into Singapore earlier this month, weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end while in Cambodia.

As the Iran war sent fuel prices soaring earlier this year, monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on 27 October.
It added that it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption" but those measures turned out to be insufficient to offset the "extraordinary increase in fuel costs".
The company also said it was working with residents to "identify temporary living arrangements" while in Cambodia.

articles.title: Vancouver Island village evacuation orders to remain in place for days after landslide
articles.summary: An evacuation order for a number of properties following a landslide in the small village of Zeballos on northwest Vancouver Island is expected to remain in place through Friday, as forecasters warn…

image.caption: The village of Zeballos is seen in this aerial shot. A number of properties in the village are under evacuation order after a landslide, with widespread rain set to arrive again on Tuesday. (Village of Zeballos)

blocks.text: British Columbia

An evacuation order for a number of properties following a landslide in the small village of Zeballos on northwest Vancouver Island is expected to remain in place through Friday, as forecasters warn of further heavy rain for the region.
Village on northwest coast of Vancouver Island is under orange rainfall warning as another storm forecast
The order covers 10 addressed properties on Pandora Crescent and Maquinna Avenue, and a number of vacant lots, in the village of around 125 people.
It came after the local Strathcona Regional District told CBC News that "debris from a landslide has affected the area" on Nov. 6.
Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) issued an orange rainfall warning for west Vancouver Island on Monday, forecasting 150 to 200 millimetres of rain beginning Tuesday morning.
State of emergency for Vancouver Island village due to flooding, risk of landslide
Bonnie Logan, the regional district's acting manager of emergency services, told CBC News that the area has been without power for multiple days, which was causing challenges.
"We can't start doing any mitigation measures until that area has been thoroughly assessed by the geotechnical engineer," she said.
"And unfortunately with these incoming storms, we just haven't had a window of opportunity to do that."

items: Landslide prompts evacuation order for Zeballos on Vancouver Island

blocks.text: Logan said the road through the village was open, but stopping was not allowed and people should only travel as necessary.
She said the regional district was monitoring the situation as they waited for the next storm to hit the area.
In an update on social media, the regional district said any update on evacuation orders and alerts would be provided on Friday after the storm systems have passed through.
Another storm expected for B.C. coast after wet, windy weekend
ECCC said the next storm is expected to arrive early Tuesday morning, and would persist for a day.
"Even though the heaviest rain eases by Wednesday morning, moderate precipitation is expected to continue until Thursday morning," the orange rainfall warning for the area reads.
An orange warning indicates major or widespread impacts, with the forecaster warning that localized flooding was likely and some roads may be impassable due to the storm.
It comes as thousands lost power across B.C. due to a series of storms over the weekend.
Mayor was just sworn in
Bob Berthelotte, who was recently sworn in as mayor of Zeballos, said his property was in the path of the debris flow on Friday morning, and his barking dog alerted him to the situation.
"I was still able to walk down, and my poor dog went out to go to the bathroom and she was right on the edge of that torrent that was coming down the hill," he said.
"And I very gently walked up, picked her up and said, 'Come on in,' so she wouldn't be whisked away."

items: Impact of Prince George windstorm still being felt, homeowners face long waits to get trees removed
Driver dead after tree hits car in Surrey as 2nd windstorm batters B.C.

blocks.text: Berthelotte said Monday that he's waiting for the power to come back on to assess the situation, and it was the first widespread evacuation order for the area since a wildfire eight years ago.
He said that despite the state of emergency in the village, and just stepping into the role as mayor, the existing relationships in the town were making the emergency response easier.
"Me being a resident there for this long, I'm not just the mayor, I'm also a neighbour and a friend," he said.
"So when something happens, we're all there for each other, which is a little bit of a blessing."
With files from Maryse Zeidler

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
articles.summary: Bookmark this page for Rappler's comprehensive coverage of Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial at the Senate

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

During the interjection of Senator Raffy Tulfo after the impeachment trial went on lunch break, Davao City assessor Engineer Jaime Adalin confirms a recent travel to China but denies recollection of a Chinese trip in November 2018.
This drew the ire of Tulfo again, who says Adalin traveled to China, and other countries including Australia.

“Gusto mo pati CCTV footage kaya ko ibigay sa ’yo. November 12, 2018, PR356 China. At two days ka lang sa China. At ang dami mong biyahe, engineer. Meron kang Hong Kong, meron kang Thailand, meron kang Australia,” says Tulfo.
“Hindi kita nilalait ha, pero magkano ba ang suweldo mo para ikaw ay palaging nag-a-abroad?” he asks, with Adalin answering he earns around P120,000 monthly.

articles.title: Senate advances bill to speed up permit reviews for infrastructure projects
articles.summary:
Chamber voted 73-25 to formally take up bill that will shorten timelines to start energy and datacenter projects

The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up…

blocks.text: The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for datacenters and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

The Senate voted 73-25 to formally take up the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as a way to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that now face years-long delays in getting to the grid.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started – both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects – and make sure datacenters pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence datacenters and rising electricity helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.

Trump urged senators to vote for it, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a social media post on Sunday. The bill will “ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families”, Trump wrote.
Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.

However, many environmental organizations have panned the deal because they say it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.
Midterm results could complicate bill’s passage in lame-duck sessions.
While the bill has received bipartisan support, the Democrats’ sweeping midterm win could complicate its passage.

Some Democrats say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that produces needed clean energy, but limits expansion of oil, natural gas and mining. Some critics have said the permitting bill as proposed could lead to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a “reckless” build-out of datacenters powered by natural gas.

Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, a New York Democrat who is expected to become speaker in January, criticized the bill last week, with his office saying it “falls short” in a number of areas.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have strongly opposed the measure in recent days, citing concerns about its limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and Endangered Species Act. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved, but supporters of an overhaul say that causes yearslong delays in federal permitting.
The bill’s four main champions – two Democrats and two Republicans – released a detailed set of amendments Saturday designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito, a Republican senator of West Virginia, Mike Lee, a Republican senator of Utah, Martin Heinrich a Democratic senator of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democratic senator of Rhode Island, say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.
“Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” said Heinrich.

If passed, the bill will save households billions on electricity costs, create jobs, cut emissions and force big corporations to pay their full share for datacenters instead of pushing energy costs on consumers, Heinrich said.

Capito called the bill “a win for America”, adding: “We cannot let this moment pass by. The reality is this, over the next several years, we will have no choice but to increase our national energy production. This is an unprecedented opportunity … to come together to show the American people we are listening to you.”

articles.title: Mother testifies police killing of autistic son in Surrey, B.C., left her 'broken'
articles.summary: At the coroner's inquest into the death of Chase de Balinhard, mother Crystal de Balinhard described the day he was been killed.

image.caption: Chase de Balinhard,15, was shot and killed by police in Surrey on Feb. 9, 2025. (GoFundMe)

blocks.text: British Columbia
At the coroner's inquest into the death of Chase de Balinhard, mother Crystal de Balinhard described the day he was been killed.
15-year-old Chase de Balinhard died last year during a confrontation with Surrey police
WARNING: This story mentions threats of suicide.
The mother of a 15-year-old autistic boy who was fatally shot by an RCMP officer in Surrey last year says her son's death has "broken" her.

Crystal de Balinhard was testifying at the B.C. Coroners Service inquest into the death of Chase de Balinhard, who died on a Surrey street corner during a confrontation with police. Chase was carrying a pellet gun that, at the time, police believed was a handgun.

De Balinhard said Chase lived with multiple challenges, including XYY syndrome, autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, anxiety disorder and intellectual disability.
De Balinhard said on Feb. 9, 2025, she drove a niece to the airport before stopping at a pub to meet her husband at a multi-family Super Bowl party on her way home.

items: B.C. police watchdog clears officers in shooting death of 15-year-old in Surrey

blocks.text: Chase had opted out of the party to stay home, saying he was tired.
De Balinhard said at the pub she received texts from two friends asking if she knew what was happening at the school near their home. One of the friends said there may be a school shooter.
De Balinhard became worried that Chase may have left the house to video the incident.
"He'd do these videos pretending that he was a YouTuber, but they were just for us," said de Balinhard.
The IIO published this image of the pellet gun Chase de Balinhard was carrying when he was shot and killed by police. (IIO B.C.)
She said she checked Chase's location on an app and it showed two addresses near a corner. When she tried to drive to where his phone was pinging, the roads were blocked off.

"So I started walking but a nice lady officer said, ‘You can't go there.' I said my 15-year-old autistic boy's phone is pinging up there. You could see the reaction on her face," said an emotional de Balinhard. "[The officer] said why don't you go sit in your car."

items: Coroner's inquest into fatal police shooting of Surrey teen begins Nov. 9

blocks.text: De Balinhard said she and her husband were prevented from getting close to Chase's body.
"We tried to get by police but they held us back," she said. "I just wanted to see him. I wanted to say goodbye."
Police responded to the Clayton Heights neighbourhood after Chase called 911 saying he was armed with a gun and threatening to harm himself.

According to a report by the Independent Investigations Office of B.C. (IIO), police attempted to apprehend the boy for 22 minutes. The report says Chase pointed what appeared to be a handgun at himself and police several times before two officers shot at him. The Grade 10 student was hit by a single bullet.
The gun was later discovered to be a pellet gun Chase had taken from the family home. De Balinhard said the pellet gun was kept locked in a location that she wasn't aware he had access to.
Chase de Balinhard, 15, was fatally shot by police in Surrey, B.C., on Feb. 9, 2025. (GoFundMe.ca)
De Balinhard said Chase could become dysregulated or upset if overstimulated by things like loud noises or people yelling at him.
"He didn't respond well," she said. "He told me loud noises hurt his body. It made him want to flee."
She also said in addition to his normal triggers, he was dealing with the aftermath of surgery on a painful cyst on his buttocks that wasn't healing.
She said the morning of his death, Chase was in good spirits after a pancake breakfast with his cousin and grandmother.
"It was the first time he cut his food with a fork and knife by himself and he was so happy," she said.
The site of the fatal police shooting, near 185 Street and 70 Avenue in Surrey, is photographed on Monday, Feb. 10, 2025 — one day after the incident. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
De Balinhard said she'd like to see first responders receive better training around dealing with people with autism.
"I wish officers could learn some of the signs," she said. "With autistics, when everything goes sideways for them they can't communicate. Why not give people the tools to do their job better?"

De Balinhard testified that Chase was a sweet, kind boy who loved Terry Fox, superheroes and playing jokes on his family. He loved his cat Ava and learned to paddle a kayak. She said his superpowers were identifying anything to do with the Titanic and mastering arcade claw machines.
"He would win all the time and would usually give his prizes away," she said. "He had a big heart."

De Balinhard said Chase did well in elementary school with the extra support provided, but once he moved to high school the support dropped off. She said in his Grade 10 year, despite the school receiving funding to help him, he received no support and had stopped attending altogether.
"Surrey started this thing where funding goes into a big pool and it wasn't going to him," said de Balinhard. "He regressed."

Dr. Patricia Frew, a psychiatrist who worked with Chase, said the teen had developed chronic suicidal thoughts, although not to the extent that he needed to be apprehended under the Mental Health Act.
A coroner's inquest is a public process involving a jury that does not find fault. At its conclusion, the jury and presiding coroner can make recommendations to prevent similar deaths.
If you or someone you know is struggling, here’s where to look for help:

items: Canada’s Suicide Crisis Helpline : Call or text 988.
Kids Help Phone: 1-800-668-6868. Text 686868. Live chat counselling on the website .
Canadian Association for Suicide Prevention: Find a 24-hour crisis centre.
This guide from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health outlines how to talk about suicide with someone you're worried about.

blocks.text: If you're worried someone you know may be at risk of suicide, you should talk to them about it, says the Canadian Association for Suicide Prevention. Here are some warning signs:

items: Suicidal thoughts.
Substance use.
Purposelessness.
Anxiety.
Feeling trapped.
Hopelessness and helplessness.
Withdrawal.
Anger.
Recklessness.
Mood changes.

articles.title: Senate advances bill to speed up projects from gas pipelines to clean energy
articles.summary:
Key environmental groups come out against bipartisan Baaja bill over fears it could spur datacenters and ICE jails

It’s a bill that would make it easier to build big infrastructure projects…

blocks.text: It’s a bill that would make it easier to build big infrastructure projects in America – everything from fossil fuel pipelines to transmission lines that would add more clean energy to the grid. And it would roll back environmental and social protections to achieve this goal. That is why climate advocates are torn over the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs act (Baaja), which was scheduled for an initial procedural Senate vote on Monday.

The Senate voted on Monday to open debate on Baaja in the first of several procedural votes. Senators voted 73 to 25 on the cloture motion, which did not result in the bill being passed, but pushed it another step forward.

Donald Trump urged all senators to vote for the 417-page bill, which is sponsored by two Republicans and two Democrats in the Senate, but after last week’s historic “blue wave” elections, some environmental and tribal advocates called on Democratic leadership to pump the brakes.

Earthjustice, the Sierra Club and the ACLU have come out against the bill because it would significantly weaken environmental laws including the National Environmental Policy Act (Nepa) and accelerate the construction of gas pipelines and ICE detention centers.

Indigenous groups held a press conference on Friday calling on senators to vote against Baaja because it would weaken the federal government’s legal obligation to consult tribes on projects that affect them.
“This is such an existential threat to Indian country,” said Mark Macarro, president of the National Congress of American Indians.

blocks.caption: Activists protested outside the home of Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer on 6 November, calling out his support for rolling back environmental laws that would increase datacenter projects. Photograph: Michael Nigro/Pacific Press/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Protesters rallied outside Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer’s building on Friday over concerns that the bill could boost datacenters. “It would be highly ironic if, having won an election where datacenter opposition was at the front and center, the first act of Congress was to make it easier to build datacenters,” said Bill McKibben.

Democrats elected in the blue wave will not take their seats until January, so the bill’s proponents still have time to rush it through the Senate, and technically there is time for it to pass in the House before new Congress and go to Trump.

But midterm success for the Democrats is dialing up the political friction. House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, expected to be the House speaker in the new Congress, said the bill “falls short in several areas”, including failing to protect tribal sovereignty, and he would not “rubber-stamp legislation without more constructive involvement with our caucus”.

Earlier on Monday, the bill’s Democratic sponsors, Senators Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse, said they had the votes to pass the bill. Heinrich said they had made last-minute changes to ensure tribal consultation, and they believed the bill would favor renewables over fossil fuels. “If we can create an open, competitive level playing field, clean is cheap, and cheap wins in the marketplace,” Heinrich said.

Whitehouse, who wore a tie with wind turbines on it, argued that passing the bill would set the stage for Democrats to work on clean energy policies next year with majorities in the House and Senate. “People should just cool their jets and have a little faith that this is not the end of the story,” he said.

Proponents of Baaja say it is needed because it takes too long to build large projects in America and the bill shortens timelines. It simplifies federal rules for building interstate transmission lines, it narrows what gets reviewed under the National Historic Preservation Act and limits tribal consultation, it limits the use of the Clean Water Act, shortens timelines for the Endangered Species Act, limits how the executive branch can interfere with federal permitting, and makes big changes to Nepa such as changing what requires Nepa review and who has standing to sue.
Baaja would expand fossil fuels
The fossil fuel industry is backing Baaja. The American Petroleum Institute (API) hailed the bill as “a historic opportunity” and called on congress to “finish permitting reform this year”.

“It creates a very accelerated fast track for gas pipelines,” said Earthjustice Action’s president, Abbie Dillen. “The gas industry is extraordinarily excited about this because they are interested in expanding existing pipeline capacity to get more liquefied natural gas out for export, and to be feeding power-hungry datacenters with gas.”

blocks.caption: The ConocoPhillips oil refinery in Wilmington, California, on 11 April. Photograph: Étienne Laurent/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: The bill could help pave the way for the Constitution gas pipeline that Williams Companies is trying to build through New York. The state denied the project’s water quality permit in 2016, but the company has revived the project under the Trump administration. The proposed pipeline could benefit from the bill’s changes to the Clean Water Act.

Baaja could also enable construction of gas pipelines in the west. Fossil fuel advocacy group Western States and Tribal Nations wants to build gas pipelines to feed domestic datacenters and export LNG from the west coast. During a 3 November election day meeting with Wyoming’s Sweetwater county board of commissioners, the advocacy group’s president, Andrew Browning, said he was talking to lawmakers about the bill: “The permitting bill’s a huge thing … We’re going to need that for everything we’re envisioning and building out.”
How the bill would increase clean energy

Some clean energy advocates want the bill to pass because it would connect renewables to the grid. Wind, solar and battery storage are now cheap to build, but the country lacks the necessary transmission lines to bring clean energy where it’s needed.

Interstate transmission lines can take a decade to get built, and energy projects also face a bottleneck in connecting to the grid. At the end of 2025, 2,060 GW of total generation and storage capacity were waiting in a queue to connect to the grid.

Ben King, energy and climate director at Rhodium Group, said Baaja would reform the interconnection queue process and unlock the ability to build the transmission that is needed. “We’re at a pretty low point for policy support for clean [energy],” he said, referring to Trump’s repeal of clean energy tax credits. “[Baaja] sets up the ability to build stuff more quickly for when the next wave of climate policy happens.”

Many experts have modeled what the bill would do to emissions, but there is a lot of uncertainty on that question. Rhodium Group’s analysis found that domestic emissions go down if Baaja passes. But another model by the Purdue engineering professor Kevin Kircher found it would increase domestic emissions.

Kircher said the optimistic case for Baaja is that there’s a huge amount of clean energy ready to go, and if we get rid of the long queues and regulations, “level the playing field and let it rip”, then clean energy wins on the economics. “I think that understanding is outdated,” he said.

What the bill does to emissions partly depends on what type of energy gets connected to the grid. Rhodium Group assumed, based on a report from 2025, that 85% of the capacity added to the grid would be renewables. But Kircher said some grid operators have updated their queues this year to remove redundant and speculative offers. (PJM’s queue as of 3 August looks quite gassy.)

blocks.caption: Wind turbines are silhouetted against the sky at dusk near Cimarron, Kansas, on 15 May. Photograph: Charlie Riedel/AP

blocks.text: King said the economics show an impressive decrease in the cost of renewables, while fossil fuels are not getting any cheaper. “Some of it is just a bet on what’s going to win out in the future,” he said. “Our modeling suggests that clean stuff is going to dominate energy expansion for the foreseeable future, and there might be people who have a different view on that. API might have a different perspective – they might bet that there’s more room for them to grow.”

Kircher emphasized that the various models have not had time for peer review since the bill was first introduced on 30 September. “We need to have some humility in recognizing that the process of taking that 417 pages of super dense legal text and mapping it … is extremely complicated and full of uncertainties,” he said.
What the bill would do to Nepa

The bill would significantly reduce the scope of Nepa. It would narrow the definition of a “major federal action” that would trigger Nepa review, and effectively eliminate the authority of courts to enforce Nepa compliance.

Nepa is the powerful law that attorneys used to block the Trump administration’s plans to convert 11 mega-warehouses into massive ICE detention centers. If the bill passes, it could accelerate the development of ICE detention centers, according to a letter the American Civil Liberties Union sent to senators. “As written, this bill would hamper, if not altogether thwart, critical work by the ACLU and our partners to halt ICE’s dangerous expansion of immigrant detention,” the letter said.

Baaja’s passage would be “the single biggest overhaul” of American environmental laws since the 1970s, said Dillen of Earthjustice. “There are legitimate concerns that Nepa has been weaponized to slow down important projects, but people have recognized this problem for years, and the law has been reformed, and it’s also been weakened very significantly by the supreme court. What this bill does is take the last pieces of it that are very relevant in an administration like this,” she said.

Trump has pushed a “drill, baby, drill” fossil fuel agenda, and Baaja’s weakening of environmental regulations would further embolden him, Dillen said. She pointed to Trump’s plan to allow drilling near Chaco Culture national historic park, a Unesco world heritage site. “Chaco Canyon is in the crosshairs,” she said.

“At Earthjustice, we are deeply committed to building clean energy and to do it in a time frame that is meaningful, given the threats that we face. But the way to do this, the way to build our country better and even faster, is not by running over tribes and by emboldening a president who voters have just come out in a historic turnout to push back on,” Dillen said.

articles.title: Premier Doug Ford suggests 'ass whooping' for 2 boys connected to alleged assault of Hamilton cadet leader
articles.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford commented on an alleged assault in Hamilton, saying the parents of two boys police say were involved should "give your kids a little ass whooping in the wood shed."

blocks.text: Hamilton·New
Ontario Premier Doug Ford commented on an alleged assault in Hamilton, saying the parents of two boys police say were involved should "give your kids a little ass whooping in the wood shed."
Police charged 12-year-old boy, 48-year-old woman with assault in Nov. 1 incident
Ford suggests ‘ass whooping’ for 2 boys connected to cadet assault
Ontario Premier Doug Ford says the parents of two boys allegedly involved in the assault of a Hamilton cadet leader should "give your kids a little ass whooping in the wood shed."

Ford's comments at a news conference come a week after the Hamilton Police Service said it charged a 12-year-old boy and a 48-year-old woman with assaulting a 59-year-old commanding officer for the Royal Canadian Air Cadets.

The cadet leader was supervising the distribution of Remembrance Day poppies at the Centre on Barton mall when two boys approached them and blew a loud air in the ears of young cadets he was with, police said in a release. The man followed the boys into a nearby restaurant to confront them and "a struggle ensued."

Police said a woman — who they later told CBC News is named Estela Quintanilla — jumped in to assist the boys and assaulted the cadet leader, causing him to fall. The 12-year-old hit him several times, police said.
The family of the cadet leader has identified him as Capt. Kenneth Kunkel. On Nov. 5, his daughter Kimberly Dietrich told CBC's Hanomansing Live that Kunkel was unable to walk.
Dietrich said her family was "taking it a day at a time," and her dad was "trying his hardest to recover."
Cadet leader faces life-altering injuries after ‘senseless’ attack | Hanomansing Live
The 12-year-old boy faces aggravated assault and assault level one charges, police said. The second boy was not arrested, police said, after officers were able to review footage of the incident.
The woman faces aggravated assault charges.
The charges have not been tested in court.

Ford has a history of commenting on criminal cases. Some lawyers have told CBC News that public officials should be careful about such comments, as they risk prejudicing juries and contributing to misinformation.

items: Ontario's premier has a habit of weighing in on criminal cases. Some lawyers say he should be more careful

blocks.text: "I just don't know how to process it," Dietrich said of the incident Thursday. "I don't know why someone would even think of doing something like that."
She said it's important to support veterans by wearing poppies.
Hamilton mayor-elect Keanin Loomis issued a statement about the incident Thursday, saying he is "deeply troubled" by it.
"My thoughts are with Kunkel, his family and the cadets during this difficult time. We wish him strength, healing and a full recovery," Loomis said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Justin Chandler is a CBC News reporter in Hamilton. He covers stories of all kinds from places including picket lines, court rooms, council meetings and research labs. Justin has a special interest in how public policy affects people, and loves a quirky human-interest story. Before CBC Hamilton, he worked for TVO and on a variety of CBC teams and programs. He co-hosted Radio Free Krypton on Met Radio.

articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon denies being ‘obsessed’ with Jesse Baird as evidence to double murder trial continues
articles.summary:
Former police officer tells jury he joked about being ‘white girl crazy’ with friends as lawyer questions him over start of relationship with Baird

Beau Lamarre-Condon has denied being…

blocks.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon has denied being “obsessed” with Jesse Baird from the start of their relationship, telling a court he would have liked the TV presenter even if he was “a garbage cleaner”.
The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Sitting in the witness box for the fourth day, Lamarre-Condon was grilled by crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC about his relationship with Baird.
The former officer told the NSW supreme court he would meet up with Baird in October and November 2022 for sexual encounters before the pair began going on romantic dates in December of that year.
Under cross-examination on Tuesday, Hatfield asked Lamarre-Condon: “You were obsessed with him right from the start?”
Lamarre-Condon denied this, telling the jury: “I never cared about showing Jesse off. I wanted Jesse to meet my friends because I thought he was genuine”.
“Jesse Baird could have been a garbage cleaner… I liked Jesse for who he was as a person,” Lamarre-Condon said.
Asked by Hatfield if Lamarre-Condon was “obsessed” with Baird in February and March 2023, the accused responded: “I don’t agree with ‘obsessed’. Smitten? Yes. Obsessed? no.”

blocks.caption: Supplied images of Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird (right). Composite: Supplied/NSW Supreme Court

blocks.text: Hatfield pointed to messages between Lamarre-Condon and his friends sent around the time the pair began going on dates, where the officer says: “it sounds crazy, I love him”.
Lamarre-Condon responded: “I say ‘I love you’ to all my friends and to people like that all the time.”
“That’s different to saying I’m ‘in’ love with him,” he said.

Asked whether he was insecure about the relationship and whether Baird liked him, Lamarre-Condon said his response was “natural” and sometimes occurred when the TV presenter did not reply to his messages straight away.
“I would always joke [with my friends], ‘we’re white girl crazy’,” Lamarre-Condon told the jury.
“It means we should stop being in our head and second-guessing ourselves.”
He told the court he would make jokes and have “banter” with his female friends, not his heterosexual male friends, telling each other things like: “you’re a crazy bitch”.
Hatfield showed screenshots of text messages between Baird and Lamarre-Condon and asked why Baird’s profile photo were low resolution.
“If you’re trying to insinuate any of these are not genuine … we’ve got videos,” the officer said, telling the court Baird’s photo was a screenshot from a video he took of the presenter.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

articles.title: Epstein associate who still runs model agency 'put me in danger' says abuse survivor
articles.summary: A woman says an agency boss sent her to photoshoots at the sex offender's Florida beach home.
articles.byline: Oana Marocico, Sheida Kiran, Haya Al Badarneh

blocks.text: A woman raped by Jeffrey Epstein says the president of the model agency representing her put her in danger, when he sent her to two photoshoots at the convicted sex offender's Florida beach house.
At the time, in 2009, Epstein was serving a jail sentence for sex offences against a minor but was allowed to work each day from his home.
"My agency's job was to protect me, and they failed. In fact, they put me in danger. And for that, they should be held accountable," she tells the BBC World Service.

Roza was 18 when she was first sent to Epstein's Palm Beach home by MC2 Model Management's US branch, having only arrived in the US from Uzbekistan about a month earlier. MC2's US president at the time, Jeff Fuller, now runs another US model agency called The Source Models.
"My agency knew exactly where I was. So Jeff knew exactly where I was going," says Roza.

She shows us an expense statement suggesting Fuller himself booked her flight home from Palm Beach, following her second shoot at Epstein's home. Fuller has previously claimed he did not know Roza was going to Epstein's house.

She says the photoshoots led to her being employed as an assistant to Epstein. Other survivors have explained how the financier used the recruitment of assistants as an elaborate ruse to allow him to continue abusing young women.
Roza says Epstein went on to systematically rape her.
Fuller has not responded to the BBC's allegations. He has previously said he did not know Roza was being abused.
We discovered through the Epstein-related documents released by the US Department of Justice [DOJ] that 10 models from MC2 met, or were in communication with, Epstein after his conviction.
The files also show Epstein gave $1m (£742,000) to MC2 in 2005 - despite the agency owners telling a US publication two years later that Epstein had no involvement in their company.

Testimony shared with BBC Eye also raises questions about the role played by two other individuals who were active in the model industry, and whom the DOJ files show had close relationships with Epstein - former agent Ramsey Elkholy and agency director Faith Kates.

A DOJ statement from last year, that no evidence has been uncovered which would warrant further investigation against "uncharged third parties", is now being challenged by New York State senator, Zellnor Myrie.
He has proposed a new sex trafficking bill to give police greater power to investigate Epstein's alleged enablers.
If you are outside the UK, please watch on YouTube, external
An email in the DOJ files, from Fuller to Epstein, makes clear the close ties between the agency and the financier.
"Had it not been for you, we would have fired her months ago," Fuller writes of another model in March 2012. "And I would be careful as she blabs about things," he says.

A month after Epstein's second arrest in 2019, MC2's US branch was dissolved and Fuller opened a new agency, The Source Models, which is still operating. The BBC has found that 50 models from MC2 were transferred to his new agency.
We asked The Source Models to comment on our findings - it did not reply.
Model agencies were useful to Epstein, says Sigrid McCawley, the lead lawyer for more than 100 of Epstein's victims.

"Epstein said to many people he wanted three different girls a day. Think about those numbers... The [model] scouts were really critical because they were the ones who were identifying the type of woman that Epstein liked."
In the case of former agent Ramsey Elkholy, BBC Eye has discovered he tried to connect 34 women to Epstein, including an 18-year-old who was still in school.
The experience of one of the women highlights how assistants would be co-opted into the structure of the abuse.
Elkholy, the DOJ files show, suggested to Epstein that one of the financier's female assistants befriend this woman, before introducing her to Epstein.
We spoke to this woman, and she revealed that at her first meeting with Epstein, aged 19, he sexually abused her in his New York townhouse.

Ramsey Elkholy told the BBC: "I completely reject any allegation that I knew of or facilitated abuse of any kind… At the time, I had no knowledge of any abuse and I knew only his own [Epstein's] account of his 2008 [legal] case, which I misguidedly believed."

He continued: "The record and published reporting show that women were often groomed by other women in his inner circle. I was never part of that circle, or indeed of any such activity… my intention was to help models find professional opportunities by introducing them to an extremely well-connected individual."

items: If you are in the UK and you have been affected by any of the issues in this story such as sexual abuse and violence, information and support is available at BBC Action Line

blocks.text: Lawyer Sigrid McCawley says these female assistants would have had "no choice" in how they conducted themselves.
"These young survivors were being abused regularly. Their livelihoods were being threatened… They had to do what they were being told to do."
Another model we have spoken to, Simona (not her real name), from eastern Europe, told us Epstein had raped her more than 200 times.
"People think that we gained something, that we agreed on this abuse in order to gain something, whether it's monetary or influential, but it's not true. We're left with deep trauma," says Simona.
She says the first time she met the financier, aged 20, she was already signed with a model agency in New York, and he offered to introduce her to his "good" friend Faith Kates.

At the time, Kates was the head of Next Management, one of the world's biggest model agencies. She stepped down from that senior executive position in December last year, but is still legally listed as a director of the company.
Simona says at this meeting, Kates suggested she undergo plastic surgery and sent details of a surgeon to Epstein.
After her meeting with Kates, Simona says Epstein convinced her to stop modelling.
And just like Roza, and several other of his victims, she became his assistant. She says he went on to rape her and control every aspect of her life for nearly two years.
The DOJ files show Epstein asked Kates to meet an additional five models, though it is not clear how many of these meetings took place.

Lawyers for Faith Kates told the BBC: "Jeffrey Epstein was a master manipulator... Ms Kates was one of those grossly misled by Epstein. Had she known then what she - and everyone else - now knows, she would have never associated with him."
They added she had never asked a model to have plastic surgery.
We approached Next Management for comment, but it did not reply.

Myrie told the BBC that if his bill were to become law, and "you were sending models to Epstein and you knew what Epstein was doing, or you should have known what he was doing, you will be held accountable".
Roza hopes sharing her story will encourage others to come forward.
"There are many, many survivors out there who never speak, because it's scary. So to all my sister survivors… you know me now. You know my name. I say, reach out."
