articles.title: Ontario university student pleads not guilty in U.S. court amid Chinese 'espionage' probe
articles.summary: An Ontario university student has pleaded not guilty in a U.S. federal court in a case a prosecutor described as involving "espionage-type activities." Weiheng (Billy) Zeng is charged with making…

image.caption: The FBI said in a criminal complaint that FedEx security cameras at Chicago O'Hare International Airport captured images of a man, later suspected of being University of Waterloo student Weiheng Zeng. (U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Michigan)

blocks.text: World·New

An Ontario university student has pleaded not guilty in a U.S. federal court in a case a prosecutor described as involving "espionage-type activities." Weiheng (Billy) Zeng is charged with making false statements following an FBI counter-intelligence investigation.
FBI says Weiheng Zeng accepted paid 'taskings' from unidentified Chinese contact
An Ontario university student has pleaded not guilty in a U.S. federal court in a case a prosecutor described as involving "espionage-type activities."

Weiheng (Billy) Zeng, a Chinese citizen studying at the University of Waterloo, is charged with making false statements following an FBI counter-intelligence investigation. He was arraigned in U.S. District Court in Detroit on Monday, according to public records reviewed by CBC News.
Court documents say Zeng was questioned by U.S. federal agents as he tried to enter Michigan on Aug. 23 after crossing the Ambassador Bridge from Windsor, Ont.

After three interviews, Zeng ultimately admitted accepting paid "taskings" on behalf of someone he believed was linked to the Chinese government, FBI special agent Robert Holbrook wrote in a sworn affidavit filed in court.
Zeng has been in custody ever since.
Weiheng Zeng was arrested at the U.S. border in Michigan in August and charged with making false statements, amid an FBI counter-intelligence investigation. (Instagram/Billy Zeng)
On Monday, U.S. Magistrate Judge Anthony P. Patti scheduled a bond hearing for next week.

A federal grand jury indicted Zeng last week on a single count of making false statements to U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents. The move indicates jurors found there are reasonable grounds to believe a crime has been committed.
Reached by CBC News last week, Zeng's Detroit-based lawyer William Swor declined to comment on the case.
Zeng allegedly paid by 'Chinese contact'

A self-described "photography lover" studying global business and digital arts, Zeng first raised U.S. authorities' suspicions in April, after an incident captured on security video at Chicago's O'Hare International Airport, according to the FBI's criminal complaint.

At the time, FedEx employees spotted a man taking photos, climbing a forklift and attempting to open a locked delivery truck and a shipping container in the company's parking lot at the Chicago airport, the FBI agent said in the court document.

When he attempted to re-enter the U.S. in August, Zeng provided conflicting reasons for trespassing and taking pictures. He initially told federal agents it was solely for hobby photography, according to the criminal complaint.

The FBI said in a criminal complaint an unidentified man was captured on security video at Chicago O'Hare International Airport on April 21 taking photos of aircraft. The incident was later linked to Zeng. (U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Michigan)

He later admitted the operation was carried out at the request of a shadowy "Chinese contact" who Zeng said he couldn't identify by name, but said he believed they worked for a Chinese government security agency.
According to court documents, Zeng told investigators his unnamed contact directed him to photograph aircraft and tail numbers, in exchange for $20-30 US per picture.

The criminal complaint also says Zeng recounted trespassing and taking pictures last year at a FedEx facility at Toronto's Pearson International Airport, at the request of the same, unidentified individual.
The allegations amount to "espionage-type activities," prosecutor Alyse Wu said at a previous hearing in Detroit.
Zeng, who lives in Cambridge, Ont., also outlined to investigators a convoluted system he purportedly used to communicate with the unnamed individual, who paid him via bank transfer in Chinese yuan.
The "Chinese contact" would mail Zeng a new SIM card every four to five months, which he was directed to use in his Huawei cell phone, according to the criminal complaint.
Ontario university student suspected of spying in Canada, U.S. for China
"Zeng, at the direction of 'Chinese Contact,' would subsequently destroy the SIM cards, delete the conversations, and delete the photos he took," wrote Holbrook, the FBI agent.
"The SIM card, which was from China Telecom, allowed Zeng to by-pass Canadian cellular network and connect directly with the Chinese provider network to send text messages to 'Chinese Contact.'"

A Chrysler Town & Country minivan with Ontario licence plates was seen in a FedEx parking lot at Chicago O'Hare International Airport on April 21, according to an FBI criminal complaint. Weiheng Zeng purportedly tried to re-enter the U.S. in August in the same vehicle. (U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Michigan)
Chinese Embassy, Zeng's sister deny allegations
A Chinese Embassy spokesperson previously sought to distance the government from Zeng's case.

"The Chinese side firmly opposes hyping up the so-called 'China spy threat' and baseless speculations and smears against China," an unnamed spokesperson for the embassy in Ottawa told CBC News in an email in September.
Zeng's sister denied her brother was knowingly involved in espionage for Beijing.
"If my brother is a Chinese spy, then I'm Trump's father," Meixuan Wang wrote in a social media post in September.

articles.title: U.S. House Republican moves to force vote on impeaching Pete Hegseth
articles.summary: Republican Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, putting pressure on his fellow Republicans to decide whether to remove one of the Trump…

image.caption: U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth in Cebu, the Philippines, Oct. 28. Fellow Republican Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote in the U.S. House on impeaching Hegseth. (Jam Sta Rosa/Pool/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, putting pressure on his fellow Republicans to decide whether to remove one of the Trump administration's most prominent figures following sweeping election losses.
Secretary of War says he is happy to litigate military actions of the administration 'all day long'
The impeachment resolution largely focuses on the war in Iran. It also includes references to Hegseth's role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.

Hegseth said earlier Monday he's eager to litigate the military actions that he and U.S. President Donald Trump have taken against Iran, Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi rebels and Venezuela's previous leaders.

"If you want to take issue with what we did in Epic Fury or Rough Rider or nabbing Nicolás Maduro, you're taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished, which is historic," Hegseth told reporters Monday, using the military code names for the Iran war and campaign of strikes to halt the Houthis' attacks on shipping in the Middle East.

items: Hegseth defends record as Pentagon chief, slams 'sham' push for his impeachment

blocks.text: Hegseth also announced that he would hold a rare news conference on Tuesday — his first in more than 180 days — on the impeachment threat. His last briefing was in May, and he has not held one on the Iran war, strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats or other U.S. military actions since then.

The Pentagon chief is bearing the brunt of anger and calls for his ouster after the Iran war and its economic impact contributed to severe Republican losses in the midterm elections that cost the party control of Congress. Massie pushed forward an impeachment resolution over the objections of House Republican leadership as momentum grows to hold Hegseth accountable for the conflict.
Hegseth gave a State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Sept. 30, but has not held a media availablity since May. (Alex Wong/Pool/The Associated Press)
Hegseth waves off impeachment push as 'noise'
Hegseth, after giving a speech at the Naval War College in Rhode Island, brushed aside the possible impeachment push.

"There's a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements, but their disagreements are with success," he told reporters. He added that "if we want to litigate" the military actions that the Trump administration has taken, "I'm happy to do it all day long."
"My team, we're not worried about the noise — it's what I told the troops, too — don't worry about the noise," he said.
Asked about U.S. Vice-President JD Vance blaming the Iran war for the massive Republican losses in the election, Hegseth noted that Trump said he would do it again, and "I agree."
He largely repeated a line that Secretary of State Marco Rubio said to reporters a day earlier: "It doesn't have to be necessarily popular, but it can be necessary."
Hegseth argued that the war was necessary because "someone had to confront the Iranian regime's pursuit of a nuclear weapon" and said "the choice was don't act and wish it away or take a bold move."

Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran has 440.9 kilograms of uranium that is enriched up to 60 per cent purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90 per cent.
Trump defended Hegseth to reporters on Sunday night.
"He's guilty of two things, basically winning two wars," Trump said. "I believe we saved the Middle East and Israel combined. And it's awfully hard to say let's impeach somebody who did that."
Trump defends Hegseth as Democrats prepare for political war
Hegseth insists 'Iran is devastated'

Hegseth reiterated that "Iran is devastated," even though the Islamic Republic has been able to keep striking military bases in the Middle East that are used by the United States, causing billions of dollars in damage, as well as commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
Disruptions to shipping in the waterway, where one-fifth of the world's oil passed before the war, have led to higher energy prices that hit voters' pocketbooks.
He said the next steps on the war are up to Trump, including telling Iran: "Hey, we're done, and we're going to watch your nuclear material. You better not move it."

With anger in Congress rising, Hegseth has been on a social media blitz, posting a video last week acknowledging the threat of impeachment. He said it would be "all about the politics of personal destruction" and insisted that "won't work with me. You can rest assured of that."

Since then, scores of political appointees within the Pentagon have posted images of Hegseth emblazoned with the words, "Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic." The White House also posted a video to social media that featured praise from Trump.

articles.title: The family business: Arnold Schwarzenegger’s son muscles into top 5 at bodybuilding competition
articles.summary: More than 60 years after Arnold Schwarzenegger first flexed his stuff on a bodybuilding stage, his youngest son is continuing the dynasty of muscle, scoring in the top five during his professional…

image.caption: Joseph Baena, the 29-year-old son of Arnold Schwarzenegger, has made his professional debut as a bodybuilder, decades after his father made a career out of muscle. (Joseph Baena/Instagram and Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

More than 60 years after Arnold Schwarzenegger first flexed his stuff on a bodybuilding stage, his youngest son is continuing the dynasty of muscle, scoring in the top five during his professional debut over the weekend.
Joseph Baena, 29, follows his father's muscular example
Joseph Baena competed in the classic physique category at the INBA PNBA Pro/AM World Cup in California on Saturday.
The 29-year-old placed fifth and said in a video on Instagram that he was happy to have achieved his goal of cracking the top five.
"I'm extremely proud of myself," said Baena, who only started competing this year. "It was an incredible experience for my first show as a pro."
This was the third-ever show for Baena, son of bodybuilder-turned-actor-turned-politician Schwarzenegger and Mildred Baena.
Under a video Baena shared on Instagram of his posing routine at the competition, several commenters noted, "Like father, like son."

It’s perhaps no surprise that the son of a man who became famous for being impressively jacked is following in his footsteps. Schwarzenegger’s physique scored him the title of Mr. Universe five times at professional bodybuilding competitions in the 60s and 70s, and he remains one of the most enduring names associated with bodybuilding.

items: Record-smashing powerlifter, 68, says she lives for the 'clang' of the weights

blocks.text: His 1977 docudrama, Pumping Iron, is credited with giving bodybuilding more exposure and having it treated more widely as a sport. High-profile roles for Schwarzenegger in Hollywood action films like Conan the Barbarian (1982) and The Terminator franchise further pushed muscle into the mainstream.

Arnold Schwarzenegger poses alongside dancers from the famous Parisian cabaret Le Paradis Latin on May 20, 1977, during the Cannes Film Festival in southern France. Schwarzenegger was there to present the docudrama Pumping Iron. (Raph Gatti/ AFP via Getty Images)

In his video reflecting on the competition, Baena said that bodybuilding was a solo sport where "it all comes down to your own discipline," but noted that he had a lot of support from family and friends.
"My father always says there's no such thing as a 'self-made man.' I have people in my corner," he said.
Baena called Schwarzenegger "the best training partner," in an interview with GQ earlier this year, saying his father makes sure he doesn’t "slack off in the gym."
He added that his father gave him "the bodybuilding encyclopedia" when he was in college, and that it sparked his interest in the sport.
Schwarzenegger and Baena attend Netflix's Los Angeles premiere of Fubar Season 2 on June 11, 2025. (Charley Gallay/Getty Images for Netfix)
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

articles.title: Skydance replaces James Gunn and Peter Safran as DC Studios chiefs following Warner Bros. takeover
articles.summary: In another major shake-up for the DC Studios, Skydance is replacing Hollywood director James Gunn and producer Peter Safran with a former Marvel executive.

image.caption: The two DC Studios chiefs are being replaced following Skydance's takeover of Warner Bros., after four years at the helm of the superhero franchise (FILE: 13/10/2026)Image: Richard Shotwell/Invision/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-heads of DC Studios after four years, Skydance Motion Picture Group announced on Monday.
Their departure marks another major shake-up for the superhero franchise following Skydance's takeover of Warner Bros, just a year after Gunn's "Superman" reached cinemas.
Who will replace Gunn and Safran?

Skydance chairman and CEO David Ellison has chosen Jeremy Latchman, a former Marvel Studios executive, to lead DC Studios. He is set to become president and chief creative officer of DC Studios on December 1.
Latchman will oversee the next phase of DC's film and television business, which includes characters such as Superman, Batman and Wonder Woman.
He was involved in major Marvel productions including "Iron Man" and "The Avengers," and previously worked with Gunn and Safran on Marvel's "Guardians of the Galaxy" movie.
What did Gunn and Safran achieve?
Gunn and Safran took charge of DC Studios in 2022, tasked with rebuilding the franchise and creating a more unified cinematic universe.
Their first film, "Superman," earned nearly $619 million (€553 million) worldwide in 2025.

But their second release, "Supergirl," flopped in June 2026, taking around $126 million worldwide against a reported production budget of $170 million. The horror-inspired "Clayface" followed in October.
Overall, DC has struggled to match immense profits and cultural impact made by Marvel in the early years of its own cinematic universe.

blocks.caption: 'Superman' was the first major theatrical release under DC Studios chiefs James Gunn and Peter SafranImage: DC Studios/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: "James and Peter launched a new era for DC Studios and led it through a period of real transformation, resetting the foundation and building a slate we're incredibly proud of," Ellison said in a statement.
"We're grateful for their passion, contributions and commitment to this legendary brand."
Gunn is currently completing "Man of Tomorrow," a sequel to "Superman." Other DC projects in development include "The Batman: Part II" and the television series "The People v. Gorilla Grodd."
Although Gunn and Safran will no longer oversee DC Studios' long-term plans, several projects developed under their leadership remain in production.
Was Gunn's Superman too 'woke' for conservatives?
Gunn's "Superman" sparked a political controversy in 2025 after the director described the superhero as an immigrant and emphasized themes of human kindness.
Conservative commentators accused the film of being "woke."
Skydance CEO Ellison has cultivated close ties with US President Donald Trump. Ellison has acknowledged having a good relationship with the administration but denied politicizing the company.
There is no evidence that the controversy surrounding "Superman" played a role in Gunn and Safran's replacement.

articles.title: US Pentagon chief Hegseth faces impeachment push over Iran war
articles.summary: Trump critic Thomas Massie is calling for a vote to impeach Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, accusing Hegseth of waging war without congressional approval.

image.caption: Hegseth previously told reporters he was not worried about the 'noise,' referring to rumors of his impeachmentImage: Matias Delacroix/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Republican lawmaker Thomas Massie, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, introduced eight articles of impeachment against US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday as pressure builds on the Trump administration over the Iran war.

The resolution proposed by the Kentucky congressman accuses Hegseth of conducting the war illegally without congressional authorization. Massie also claims Hegseth has abused his powers as the head of the Pentagon.
Massie is using a special procedure that could see the US House of Representatives vote on the resolution within two days, with the legislative chamber still dominated by Republicans.
Trump told reporters at the White House that Hegseth had done a "good job" and had "won" wars in Venezuela and Iran.
"I'll stand by him... He won two wars. He was in charge," Trump said.
How has Hegseth responded?
Earlier on Monday, Hegseth sought to downplay rumors about the push against him.
"My team, we’re not worried about the noise," he told reporters.
Hegseth said he would hold a press conference Tuesday — his first in more than 180 days — and defended the war as necessary, even if unpopular.
Who supports impeachment?
Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries backed the effort Sunday.
"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," he told ABC News. "Pete Hegseth has got to go."
Some Republicans have signaled they might support the charges. Arkansas congressman French Hill said he wanted to hear the debate before deciding.
The push follows Democrats' victories in both chambers of Congress in last week's midterm elections amid anger over the Iran war and soaring fuel prices. Republicans retain control until January 3.
Would impeachment remove Hegseth from office?
Impeachment requires a simple majority in the House and amounts to bringing formal charges. Removal would require a Senate trial and conviction by two-thirds of senators present.
Even with their enlarged majority next year, Democrats would need substantial Republican backing to reach that threshold.
What will Democrats do with their midterm mandate?

articles.title: Payments Canada launches long-delayed instant payments system
articles.summary: Payments Canada says it has launched its real-time rail national payment system, which is expected to speed day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses and consumers.

image.caption: The system is expected to generate savings from lower processing costs, reduced use of cash and cheques and a shorter period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to the recipient. (Jenny Kane/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Business
Payments Canada says it has launched its real-time rail national payment system, which is expected to speed day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses and consumers.
The new system is expected to enable members to exchange, clear and settle payments in real time
It says the new system is expected to enable participating members to exchange, clear and settle payments securely in real time.
"The launch of Canada's real-time rail marks the beginning of a new era for payments in our country," Payments Canada CEO Susan Hawkins said in a news release Monday.
"As a national asset that's designed specifically for our country, the [real-time rail] gives the payment ecosystem a modern foundation to build on."

items: BMO, CIBC, RBC, TD Bank block personal AI agents, citing safety and security

blocks.text: The system is expected to generate savings from lower processing costs, reduced use of cash and cheques and a shorter period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to the recipient.

The initial participants include Wealthsimple, Questbank, Peoples Trust Co., Paramount Commerce, Koho, DoBusiness.com, Digital Commerce Bank and Bank of America. Additional participants are expected to be added in the coming months, including all of the major Canadian financial institutions.
Marketplace investigates global bank scam industry
Transactions that pass through Payments Canada systems include debit card payments, pre-authorized debits, direct deposits, bill payments, wire payments and cheques.
Henry Kim, a professor at York University's Schulich School of Business, said the announcement is a step in the right direction.

"There's a thread that we have to do this for our sovereignty, and we just have to keep up with the rest of the world. A lot of the world has real-time settlement," he said in an interview, adding it already exists in the U.S.

Payments Canada has been years behind schedule on getting real-time rail in place, which allows near-instant payments clearing 24 hours a day, along with other improvements. The organization originally aimed to have the system in place by 2019.
The ability to more rapidly clear payments is particularly helpful for businesses, Kim said
"It also means that if you're tight for cash, if you're a business and your working capital runs low, you can get paid much faster by other businesses," he said.

Payments Canada said the real-time rail system will also come with mandatory centralized fraud services and controls, including confirmation of payee, a fraud transaction safety score, a list of fraud risks and a platform for fraud reporting.

items: BMO CEO says don't give AI agents your banking info

blocks.text: Kim, who works with U.S. credit unions on payment technology, said there are some concerns among U.S. financial institutions about fraud-related risks from real-time payments, with some U.S. banks electing not to provide the feature to customers.

"Because when you get rid of that lag, there's less time for verification so someone could actually make a fraudulent transaction. And with the real-time rail, oftentimes you don't get that back," he said.
"Canada's actually done something different from the U.S., and I think it's actually really good to have that centralized."

articles.title: Tommy Walsh, co-presenter of BBC’s Ground Force, dies aged 69
articles.summary:
Former builder got his big break after restoring the home of a producer who was working on a precursor to the show

Tommy Walsh, the building and DIY expert who appeared on television shows…

blocks.text: Tommy Walsh, the building and DIY expert who appeared on television shows including Ground Force, has died aged 69 after a long illness.
Walsh started his career as a professional builder before rising to fame alongside Alan Titchmarsh and Charlie Dimmock on the popular BBC garden makeover show from 1997 to 2005.
He went on to front programmes including Clean It, Fix It and Cowboys and Angels and joined the BBC show Homes Under the Hammer in 2021, following renovation projects and attending property auctions.
Walsh’s agent, Debbie Schiesser, told the Press Association: “Tommy died peacefully after a long illness surrounded by his family.
“As this has only just happened, we would ask everyone to please respect the family’s privacy.”

blocks.caption: Tommy Walsh (left), Alan Titchmarsh and Charlie Dimmock  receive the 2004 Television and Radio Industries Club special award for Ground Force. Photograph: Ian West/PA

blocks.text: Walsh, from Hackney in east London, ran his own property business before his television career. He got his big break after restoring the house of a BBC producer who was working on ideas for a show that would become Ground Force.
He told the BBC in 2004: “She asked me to look at a couple of pilots. One of them was the precursor to Ground Force, called Over the Garden Wall.
“It was like watching paint dry. It was terrible.”
Walsh turned down the chance to star on the show three times, but agreed when his eight-year-old daughter told him she had made a £10 bet with a boy at school that her dad was going to be on TV.
At its peak, Ground Force attracted 12 million viewers. In one episode, the team was flown out to South Africa to work in secret on Nelson Mandela’s garden, building a pergola and water feature.

blocks.caption: Tommy Walsh (right), Charlie Dimmock and Alan Titchmarsh with Nelson Mandela. Photograph: Susan Bell/PA

blocks.text: Walsh attended Parmiter’s grammar school in Bethnal Green, east London, and played football for the Old Parmiterians.

The club wrote on X: “It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of Tommy Walsh. A Parmiters boy he played for the club for many years in goal but made a great career as a TV personality in shows such as Ground Force. He will be sorely missed. RIP Tommy.”
He was married to Marie Walsh and was a father to three children: Charlotte, Natalie and Jonjo.

articles.title: Cyber-attack on French supermarket freezers has geopolitical context
articles.summary:
‘Not particularly complex’ defrosting hack has been attributed to Iran, with presumption it is linked to others across Europe

Iranian hackers like to send a message.

In 2023 a…

blocks.text: Iranian hackers like to send a message.

In 2023 a state-backed group interrupted TV streaming services in the United Arab Emirates to broadcast a deepfake report on the war in Gaza. In the same year, hackers affiliated with Iran displayed the slogan “down with Israel” on the screens of water-control equipment made by an Israeli firm.
Now France has attributed an attack on supermarket fridges to hackers operating under the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a key branch of Iran’s military establishment.

There was no message this time, but the disruption made headlines around the world. Some refrigerators had their temperature turned up so high they caught fire. ‌In the hours after the hack, supermarket employees dumped piles of perished meat and melted ice-cream into rubbish containers.
France’s foreign minister described it as an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” and promised “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible.

blocks.caption: An employee fills boxes of perished goods outside an Intermarche supermarket in Paris the day after the cyber-attack. Photograph: Lucien Libert/Reuters

blocks.text: It follows attacks on industrial freezers at an Israeli food production plant in May and a wave of freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at US military bases in August that are now reportedly being treated as a suspected hack. Those attacks have not been officially attributed to Iran, but the French announcement is the first to implicate the state in this type of hack.
after newsletter promotion

Rafe Pilling, a senior director at Sophos, a cybersecurity firm, said the relatively unsophisticated nature of the attack – hackers used default passwords to access fridge controls – was in line with Iranian capabilities. “The attacks themselves were not particularly complex,” he said.
Pilling said there was now a presumption the French attacks and a wave of rogue defrosting hacks across Europe last week were linked.

Hostile cyber operations against the west tend to come from a vexatious quartet of China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. All have different aims and characteristics: China has focused on industrial espionage and mass data gathering, Russia on disrupting enemy infrastructure and spreading disinformation, and North Korea on hacking crypto exchanges because it needs money. Iran, according to Pilling, wants to put a shot across the bow of its enemies.

blocks.caption: Boxes of perished goods outside an Intermarche supermarket in Paris the day after the cyber-attack.  Photograph: Lucien Libert/Reuters

blocks.text: “In general Iran uses cyber-attacks to project power internationally and to signal their political displeasure with regional and international adversaries,” Pilling said.

The fridge hacks came as the UK’s national cybersecurity centre warned the country is in the “foothills” of a new level of cyber threat – and should expect a “huge rise” in the volume of incidents. The main concern is AI, a technology now capable of highlighting previously unforeseen flaws in IT systems and helping attackers plan and carry out attacks.

However, the underlying context of the fridge attacks is not AI but geopolitics. After all, the refrigeration system vulnerabilities were relatively easy to find and exploit. But a combination of groundbreaking technology and tense global relations makes for an alarming landscape.

articles.title: Jemima Goldsmith says ex-partner Russell Brand physically assaulted her
articles.summary: TV producer, who was in relationship with ex-comedian that reportedly ended in 2014, accuses him of ‘violence, coercive control and abuse’

blocks.text: Jemima Goldsmith has said Russell Brand physically assaulted her and she accused him of “violence, coercive control and abuse”.

The 52-year-old TV producer said she has always been “strongly and unequivocally” on the side of Brand’s victims as she opened up about her own “painful” experience with her former partner in a social media post on Monday.

Shortly after Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison, Goldsmith posted on X: “I am in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand’s trial, told their stories, testified and ensured justice was done.

“I have had my own personal experience of his violence, coercive control and abuse. I had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident. I chose not to press charges at the time and not to go public with this, as I was worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children.

“I have neither seen nor spoken to Brand since that period in 2014. Whilst my pain in relation to this, pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact.”

On Thursday, Brand was found guilty of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.

Goldsmith, known professionally as Jemima Khan, is reported to have been in a relationship with Brand for a year from around September 2013. On X, Goldsmith said she had assisted the journalists who had exposed Brand in a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary and in reports in the Times and Sunday Times in 2023.
“I also undertook to testify in court to his abusiveness, if the newspaper that published the victims’ accounts were ever to be sued,” she said.
Goldsmith made the comments in light of renewed press reporting about a harassment injunction that she and Brand had taken out against a woman named Szilvia Berki in 2014.

Goldsmith, who married former Pakistan cricket captain Imran Khan in 1995, said the online commentary and media reporting about the injunction had presented “an untrue narrative” and opened her up to “vile hatred and abuse online”.
Berki had made allegations against Brand to the police after she had been booked to give him a massage at Goldsmith’s home in June 2014.

“I was present the whole time he was with her, and I did not see anything untoward, despite the fact that he was later found guilty of sexually assaulting other women and he later physically assaulted me. If I saw any man abuse any woman under any circumstances, I would do my utmost to stop them, without hesitation,” Goldsmith said in her statement.

Goldsmith alleged that a series of “untrue stories” appeared in the tabloid press and that Berki embarked on a campaign of “threatening abuse online and in emails”. The Guardian has not been able to reach Berki.
Brand and Goldsmith took out a harassment order against Berki, which meant she was banned from speaking to anyone about her allegations against Brand.

The injunction was granted by the high court judge and former leading counsel in the Leveson inquiry Mr Justice Jay. It was brought to light by the non-profit campaigning thinktank Tax Policy Associates, founded by the former tax lawyer Dan Neidle, after Brand’s conviction.

articles.title: $276 for hair ties? Skims offers advent calendar refunds after online backlash
articles.summary: After intense customer backlash, Kim Kardashian's apparel brand Skims is offering refunds to anyone who purchased its 2026 accessories advent calendar, which costs $276 and was advertised as "12 fun…

image.caption: Skims underwear is displayed on a shelf at a Nordstrom store on March 25, 2025 in Corte Madera, Calif. The apparel brand is offering refunds to anyone who purchased its 2026 accessories advent calendar, which is being roasted online. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

After intense customer backlash, Kim Kardashian's apparel brand Skims is offering refunds to anyone who purchased its 2026 accessories advent calendar, which costs $276 and was advertised as "12 fun days of surprises."
'For some, the calendar didn't meet expectations,' says rep from Kim Kardashian's apparel brand

The contents of the Skims 2026 accessories advent calendar have been described as what you might find in the bottom of your purse, on the floor of a car, or behind your dresser when you pull it away from the wall.

After intense customer backlash, Kim Kardashian's apparel brand is offering refunds to anyone who purchased the calendar. The package costs $276 Cdn (or $148 US — a relative premium), is advertised as "12 fun days of surprises" and contains an assortment of hair ties, bobby pins and key chains.
Viral unboxing videos posted over the weekend by disappointed customers have called the pricey calendar "a mess" and a scam.

"Are we serious right now?" exclaimed influencer Kayla Ryan as she opened the package for Day 4 to reveal three pink bobby pins. She called it "the worst advent calendar I have ever seen" in her Saturday video which accrued more than 20 million views as of Monday morning.
"I’m hoping this is a prank and the last one is a $150 gift card for all my money back," she added, after opening Day 9 to reveal an ornamental keychain comb that can't actually comb hair.

"This is the last one and it better be made of gold," another content creator says in a TikTok video with nearly 65 million views before opening Day 12 to reveal a furry compact mirror on a key chain and then grimacing.
"So, basically, everything that falls between my car seats," one person commented on the video; another described it as "wild for maybe $20 worth of stuff."

A composite of three screen grabs from TikTok unboxing videos for the new 2026 Skims advent calendar by, from left, @wetsloppyswollen, Brittany Shaw, and influencer Kayla Ryan. (@wetsloppyswollen/TikTok, @kaylaryan/TikTok, @brittanyshaw2.0/TikTok)

In statements provided to multiple media outlets, a Skims spokesperson said the company was "aware of the feedback" about the advent calendar and acknowledged that "for some, the calendar didn't meet expectations."
The company told told Page Six they "personally contacted every customer who purchased the calendar" and offered either a full refund or credit towards their other products.
CBC News reached out to Skims for further comment but has not received a reply.
Chanel advent calendar lambasted on social media
'Disappointed they got what they paid for'

This is far from the first advent calendar controversy. In 2021, Chanel was roasted online for a $1,025 calendar full of stickers, a magnet, a keychain and other miscellaneous branded items in addition to a miniature lipstick, hand cream and small bottle of perfume.
A year later, Dior was slammed for a nearly $5,000 advent calendar that mostly contained candle accessories and scented soaps in addition to small bottles of perfume.

Some commentators have criticized high-end advent calendars for being little more than luxury status symbols driven by the unboxing craze. Last year, for instance, Dior sold an $11,000 calendar. In 2019, Tiffany & Co. released a limited advent calendar that contained 24 pieces of jewelry and cost $158,000.

items: A Dior calendar for $11K? Here’s how the humble advent calendar has gone bananas
Luxury brand Chanel roasted online for $1,025 Advent calendar full of stickers, other trinkets

blocks.text: The Skims advent calendar is currently sold out with a waitlist. Some people have noted, the product description online details exactly what can be found in the calendar each day: a bear keychain, hair elastics, scrunchies, bobby pins, a squishie, bra elastic hairbands, more bobby pins, a comb keychain, a logo keychain, more scrunchies and a faux fur compact mirror keychain.
"While I agree the contents are ridiculously overpriced, we need to have a conversation about personal accountability as consumers," one person wrote on Threads.
LISTEN | Extravagant advent calendars:
Radio Noon Manitoba18:11Extravagant Advent Calendars and the Evolution of Adult Holiday Traditions
"If the contents were disclosed, you ignored the description, spent $148 [US], and then acted completely blindsided by what you received, some of that responsibility belongs to YOU."

A Toronto influencer who goes by the name Glamzilla online defended the advent calendar in a TikTok video, where she argued it's about the experience of opening something leading up to the holidays rather than a "big gift."
She was dragged in the video's comments, with some accusing of "gaslighting" and being insensitive to the price.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Millions fill Buenos Aires streets to welcome Pope Leo XIV
articles.summary: The Pope celebrated an outdoor Mass in Argentina's capital, the second stop on a 12-day tour of Latin America, just three weeks after having had surgery for lung cancer.

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV celebrated an outdoor Mass in Buenos Aires, Argentina, the second stop on a 12-day tour of Latin America, only three weeks after having had surgery for lung cancer.
An estimated 2.5 million people filled the streets to welcome him and attend the historic Mass.

articles.title: Pope Leo draws 2.5 million in Buenos Aires, renews warning over Milei's austerity
articles.summary: An estimated 2.5 million people have attended Pope Leo's mass in Buenos Aires, his largest gathering yet. The pontiff once called for protecting the vulnerable as President Milei cuts disability care…

image.caption: Argentina had not hosted a papal visit since 1987, despite being the homeland of Leo's predecessor, FrancisImage: Andrew Medichini/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: An estimated 2.5 million people attended Pope Leo XIV's open-air mass in Buenos Aires on Monday, according to local authorities, making the event the largest gathering of his papacy so far.

Crowds stretched for miles along Avenida del Libertador in Argentina's capital, with the faithful waving Vatican flags and chanting "Long live Pope Leo!" as the US-born pope passed in an open-top popemobile.
"It fills my heart with joy to celebrate... with you," Leo said in his sermon.

The pope also reinforced an appeal to President Javier Milei to protect vulnerable Argentines, visiting a disability care home struggling with the government's cuts to health care and social services.
What did Pope Leo say about Milei's spending cuts?
Before the mass, Leo visited the Cottolengo Don Orione care center in Claypole, south of Buenos Aires, which houses more than 400 people with disabilities.
He told residents their lives were a blessing rather than a burden, and challenged the idea that economic success alone measures a country's achievements.
"A nation's progress is also measured by how it welcomes all people with disabilities and particular needs," he said.

blocks.caption: Some worshippers had camped overnight to secure a place at Argentina's first papal massImage: Andrew Medichini/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The remarks followed his appeal Sunday, at a reception attended by Milei, for economic growth to benefit people facing the greatest difficulties. He also urged leaders to choose their words carefully and recognize the limits of their power.

Milei became the president of Argentina some three years ago, Since then, his government has cut disability services and resisted implementing a law increasing funding for care, despite Congress overriding Milei's veto in 2025. The Senate is due to consider next year's disability funding in the coming days.
Argentina declares national holiday over Pope Leo's visit
Some worshippers camped overnight to secure a place near the Monumento a los Espanoles, where Pope John Paul II celebrated Argentina's last papal mass in 1987.
Monday was declared a national holiday to allow people to attend. President Milei and his sister Karina were among those present.
Pope's message for Milei
In his sermon, Leo spoke of families facing unstable employment, violence and addiction, while describing them as a pillar of society.
Where is the pope traveling next?
The visit is Argentina's first by a pope in nearly four decades. Leo's predecessor Francis, despite being born in Argentina, never returned to his homeland during his papacy.
Leo, 71, visited Uruguay before arriving in Argentina on Sunday. He is due to travel to Peru on Wednesday and return to Rome on November 17.
The first US-born pope spent decades in Peru as a missionary and bishop. The Vatican has described his South American tour as a "homecoming."
The demanding trip comes less than a month after surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his lung.

articles.title: Witnesses recount struggle to save people buried in ‘horrifying’ Gaza landslide
articles.summary:
High winds and heavy train triggered collapse of sand bank overlooking camp for displaced families

Witnesses have described the frantic struggle to save three members of a family buried by a…
articles.byline: Seham Tantesh in Gaza and Jason Burke

blocks.text: Witnesses have described the frantic struggle to save three members of a family buried by a landslide triggered by high winds and heavy rain in Gaza.
A sand bank overlooking a camp for displaced families south of Deir al-Balah collapsed on Sunday, killing five people and crushing at least three tents.

“It was a horrifying sight,” said Abdul Karim al-Sahhar, 30, originally from Izbat Beit Hanoun in northern Gaza. “We saw people buried beneath the sand and rocks. None of them was moving or making a sound. Even the tent had disappeared completely. There was no trace of it left.”
Among the casualties was an eight-year-old, a six-year-old and their mother.

Sahhar, whose own shelter was badly damaged in the landslide, said the children’s father was outside the family tent and so survived. “One of his children had called him to come and eat with them,” he said. “He was a little late returning, and then the collapse happened.

“The father started shouting: ‘Save my children! Save my children!’ People came and started digging [but] there was a huge boulder on top of the victims. The young men had to break it into pieces so they could reach the people buried underneath.”

Abu Darbali, another witness, said the collapse of the embankment sounded like an explosion. “We found that three tents were covered completely after the mountain collapsed on top of them,” he told Reuters. “People were under the rubble and we couldn’t see them.”
Video posted to social media showed residents using hammers to break large rocks and others removing sand with shovels, searching for people trapped underneath using flashlights.

blocks.caption: Palestinians remove sand at the site of the deadly sand bank collapse. Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/Reuters

blocks.text: The UN said more than 26,000 households had reported damage to shelters or belongings after the weekend’s rainstorms.

The vast majority of Gaza’s population of 2.3 million live in tent encampments or the ruins of bombed-out buildings, ‌with reconstruction yet to begin after Israel’s relentless two-year military assault launched after the Hamas attacks on southern Israel in October 2023.

“The collapse [this weekend] was waiting to happen. [Gaza] is extremely overcrowded. People are just trying to find a place wherever,” said Toby Fricker, a spokesperson for Unicef, which has been working to prevent similar tragedies and improve drainage in camps for the displaced.

In a statement, the Hamas-run government media office said about “70,000 tents sheltering tens of thousands of displaced people were flooded on the first day” of rains. It also noted the “collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs, which caused injuries”, some critical, in various areas of the tiny territory.

A US-brokered ceasefire last year called for the eventual reconstruction of Gaza, but little progress has been made. Negotiators have failed to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm or for Israel to withdraw its troops, which control about two-thirds of the territory ‌from which residents have been ordered to leave.
Israel says no reconstruction can happen before Hamas is disarmed.

Sahhar said he and his family were now homeless. “My tent and everything I own are now buried under the sand. My mattress, household utensils and all my belongings – everything was buried. I could not retrieve anything,” he said.

blocks.caption: Palestinians inspect tents buried under rocks following the collapse of a large sandstone slab. Photograph: Abdel Kareem Hana/AP

blocks.text: Mustafa Qazzaat, a member of the Gaza City council, said Israel had not allowed prefabricated homes to shelter the displaced since the truce was announced, and only permitted the entry of limited numbers of tents.
Many so-called “dual use” items remain restricted, such as metal tent poles. Humanitarian workers said they instead had used wooden poles fashioned from palettes used to transport food.

Cogat, the Israeli defence ministry body that oversees aid to Gaza, said over 91,000 tents and over 8,200 trucks containing tarpaulins, blankets and winter clothinghad reached Gaza, as well as convoys carrying supplies of fuel and engine oil to power pumping facilities and other humanitarian installations.

Earlier this year, an assessment compiled by shelter specialists in Gaza revealed that thousands of tents supplied by China, Egypt and Saudi Arabia to shelter displaced Palestinians offered only limited protection against rain and wind.

articles.title: Republican congressman to force impeachment vote on Defence Secretary Hegseth
articles.summary: The effort will likely fail, but Representative Thomas Massie wants to push Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch their own impeachment process.

blocks.text: A Republican congressman plans to force a vote in the House of Representatives this week to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, alleging he has violated the US Constitution.
"By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable," Representative Thomas Massie said.

The effort will likely fail, given Republicans will remain in power in Congress until January. But Massie says he wants to push President Donald Trump to fire Hegseth before Democrats can launch an impeachment process.
Hegseth, who will hold a news conference on Tuesday about Massie's move, said he was not concerned.
"We're not worried about that," Hegseth said when asked by reporters about the impending resolution on Monday, adding he would hold a news conference Tuesday morning "on that very topic".
Hegseth's last news conference was in May.
Massie, who lost re-election earlier this year, is among the few Republicans who have been critical of Trump and the war that started earlier in this year in Iran.

The Kentucky congressman first introduced impeachment articles in September and is now pressing for a vote in the wake of Republicans losing control of both the House and Senate in last week's midterm elections. He has said his push to rid the administration of Hegseth is meant to prevent a Democrat spectacle next year.

"My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what's coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie also said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials."
"President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate," he also said.

Impeaching a cabinet secretary is very rare. The impeachment must be approved by both chambers for the secretary to be removed from office. The House has voted to impeach only two cabinet members in US history, but the Senate did not agree on either one.

Once Massie introduces his resolution - expected later on Monday - Speaker of the House Mike Johnson must schedule a time to consider it within two days. Along with voting on the resolution directly, the House has the option to vote to refer it to committee or to set it aside.

Massie will likely have the support of the Democrats in the House, with that party's leader, Hakeem Jeffries, saying on Sunday that he is a "hard yes" on impeachment. But Massie would still need to win over members of his own party.
The House has passed a War Powers resolution - a measure that seeks to halt Trump from taking further military action in Iran - multiple times this year, with Massie's support.
But Massie's disagreement with Hegseth also goes beyond Iran, he said in the statement.
He has accused Hegseth of intimidating critics of the Trump administration, kidnapping foreign leaders and ignoring congressional war powers resolutions.

articles.title: Russia's leading independent newspaper closes after eviction

blocks.text: Russia's leading independent newspaper has closed after being evicted from its offices and facing pressure from authorities.
For 30 years, Novaya Gazeta published investigations into corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power in the country.
On Monday, the team behind the newspaper had a final editorial meeting before packing up their belongings and leaving.
The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia's media was highly diverse and that the newspaper's closure was part of "a standard rotational process".
The BBC spoke to its co-founder Dmitry Muratov, a Nobel Peace Prize winner, about the closure.

articles.title: Turkey steel factory blast kills at least 16 people
articles.summary: Eyewitnesses say the explosion shook the ground, with one believing an earthquake had hit near the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga.

blocks.text: At least 16 people have died and 13 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey.

All those killed and injured were workers at the Habas plant, one of the country's leading steel producers, authorities said. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air.
The local governor said the blast happened around midday after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below.
Workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey, the Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said.
Eyewitnesses said the explosion shook the ground, with one person initially believing an earthquake had struck.
In a statement, the company said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces.
Izmir Governor Süleyman Elban told media that some people are believed to be still under the rubble.

Speaking after a cabinet meeting on Monday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way, while search and rescue operations continued. He also said two of the injured were in a serious condition.
At least five people have been arrested, according BBC News's Turkish service, citing local media reports.
The Habas plant is in the Izmir district of Aliaga which is a major port and one of Turkey's main shipbreaking hubs.

articles.title: France blames Iran’s Revolutionary Guards for cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges
articles.summary: French foreign minister vows European sanctions against Tehran over ‘unprecedented’ hacks last month

blocks.text: France has said Iran’s Revolutionary Guards were behind “unprecedented” cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges in the country last month, vowing European sanctions against Tehran.

“I can confirm that this attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” the French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, said on Monday of the hacks on 11 and 12 October.
“This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression,” he said, adding, “We will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack.”
Iran’s mission to the United Nations did not return messages seeking comment. Iran routinely denies carrying out malicious cyber operations.

The October hacks were followed this month by a second wave of hacking ‌that hit more than 100 establishments across Europe and even affected refrigerators used by French blood banks, prompting employees to move some of the blood to other cold storage units.

The seemingly straightforward nature of the refrigerator hacks – and their repetition ​across multiple countries – prompted speculation about who might be responsible amid ongoing concerns over Russia’s suspected sabotage campaign in Europe, the war between the US and Iran and the global rise of AI-powered cyberattacks.

articles.title: Men recruited to French gang as children to kill give rare insight into drug underworld
articles.summary: "It destroys people, but we all make our own choices" - Marseille drug-gang members spoke to the BBC.

blocks.text: A BBC investigation has found one of Europe's most powerful drug gangs in France is recruiting teenage children from across the country to commit kidnap and murder.
Known as the "DZ Mafia", the gang won a bloody turf war against a rival group in Marseille during 2023, and is now recruiting from further afield.
One member who is in prison awaiting trial after being implicated in several murders told the BBC he was part of a DZ Mafia hit squad.
He agrees the killings he has been charged with were "quite shocking".

"Attempts in broad daylight, in traffic jams… it can range from going to hit a guy, slap him to taking him in front of his mother and burning him up in a car. I think I have good composure, I handle it fairly well."
When challenged over whether he feels regret when carrying out such acts of brutality, he says he feels "guilty in-part" but claims to have no regrets.
Like so many teenagers from Marseille, he knew large sums of money could be earned quickly in drug trafficking. Now in his twenties, he admits the environment he entered was a "trap".
The BBC's Paris Correspondent, James Waterhouse, reports from Marseille.

articles.title: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
articles.summary: The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up.

blocks.text: France has accused Iran of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers.
Speaking at a news conference, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of Iran.

He said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding that the country would "implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack."
The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up, which spoilt fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Then last week, dozens of supermarkets across seven other European countries were also impacted by a cyber-attack that targeted fridges and freezers. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Iran is yet to respond to Barrot's allegations.

Separately on Monday, the Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as well as his two deputies.
Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.

More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.

articles.title: Trump questions midterm elections integrity after previously accepting results
articles.summary: Trump made the claims, without evidence, on Truth Social on Monday.

blocks.text: In the Truth Social post, Trump made vague claims about polling, voting "dumps", and "machines" without providing specific evidence of error or wrongdoing.
He has previously attempted to cast doubts on the integrity of elections he has lost, although he himself was not on the ballot in the midterms.
"We would have won easily if I was on the ballot," Trump told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, after it was confirmed his party had lost both the Senate and the House.
As it stands, Democrats have won 54 US Senate seats and 254 US House seats, giving them comfortable majorities in both chambers even as counting continues in some races.

image.caption: Stores in several countries across Europe recently experienced fridge and freezer issuesImage: Elsa Rancel/Ouest-France/PHOTOPQR/MAXPPP/IMAGO

blocks.text: French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the attacks on French supermarkets last month came from Iran, and were carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), a powerful paramilitary force loyal to the Iranian regime.
"This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression," Barrot said, adding "we will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack."
The comparatively simple cyberattack nevertheless had dramatic consequences, spoiling large quantities of produce and in some cases setting temperatures so high that refrigeration units caught fire.
It was launched on October 11 but last week a series of similar incidents affected French supermarkets and authorities even reported a failed attempt to hack cooling units at blood banks.

articles.title: Russia: Independent Novaya Gazeta shuts its Moscow newsroom
articles.summary: The investigative newspaper is closing its doors after Russian authorities labeled it a "foreign agent" and ordered it vacate its Moscow premises.

image.caption: Launched in 1993, Novaya Gazeta often took on Russia's criminal and political elites Image: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Novaya Gazeta newspaper closed its Moscow office on Monday, saying it was not able to continue reporting amid a campaign of state pressure in Russia.

The investigative outlet, co-founded by late USSR chief Mikhail Gorbachev, had long been a thorn in the Kremlin's side. In recent years, it ran into increasing roadblocks amid its critical coverage of the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
It was branded a "foreign agent," a Soviet-era term resuscitated by President Vladimir Putin's administration, with officials ordering it to vacate its Moscow offices.

Russian banks were also forbidden from processing donations from readers and supporters. The paper had been heavily dependent on this income stream after moving wholly into online publishing, with the transition taking place shortly after the invasion of Ukraine. Russian authorities introduced new wartime censorship rules in the wake of the full-scale invasion.

blocks.caption: Founding editor Dmitry Muratov shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize for his work with the paperImage: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nobel Prize winner Muratov calls for free speech
2021 Nobel Peace Prize-winning founding editor Dmitry Muratov issued an appeal for free speech in wartime Russia as journalists gathered in the Novaya Gazeta offices to witness its closure.

"Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today," he said. "We are currently at a point where the section of the Russian constitution that guarantees political and civil rights has ceased to function."

Russia's government meanwhile sought to play down the significance of the closure, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying it was part of a "rotational process" in a fiercely competitive media landscape.
What is Novaya Gazeta?

Novaya Gazeta was a flagship for post-Soviet democratic Russia and the era of "glasnost" or openness, also launched by Mikhail Gorbachev. The reformist Soviet leader used some of the prize fund for his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize as seed money for the publication.

The paper has built a reputation for fearless reporting, which has also put it in the crosshairs of Russia's wealthy and powerful. Six of its journalists were murdered since the paper was launched in 1993.

They included Anna Politkovskaya, who spent years investigating allegations of abuses by Russia's military during its campaigns in Chechnya. An early critic of Putin, she was found dead in her apartment bloc on the president's birthday in 2006.

Images published in Russian media on Monday showed the paper's editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, taking down photographs of Polikovskaya and other reporters murdered in what's thought to be retribution for their work.

blocks.caption: The paper moved online soon after Russia's invasion of UkraineImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Last month, when first announcing that the paper would close, Sokolov said the outlet had "been killed." The paper was shutting down after "the Russian authorities — the Russian special services — have forced the editorial team to end its work," he said.
Will closure in Moscow mark a definitive end?

Muratov called for a ceasefire in Ukraine and urged foreign observers to remember the strength of dissent that endured in Russia, even if it was being pushed underground by censorship laws and other repression or intimidation.
"We canot blame the citizens themselves for this," Muratov said, "especially the wonderful, truly remarkable younger generation."
"I urge you to distinguish between the Russian authorities and the Russian people," he added.
Muratov also called for the release of around 4,000 people he termed political prisoners in Russia.

Novaya Gazeta's leadership has not made it entirely clear whether its closing down in Moscow marks a defeinitive end to the outlet's reporting, or whether they might perhaps seek to regroup and begin operating in some form from outisde Russia, as several other publications including DW have been forced to in recent years.
One of its journalists, Irina Vorobyova, said that the paper's spirit would survive like a "good virus" and would "continue in everyone that was part of it."
