articles.title: India’s demonetization: 10 years on, promises remain unfulfilled
articles.summary: A decade after the 2016 currency ban, its impact on India's economy and the fight against black money remains contested.

image.caption: Digital payments in India have expanded rapidly since the demonetization move in 2016Image: Amit Dave/REUTERS

blocks.text: On November 8, 2016, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced in a televised address to the nation that he was withdrawing all 500- and 1,000-rupee banknotes from circulation at midnight.
The surprise move invalidated 86.9% of the value of currency in circulation in a single stroke.
Modi asked Indians to make a "grand sacrifice for cleansing our country."

He promised that the hardship would help eliminate black money, corruption, counterfeit currency and terrorist financing. The exercise was presented as a major step towards a cleaner and more transparent economy.
The cost to the informal economy
Millions of Indians rushed to banks to exchange their savings. Long queues formed outside banks and ATMs, with people waiting for hours, sometimes without knowing when they would get their money.
Workers missed wages, small businesses struggled to pay employees and families found it difficult to buy everyday essentials. Reports of people dying during the cash crisis added to the distress.

"I still remember my domestic help's father," businessman Prakash Patra from Jaipur city told DW. "He panicked, collapsed, and passed away right there, standing in a long queue just trying to exchange his family's life savings. It wasn't just cash that was lost in those lines. It was human lives."
Is India ready to become a ‘global power’?

For India's most vulnerable, particularly rural women and people without bank accounts, the sudden cash shortage made savings difficult to access. Money set aside for family weddings, medical emergencies and basic survival was suddenly compromised.
Joe Athialy, executive director of the Centre for Financial Accountability, a financial watchdog, says the impact fell disproportionately on the poor and the informal economy.

"Demonetization destroyed livelihoods, disrupted small businesses and pushed millions into deeper economic insecurity. The poor and those dependent on the informal sector bore the greatest cost," Athialy told DW.

Arun Kumar, former professor of economics at Jawaharlal Nehru University and author of "The Black Economy in India," shared a similar assessment. The government wrongly assumed that illicit wealth was primarily held in cash, he said.
"And it penalized the cash-dependent informal sector while leaving the real engines of the black economy untouched," Kumar told DW.
Did it solve the black money problem?
The first major setback came in 2018, when the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) reported that 99.3% of the demonetized currency had returned to the banking system.
Only a small fraction of the withdrawn money had failed to come back, undermining the expectation that large amounts of undeclared cash would be extinguished.
India's AI ambitions: Can it become a global tech superpower?

A decade later, there is little evidence that demonetization made a significant dent in black money or corruption. Economists have long pointed out that much illicit wealth in India is held in property, gold and other assets rather than cash.

Some supporters of the policy argued that forcing cash into the banking system would help formalize the economy and widen the tax base. But the extent to which these changes could be attributed to the currency withdrawal remains contested.
Lekha Chakraborty, a professor at the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy, said research after the exercise pointed to limited success in achieving its stated objectives.
She draws on studies that examined both the immediate economic shock and its longer-term effects.

"The research points to modest gains against demonetization's primary objectives, alongside temporary but real economic costs. The impact was particularly severe in the informal sector, where cash remains central to everyday transactions," Chakraborty told DW.
"The economic shock was real, even if much of it faded over time. But there is little to suggest that demonetization produced a lasting change in the way black wealth is generated or concealed."
Athialy argues that the policy was based on a flawed understanding of how illicit wealth is held in India.
"Cash is only an insignificant part of the black economy. Much of India's unaccounted wealth is held in assets such as real estate and in tax havens, not currency," he said.
He also questions the absence of accountability for the disruption and its institutional consequences.
"Nobody has been held accountable for the economic disruption or the undermining of institutions such as the RBI."
Comparing mobile payment systems: India vs. Germany
Boost to digital payments
Digital payments have expanded rapidly since 2016. The Unified Payments Interface (UPI), launched in August that year, has become a major part of India's retail payment system today.
In 2025-26, UPI processed 241.6 billion transactions, worth 314.2 trillion rupees (approximately €2.95 trillion), according to the RBI.
Yet the growth of digital payments has not reduced the amount of physical currency in circulation.
RBI data show that the value of banknotes in circulation stood at 43.15 trillion rupees (about €405 billion) on October 23, 2026, compared with 17.97 trillion rupees (€169 billion) in November 2016.
The figures show that Indians are increasingly using digital platforms for everyday payments, but cash remains firmly in circulation.
Chakraborty cautions against attributing the growth of digital payments to demonetization. "Digital payments largely continued a trend that was already under way before the currency ban," she said.
A decade after the unprecedented move, the gap between the government's promises and what demonetization ultimately delivered remains central to its legacy.

articles.title: Ice hockey: Norway says it's been kicked out of World Juniors in favor of Russia
articles.summary: The wrangling over Russia's return to international ice hockey continues, with Norway saying it has been kicked out of the next major tournament – to accommodate Russia. Switzerland has joined a…

image.caption: The last time Germany hosted the World Championship in 2017, Russia won the bronze medalImage: Andreas Dick/Beautiful Sports/IMAGO

blocks.text: With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th (of 10) participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) said that the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had informed it that it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

The move, which has yet to be publicly announced by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to last month's Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision. The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued on Saturday, the IIHF said it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey."

As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta beginning on December 26. Still, Swiss Ice Hockey responded to Norway's statement, saying it's team would not face Russia at the World Juniors – as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.
However, it is far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," Mark Carney said.
"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

How this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the NIHF hope that its team could still play in the upcoming World Juniors. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.
"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten said.
"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days."
Hosts Germany continue to explore options

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed – or not – with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship next May.

"We intend to host the World Championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.
While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.
Lutz, who said he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility – if only as a last resort.
On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

"However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore — through dialogue — how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.
"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.
However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.
Could Munich's Olympic bid be a factor?
It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040, or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee – opening the door for their return to competition, despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.
The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games – like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) – to follow its lead.
Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius said he didn't wish to "speculate on implications."

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the issue could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

articles.title: Fake news in Africa: In an age of disinformation, who decides what's true?
articles.summary: From Ghana to Mozambique, the fight against fake news keeps gaining momentum. But combating disinformation also requires safeguards for free speech, leaving some governments in an inconvenient…

image.caption: In junta-run countries like Burkina Faso, fact-checking initiatives like Fasocheck are under increased government scrutinyImage: Boureima Salouka/DW

blocks.text: Misinformation poses a threat to democracy worldwide: An exaggerated WhatsApp message, a manipulated TikTok video or an apparent breaking news alert on Facebook can all misguide people in Africa and beyond — particularly in the run-up to elections.

As artificial intelligence is making it increasingly easy to manipulate images, voices and videos, more and more countries are trying to equip their populations with skills to identify and counter fake news.

But are these efforts really about raising awareness, or are certain governments using this fight to control public opinion, silence dissident voices and misguide the populace — from both within and outside of these respective nations?
Civil society groups fill gaps left by governments

Journalism lecturer Dani Madrid-Morales at the University of Sheffield believes that African governments must significantly step up their efforts to combat sources of disinformation and misinformation.
He told DW that "there are very few countries — if any — that are actually doing a good job" to beat the influence of fake news.

blocks.caption: Dani Madrid-Morales believes that civil society has an important role to play in fighting disinformationImage: Privat

blocks.text: Meanwhile, he also points out that there also are civil society initiatives in various African nations which help inform people about the dangers of such false narratives.

For instance in South Africa, organizations like Africa Check and Media Monitoring Africa work together to highlight the impact of fake news on elections. Similar coalitions also exist in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Senegal.

However, these initiative mostly focus on fighting disinformation during election periods; the rest of the time, they typically lack funding and sustained engagement with civil society to continue to make a change.
When African governments become part of the problem
There also are deliberate efforts by certain governments not to battle fake news; some let it happen while others engage in deliberately spreading this.

Madrid-Morales distinguishes between three types of disinformation within this context: There are scams and similar schemes, which some governments, he says, fail to sufficiently fight, leaving people susceptible to financial losses.
He adds that there also are certain foreign influence operations trying to impact public opinion from outside a country and, in many instances, outside of the continent.
Finally, there are political disinformation campaings which originate from within a country, he explains.
"Governments are particularly interested in the third category," says Madrid-Morales, adding that this is particularly prevalent in the Sahel region.
He highlights how in nations like Burkina Faso and Mali, military governments have shut down media outlets, prosecuted journalists and expelled foreign correspondents to silence free speech.
In his view, these junta governments are primarily concerned with preventing negative or false information about themselves from circulating.
Why we need fact-checking more than ever
Do outside forces shape public opinion in Africa?
Foreign powers meanwhile also appear to play a considerable role in shaping public opinion across the continent.
Afrobarometer, a pan-African research network, examined the influence of international actors in terms of their influence over the continent.
The study found that over 60% of respondents viewed China's political and economic influence positively; this was followed by 52% for the United States.

Both countries have no past colonial history in Africa, although they are now vying for economic gains while focusing on infrastructure projects — partly to maintain this largely benevolent perception.

However, perceptions of other former colonial powers varied notabbly depending on factors such as the impact of past injustices: For example, in French-speaking countries, only 34% of respondents viewed France's ongoing influence positively.

Komi Amewonou from Afrobarometer meanwhile told DW that such attitudes are not necessarily the result of targeted propaganda campaigns but rather of African governments letting negative perceptions simpy run their course.

blocks.caption: Komi Amewonou stresses the dangers of foreign powers also influencing public opinion across AfricaImage: Africa-Fact Summit 2026

blocks.text: The mixed role of media literacy initiatives
In some countries, there are media development project trying to educate people and animate them to think for themselves.
Ghana, the NGO Penplusbytes runs the "Caravan of Hope" — a project supported German development agency GIZ and the by DW Akademie.

This mobile campaign brings media literacy training to rural communities through theater, role-playing exercises, public discussions and videos in local languages. The initiative has managed to reach 3,000 people in five districts to date.
The campaign also involves trusted community figures, as studies show that locals mostly trust people they know personally — particularly traditional village leaders and community representatives.

Rebecca Avusu from Penplusbytes, who helped develop the project, told DW that "information must be verified before people believe it or pass it on. This is particularly important for those without smartphones or with limited formal education."

blocks.caption: This event in the village of Odomase is part of the "Caravan of Hope" media literacy projectImage: Penplusbytes

blocks.text: Initiatives in South Africa take a similar approach: The country is home to Africa Check — one of the continent's best-known fact-checking initiatives.
The organization visits schools and teaches classes how to identify manipulated images, verify sources and deal with misinformation circulating in WhatsApp groups.

However, Madrid-Morales says that there can be a downside to such media literacy programs as well; pointing to research conducted in South Africa, he highlights that while some young people do become more discerning consumers of information, others eventually lose trust in almost every source, resulting in a complete lack of knowledge about important developments.
Limited powers elsewhere in Africa
In other parts of the continent, there's greater resistance against such media literacy initiaves — chiefly by their own governments.

In 2026, the International Media and Information Literacy Institute (IMILI) was opened in the Nigerian capital Abuja under the auspices of UNESCO, with a mission is to promote research, training and international cooperation in media literacy initiatives.

The government has said that it aims to play a leading international role in Africa in the fight against fake news; however, civil rights groups say the state often blurs the line between genuinely battling disinformation and silencing public dissent in the country.

blocks.caption: Rebecca Avusu, project coordinator of "Caravan of Hope" incorporates local leaders in media literacy projectsImage: privat

blocks.text: In Kenya, there are similar concerns: The Media Council of Kenya has the role of supporting journalists and fact-checking initiatives.

However, it's scope of operations is limited, as the organization abides by the country's laws to remain in operation — in particular legislation supposedly designed to target the spreading of false information.
Conversely, these laws have come under increased scrutiny, as they can also be abused the silence views against the government.
Madrid-Morales says that in such contexts, there need to be independent oversight bodies to ensure that people do not refrain from expressing themselves publicly for fear of reprisal.
Mozambique: Fighting disinformation as a tool of control

Meanwhile in Mozambique, the media institute MISA has also launched a series of fact-checking initiatives such as MISACheck. The program is designed to train young journalists and social activists in fact-checking techniques.
Olivia Massango, the vice-president of MISA, says however that the efforts of such civil society groups may seem like a drop in the ocean.

Massango is particularly critical of how state authorities deal with misinformation: "When something becomes inconvenient, the government ... invokes public interest, but ultimately often ends up protecting only what suits it, or what it finds troubling," she told DW.
As an example, she cites an internet blackout justified on the grounds of protecting public safety.
"Combating disinformation must not mean criminalizing opinions, criticism or journalistic work," she warns.

blocks.caption: Olivia Massango highlights that governments can abuse fake news initiatives to suppress press freedomImage: Privat

blocks.text: Guidance from Europe — with limited safeguards
More and more African nations meanwhile are turning to Europe in hopes of adopting mechanisms to fight fake news.

Morocco and Senegal are among the examples where proposed legislation is inspired by EU standards. Madrid-Morales however stresses that while following strong EU legislation in the battle against disinformation, there also need to be independent oversight and enforcement mechanisms to make them work.
In the cases of Senegal and Morocco, these are yet to be established.

Rebecca Avusu is also concerned about such efforts maintaining loopholes to suit governments is and as needed: "We do not want laws designed to combat disinformation to become instruments for silencing people who question government decisions or express legitimate opinions," Avusu warns.
A journalist's guide to spotting fake news

articles.title: Turkey: Workers killed in Izmir steel plant blast
articles.summary: At least 10 workers lost their lives in an explosion at a steel factory in Izmir, with the Turkish authorities warning more people are trapped under the debris.

image.caption: An eyewitness said the Izmir blast felt similar to an 'earthquake'Image: Servet Ulku/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: An explosion and fire at a factory in western Turkey left 10 workers dead, while rescuers searched for four more believed to be trapped under the debris.

The blast took place at the HABAS steel plant in Aliaga, in the port city of Izmir. The city's governor Suleyman Elban told reporters that 15 people were injured, two of them critically, and that further search and rescue efforts were underway.
The plant's production line was in the middle of a shift change rather than active production, according to the governor. Only some 200 workers were present instead of the expected 300.

An earlier statement from the governor's office said that the blast happened around noon (09:00 GMT) when an overhead crane toppled into a furnace during the casting of liquid steel. It also said that the authorities were investigating the incident.
Izmir mayor fears death toll could rise
Mayor Cemil Tugay wrote on X that the initial fire following the blast had been extinguished, but the exact number of dead and injured would become clear only after the debris had been cleared.
Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci, announced that those injured in the incident have been taken to hospital and their condition is being closely monitored.

blocks.caption: The governor's office said search and rescue efforts were underwayImage: Kadir Özen/DHA

blocks.text: Minister of Justice Akın Gürlek announced four public prosecutors have been assigned to the case.
'I thought it was an earthquake'
Eyewitness Nuri Ali Ulker described the blast as "very intense."
"The ground shook," he was quoted as saying by the state-run Anadolu news agency.
Another witness, Deniz Ulker, told the agency that the explosion "felt like the earth's crust was shifting beneath us. I thought it was an earthquake."
Turkey's big bet to become the new energy hub
The HABAS plant was established in 1987 and can produce 4.5 million tons of steel annually, according to the company's website.
Leftist opposition lashes out at the government
Turkey's leftist opposition party TIP lashed out at the government saying that the blast has once again laid bare how occupational health and safety are completely disregarded in the country.
The described the incident as "workplace homicide."
In an online post, TIP leader Erkan Bas said that "[t]he regime of bosses has declared war on the workers."
Union leader Basaran Aksu said that "the massacre calls for the resignation of the minister of labor."
He warned that "workers' blood" was being shed for profit.
According to the Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent NGO in Turkey, there were 226 workplace deaths reported across the country in September this year.

articles.title: Russia's top independent newspaper closes under relentless government pressure
articles.summary: Novaya Gazeta, Russia's most celebrated independent newspaper, closed its Moscow offices Monday, citing relentless pressure from government officials.

image.caption: Dmitry Muratov, former editor-in-chief of the Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta, holds a poster in support of jailed reporters outside the outlet's office as the newspaper shuts down, citing what it describes as a relentless campaign by the authorities, in Moscow on Monday. (Ramil Sitdikov/Reuters)

blocks.text: World
Novaya Gazeta, Russia's most celebrated independent newspaper, closed its Moscow offices Monday, citing relentless pressure from government officials.
Novaya Gazeta, last major independent media critical of Kremlin, saw staff killed, attacked in Putin's Russia

It was the last major independent media outlet critical of the Kremlin that remained active in Russia. Others closed or moved their operations abroad after President Vladimir Putin launched Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
In a statement published Oct. 30, the newspaper said the Russian authorities and the security services had "forced our editorial team to cease operations."

"Human rights and freedoms have been abolished in this country, and defending them is now treated as a crime," the newspaper said. "Elections and elected governing bodies have been effectively dismantled, civil society institutions have been wiped out, freedom of conscience and human dignity have been trampled underfoot."
The newspaper was launched in 1993 by Dmitry Muratov and the last Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, using money from Gorbachev's 1990 Nobel Peace Prize.
6 journalists killed

Novaya Gazeta quickly became known for its fierce reporting and dedication to uncovering Russian human rights abuses and corruption. Six of its journalists have been killed, including Anna Politkovskaya, who reported on atrocities during the second Chechen War at the start of Putin's first term as president. She was fatally shot in her apartment building in 2006.
On the newspaper's final day in its office Monday, journalists slowly removed the portraits of their slain colleagues from the newsroom where reporters and editors planned their work.

Sergei Sokolov, editor-in-chief of the Novaya Gazeta daily, collects portraits of slain journalists from the offices as the newspaper closes down in Moscow on Monday. (Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP/Getty Images)
Tatiana Britskaya, the editor of Novaya Gazeta's investigations desk, said she had expected the outlet's closure almost every day for the past 4½ years.
"It is an incredibly difficult decision, because this is more than a workplace, more than an office — this is our home, and we're losing it," she said.
Novaya Gazeta had faced growing government pressure as the Kremlin cracked down on critics, with repression sharply intensifying after the start of the conflict in Ukraine.
Editor attacked on train

Longtime editor-in-chief Muratov, who shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize with Philippine journalist Maria Ressa, was attacked on a train in 2022 by an assailant who poured red paint over him, causing severe irritation in his eyes. Muratov stepped down as editor in 2023 after being named a "foreign agent" by Russian authorities. The designation carries strong pejorative connotations in the country and can bring additional government scrutiny.

The newspaper was fined after it was accused of discrediting Russia's armed forces, and it also was declared a foreign agent. Authorities blocked all of its online platforms, seized its printing house, revoked its media registration and shut down the donation system that allowed it to receive support from readers.
Kremlin tightens grip on Russians' access to media with misinformation law
In a final blow, the newspaper was ordered to clear out its Moscow offices.
As reporters left the building and gathered in the street, a new sign was affixed atop the nameplate that once announced the newspaper's office. It read, "Here lived Novaya Gazeta."
Sergei Sokolov, Novaya Gazeta's editor-in-chief, said he believed the newspaper would return one day "with renewed strength."

"We will live, and I am sure that this country, caught in such a terrible era, will eventually stir. As soon as those first signs appear, Novaya Gazeta will return, to our readers and to our colleagues."
'You cannot blame citizens for this'
Muratov said people needed to understand ​that it was the Kremlin that was to blame for waging the war and suppressing free speech.

"We cannot blame the citizens themselves for this — especially the wonderful, truly remarkable younger generation. I urge you to distinguish between the Russian authorities and the Russian people," he said.

items: Canada's Russian envoy returns with advice on how to hit back against Putin
Russia denies think-tank assessment that 1.2 million of its troops have been killed or injured in Ukraine war

blocks.text: The Kremlin defends the need for censorship laws, denies there are any ​political prisoners and says that Russia is taking necessary action at a time of war to prosecute people engaged in subversive activity.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the newspaper's closure was part of a "rotational process" ⁠in a fiercely competitive media environment.
Some of Novaya Gazeta's staff left Russia in 2022 and opened a separate project, Novaya Gazeta Europe. The new outlet has been sharply critical of the Kremlin and its military action in Ukraine.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: Strait of Hormuz still a source of leverage for Iran
articles.summary: Attacks in the Strait of Hormuz put crews at risk and drive up energy shipping costs. Iran's ability to sustain them and the limits of US protection will shape how much trade can continue and at what…

image.caption: Latest data from the UKMTO show increased shipping traffic through HormuzImage: Atta Kenare/AFP

blocks.text: Since the Iran war started, attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz have put crews at risk of death and injury, forcing shipping companies to choose whether to attempt the passage or delay cargoes and face higher costs.

Merchant vessels continue to use the strait despite the danger but how long that can continue depends partly on Iran's ability to sustain its attacks and the United States' capacity to protect shipping and bear the cost.
Ali Mohammadi, an expert in Iranian affairs based in France, believes Iran's geography and the equipment it uses allow it to keep attacking ships.
But he sees the economic burden of the war as Tehran's main constraint.
"Iran's limitation in the Strait of Hormuz is economic rather than military, because continuing the war has a significant impact on its economy," he said.

It's unclear how long Iran can sustain attacks given the lack of reliable information on the nation's weapons stocks and its ability to replenish supplies. And sporadic attacks in the crucial waterway are also different from closing the strait completely.

"Even if a complete closure of the Strait of Hormuz were possible, it would not be sustainable because it could carry high political costs for Iran," Mohammadi told DW. "Iran cannot indefinitely disrupt its allies' access to the strait."
By threatening shipping, Iran can raise the cost of confrontation and seek leverage in negotiations but that may not guarantee success or yield concessions, the expert said.
Shipping crews caught in the crossfire of the Hormuz conflict
More crossings, but traffic remains depressed

Data from the UK Maritime Trade Operations Center's (UKMTO) weekly report, released on November 6, show 325 reported transits through Hormuz between October 29 and November 4. That was up from 277 the previous week, an increase of about 17%.
It's still roughly 65% below pre-war levels, the UKMTO assessed.
But vessel numbers alone cannot explain what is happening to energy supplies as cargo volumes and the routes used also matter, said Dalga Khatinoglu, an expert on Iran's energy and macroeconomics.

"If we look only at crude oil, Middle Eastern exports across all routes, from the Gulf of Oman and the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea, have largely recovered to pre-war levels," he told DW. "In some weeks in September and October, they even exceeded those levels."
His assessment covers the region's overall crude exports across all routes, not just shipments passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

The picture for refined petroleum products is different, Khatinoglu said. "Before the war, the Middle East exported about 6.2 million barrels of petroleum products a day. That figure has now roughly halved."

Liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports have also suffered. "As of September, exports from Qatar and the UAE were about 10% below pre-war levels. Although there has been some improvement, they remain severely disrupted," the expert underscored.
The cost of getting through spikes
Khatinoglu said recovering energy exports have not eliminated the costs associated with ongoing insecurity.
"Although oil exports from Middle Eastern countries have approached pre-war levels, shipping and insurance costs have remained very high," he stressed.

Citing recent figures from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), he said that average freight rates for a large tanker carrying crude from the Middle East to East Asia has risen about 12 times, from $3.18 (€2,84) per barrel at the beginning of the year to $37.13 a barrel at the end of October.
This means elevated costs for Asian importers even when crude is available.
Reducing costs and restoring commercial confidence in the safety of the strait requires more than a US military presence, Mohammadi said.
"There is only one solution to the Strait of Hormuz issue and that's an end to the war, accompanied by a lasting agreement that brings lasting security," he said.
Khatinoglu shared a similar view. "You cannot expect oil prices to return to pre-war levels simply by relying on US protection for ships in the Strait of Hormuz," he said.

articles.title: Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault convictions
articles.summary: The former comedian was found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others last week. The judge referred to Brand as a "predator."

image.caption: Russell Brand built his comedy career with jokes about his sexual exploitsImage: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/IMAGO

blocks.text: British media personality Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years and 6 months imprisonment on Monday after being found guilty of rape and assault.
He is required to spend at least two-thirds of that time in prison, and may be released under supervision after that if he displays good conduct while in jail.
Judge Joel Bennathan called Brand a "predator," and said that the sentence "just and proportionate...to the overall gravity of your criminality."
Bennathan also praised the "determination and bravery" of the survivors who came forward.
The 51-year-old had consistently denied the charges, brought about by six victims on allegations going back as far as 1999.
A jury of four women and eight men did not find his defense that all the encounters were consensual to be plausible, and found him guilty of raping or sexually assaulting four of his accusers.
Survivors, PM Burnham speak out
At the sentencing hearing, some of his victims gave victim impact statements to the court.

"I wanted ‌to express how this crime has affected me over the years," one woman said from behind a screen to protect her privacy, adding that the attack led to an "undeserved feeling of shame" she had carried for 20 years.
Another survivor called Brand a "sexual predator who has no remorse."

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham hailed the bravery of the survivors in a statement, and said his government would be "relentless in making whatever improvements we can” to provide more support for victims and make sure every police station has a sexual assault response team.
Who is Russell Brand?
Brand rose to prominence in the UK stand-up scene in the early 2000s with sets focused on his sex life, alcoholism, and heroin addiction.
He then became a presenter for several British televisions shows before starring in several Hollywood movies and being in a brief, high-profile marriage to American pop star Katy Perry.

As accusations of predatory behavior towards women began to mount, Brand left London and Hollywood behind for Florida. His politics changed from left-wing activism to promoting conservative ideas and conspiracy theories on his podcast.

He has said he underwent a religious conversion around this time. In 2016 he resumed his relationship with restauranteur Laura Gallacher, whom he first dated in 2007 when he was 31 and she was 19. They have since had three children together. Gallacher has remained by Brand's side throughout the court proceedings.

articles.title: 37 years after fall of Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans?
articles.summary: Three artists share their thoughts on the reunification of East and West Germany. How do they perceive a shared "we" and what gives them cause for optimism?

image.caption: The Berlin Wall came down on November 9, 1989Image: Norbert Michalke/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: When the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the wall. Yet, 37 years later, many people on both sides remain deeply skeptical of each other.
Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.
Does Germany's Gen Z still feel the East-West divide?
We asked three artists from Germany with different perspectives on the history of the country's division to share their views.
Winter shoes? Candy!
Author Lea Streisand was born in 1979 and experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall firsthand while growing up in East Berlin.
In her books and essays, she has returned to her East German upbringing many times, using literature to process it.
The novel "Hufeland, at the corner of Bötzow" (2019, Ullstein), for example, recounts the period of reunification from a child's perspective.

"November 9, 1989, was simply incredible," she told DW. She was 10 years old at the time. When her mother bought her winter boots with the 100 Deutsche Marks she received from the West German state — a welcome gift given to all East German citizens — she was so disappointed that she felt like crying. But later, a friend of her parents' let her buy so many sweets at the supermarket that they lasted until Christmas.

"The disappointment really set in afterwards, with what happened over the course of the following year. It was unbelievable how quickly an entire system was suddenly swept away and a new one built up, as if to say, 'There you go. You're welcome'," Streisand recalls. "I think it was just too fast for people."

blocks.caption: After the fall of the Berlin Wall, author Lea Streisand was finally able to visit her great-grandmother in the western part of BerlinImage: Marlene Gawrisch

blocks.text: The people of East Germany, or the GDR, had brought about the fall of the Berlin Wall themselves through a civil rights movement and numerous demonstrations. For many, however, the goal was not to dissolve the state immediately but to reform it.

Among them was Anke Feuchtenberger, born in 1963 in East Berlin. Her childhood was spent in East Berlin and in the East German region of Vorpommern, where she now lives again and feels "very much at home."

Today, she teaches at the University of Applied Sciences in Hamburg, meaning she spends time on both sides of the former divide. Feuchtenberger is often described as Germany’s most influential comic artist. Her work has also garnered international acclaim.
"Back then, as artists, we tried to bring about a change through posters and flyers — to gain more freedom without immediately abolishing socialism," she explained.

At the time, the fall of the Berlin Wall stirred up mixed feelings in her: "I quickly realized that the creative and revolutionary aspects of our movement were very quickly being smothered by consumerism, and that nationalist tendencies — which had already been noticeable before — were coming to the fore," Feuchtenberger recalls. "That made me afraid."

blocks.caption: Photo artist Simon Menner is interested in how images are instrumentalized in advertising, propaganda and warfareImage: Simon Menner

blocks.text: Meanwhile, for photographic artist Simon Menner, born in 1978 in Emmendingen, in the West German state of Baden-Württemberg, Berlin was very far away. As he put it, he experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall as a child in a "rather abstract" way. Today, Berlin is his home.
In his experience, the way films and documentaries portrayed East Germany around the time of reunification was very bleak. "But West Germany in the '80s," he said, "was also bleak and very staid."
The Stasi's photo treasure trove

This uneven portrayal of the two parts of Germany is an issue that deeply concerns him — partly because he unwittingly contributed to it in a small way. Among other things, Menner's work explores the topic of surveillance and how it works.

In the archives of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi — which are freely accessible today as part of the National Archives — he discovered a massive collection of photographs that both fascinated and horrified him and which he wanted to bring to the attention of a wider public.
His photo book "Top Secret" (2012, Hatje Cantz) features a selection of photos that offer a unique insight into the work of the Stasi. Sometimes eerie, sometimes curious, even absurd.

blocks.caption: Before searching an apartment, the Stasi would take Polaroid photographs so that they could subsequently restore the rooms to the state in which they had found themImage: Simon Menner/BStU 2013

blocks.text: Simon Menner also tried to look into the photo archive of West Germany's Federal Intelligence Service. "I spent a year trying to gain access — without success."
In hindsight, he now finds his artistic project problematic because he believes it is too one-sided, focusing exclusively on East Germany’s past.

According to Menner, West Germany's intelligence services in the 1960s were not exactly models of virtue either, and he believes it is "actually high time" to critically examine this part of history as well. In his view, an honest examination of Germany's past as a whole is a prerequisite for genuine reconciliation.

According to Lea Streisand, literature can help foster mutual understanding. "Literature opens a window into experiences we haven't had ourselves," she says. "You can immerse yourself in the mind of someone who has had a different life than you have and understand what happened."

Interest in these stories remains strong. In 2023, Anke Feuchtenberger published the nearly 500-page graphic novel "Comrade Cuckoo" (published by Reprodukt), which was the first graphic novel to be nominated for the Leipzig Book Fair Prize in the fiction category.

blocks.caption: 'May Day' from the comic book 'Comrade Cuckoo' by Anke FeuchtenbergerImage: Anke Feuchtenberger

blocks.text: The story spans a childhood in the fictional East German village of Pritschitanow in the 1960s in the GDR to the post-Reunification era. In it, Feuchtenberger weaves autobiographical memories of her upbringing with fantastical and fictional elements.
The artist says she was surprised "that, so long after the fall of the Wall, my stories have sparked such great interest in the West."

In particular, the fact that the main character, Kerstin, rarely sees her parents because they both work full-time is a topic that often comes up at readings. In the GDR, everyone had the right to work, she said. At the same time, it was a civic duty. Could the West German interest in this stem from the fact that full-time employment for both parents has long been less common in the West? It's possible, says Feuchtenberger.
What does the future hold?

When looking toward their shared future, the two East German women are more optimistic than the West German man. "In Berlin, I often don't even notice anymore whether I'm in the West or the East," says Simon Menner. "But when it comes to sociopolitical issues, politicians should listen to older and younger people more closely," he said, referring to the recent election successes of far-right party Alternative for Germany, or AfD . "Otherwise, things are going to get difficult in the near future."

"It's very important to step outside our own bubble because people all over the world are facing problems. Constantly focusing on this German-German divide that has emerged between the groups doesn't help," said Anke Feuchtenberger.

"For me personally, the whole issue of borders has somehow dissolved," she explains. This is due in no small part to the many trips abroad that have taken her to various places around the world. Moreover, in her hometown near the Polish border, she observes how animals couldn't care less about the border: "They come from the east and the west and do whatever they want." That's why she also gave "Comrade Cuckoo" the working title "A German Animal in a German Forest," "because I found the absurdity of an animal having a nationality so funny."

"This East-West thing — our children won't have any interest in it at all," thinks Lea Streisand. "Young people don't care where their parents come from. Can I get a job that will support a family? Do I have to go to war? Right now, completely different things are relevant."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Thirteen migrants die after boat sinks off Crete
articles.summary: The Greek coastguard says it has rescued 18 people, all of whom were Sudanese nationals.

blocks.text: At least 13 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of the Greek island of Crete.
The coastguard said it had rescued 18 people, all of whom were Sudanese nationals. Four of the survivors were taken to hospital, including a toddler.
Authorities said it was not immediately clear what caused the deaths, but they believe the boat had been at sea for days and had struggled to reach shore due to strong winds.

Crete remains one of several key gateways for migrants attempting to reach Europe from the Middle East and North Africa, with more than 22,000 of the 86,400 sea arrivals so far this year landing in Crete alone.
One unnamed coastguard official who spoke to news agency Reuters on condition of anonymity said the survivors were "shivering from the cold".
The migrants' boat was spotted by a Moroccan-flagged container ship about 15 nautical miles (28km) off Crete's coast.
The Greek coastguard rescued another 187 people in three separate incidents off the coast of Greece on Monday.
More than 37,000 migrants have arrived in Greece so far this year, UN figures show, already surpassing the number who arrived in the entirety of 2025.
The Greek government has announced plans to deal with the influx, including opening a temporary housing complex near the Cretan capital, Heraklion.
Greece was at the heart of Europe's migration crisis in 2015-16, when nearly a million people arrived on its islands, mostly from Turkey.

Arrivals later fell as border controls tightened, but crossings from Libya have surged in recent years, particularly among people fleeing conflict in Sudan and seeking better economic opportunities from countries including Bangladesh.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is embroiled in a spying scandal. Could the AI chipmaker survive without him?

image.caption: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang delivers his keynote on the company's GTC event in Berlin, Germany, on Oct. 21. As the CEO is investigated to determine whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort, analysts worry what the future would look like for Nvidia if Huang had to step down. (Markus Schre

blocks.text: Business·New

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has helmed the company since starting it in 1993, guiding it from a graphics card maker to the AI behemoth it is today. But with an investigation now underway into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort and no clear successor in sight, analysts say a change at the top — if it were deemed necessary — would be massive.
Analysts say change at the top would be a big shakeup, but company would go on
Jensen Huang, the leather-jacket-wearing and autograph-signing co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, has made himself a seemingly inseparable part of the AI chipmaker.

But now that an investigation is underway into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, that tight control at the company's helm is creating worries about whether he could actually be replaced, if such a move were deemed necessary.

The investigation comes after the New York Times reported late last week that Huang had a close romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese tech executive who was spying on behalf of China. It's unclear when he met the executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, but the two were photographed together in 2024.

Nvidia's board said Sunday it had no reason to believe that state or company secrets were compromised, but was undertaking an independent investigation in light of the reports. U.S. House Republican committee leaders have also called on Huang to sit for a briefing on his relationship with the woman.

items: Nvidia's shares slide as chip giant probes CEO Jensen Huang over spy claims

blocks.text: In a message to his staff, Huang admitted to having an affair and apologized to his family and colleagues for breaking their trust.
"I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence," he wrote.

Huang will stay on as CEO while the investigation takes place. But if the board were to oust him, or if he changed course and stepped down, tech analysts like Dan Ives say finding someone to take his place would be nearly impossible.
"In my opinion, Jensen is a one of one," said Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., a New York-based modern merchant bank. "Nvidia is here because of Jensen."
'The king of tech'

Nvidia began as a graphics card maker in 1993 until company leaders — Huang in particular — realized that its graphics processor units could power more than just games. The company pivoted to making chips for supercomputers in the early 2010s, betting on an artificial intelligence boom that wouldn't come for many years.

An early partnership with OpenAI led to a long-term relationship with the ChatGPT creator, which still relies on Nvidia's chips to power its technology today. Amazon, Meta, Google and virtually every other company building AI tools rely on the chipmaker's hardware to power their systems.
Worth about $4.5 trillion US today, Nvidia is the second most valuable company in the world, and invaluable to the AI ecosystem as a whole, according to Ives.

items: Nvidia probes whether CEO Jensen Huang targeted by foreign intelligence as he admits affair
Can AI be regulated? Why experts say government intervention is needed — but could be tricky

blocks.text: From his place atop the massive company, Huang became something of a rock star, routinely signing fan autographs at public appearances. One of his signature leather jackets sold for more than $1 million at an auction earlier this year.
"He's gotten to the point where he's sort of like the king of tech. Everybody listens to what Jensen has to say," said Bob O'Donnell, president and chief analyst at Technalysis Research.

Outside of his own company, Huang has also championed the AI buildout, financially backing companies like cloud computing company CoreWeave and Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot. He has also dismissed fears about an AI bubble and challenged apocalyptic warnings about the technology's existential threat to humanity, and has forged a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump.
Nvidia shares tumble as company investigates CEO Jensen Huang
Ives says the loss of Huang's advocacy would be a major hit to the industry if he had to step away.

Meanwhile, within the company, Huang created an unusually flat chain of command, with many employees reporting directly to him rather than to high-level executives. On a podcast earlier this year, Huang said as many as 60 people reported to him directly.
The company's site lists only a handful of high-ranking executives aside from Huang.
Two of Huang's children are also on staff at the company — his son Spencer is director of product for robotics, while his daughter Madison is senior director of product marketing.
No clear successor
With Huang having held control at Nvidia for so long, analysts say there is no clear successor.
"There's no one person or two people or three people that could replace Jensen. And that's a scary thing for investors, given this … black-eye moment that we're seeing," Ives said.
If Huang were forced to step down, Ives worries Nvidia would never fully recover from the loss of his leadership, given his integral role in the company's growth.
But others say with a firm as big as Nvidia, there are others who could take on the top job.
The falling star of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang | About That
"You don't create a company that large by yourself, right? It's just not possible. There's a huge team of very strong, smart, capable people," O'Donnell said.
While he agrees that Huang's loss would be massive, he says the company's technology roadmap — used to plan the next few years — is already laid out, making any potential successor's job easier.
O'Donnell expects Nvidia is on track to keep its leadership position among chipmakers for now, and doesn't expect a shakeup at the top would change that.
Furthermore, with the board saying it has confidence in Huang, O'Donnell says he doesn't expect those members would try to oust him.

Still, if Huang does stay on as CEO, his grip on the company likely won't be so tight going forward, O'Donnell says, as other high-ranking executives are likely to take centre stage as spokespeople and dealmakers at least some of the time.

"It's hard to replace an iconic figure who just lights up a room," he said. But "if the board is smart, and I'm sure they are, they recognize they're going to have to address this so people can regain confidence in the company."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Nine foreigners caught allegedly trying to leave South Africa to fight in Ukraine
articles.summary: Police declined to disclose their nationalities but said none of them lived in South Africa.

blocks.text: Nine foreigners have been arrested in South Africa after they were caught allegedly trying to leave the country to fight in the war between Russia and the Ukraine, police say.
The group, aged between 20 and 26, were arrested in and around Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team on Sunday evening.
They were caught as they were "preparing to board flights out of the country", authorities added, but their final destination is unclear.
The group is accused of contravening South Africa's laws, which outlaw mercenary activity without government permission.
Police said the group were arrested at South Africa's biggest airport, OR Tambo, and a hotel in Bruma, east of Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team that involved Interpol.

The police statement added that the involvement of Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies indicated that the suspects had also allegedly violated laws in their respective home countries, prompting cooperation with South African authorities.
Authorities declined to disclose the group's nationalities but confirmed that none of them resided in South Africa.
They have also not said whether the group allegedly intended to fight for Russia or Ukraine nor provided details of the organisations allegedly involved in facilitating their travel.
Citizens of several African countries, including Kenya, Ghana and South Africa, have gone to fight for Russia in Ukraine - some they had been duped and had not realised where they were going.
A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.
Kenya at the time estimated that 252 citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia. In March, Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue.
He said at the time that an agreement had been reached to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.
In February, Ghana said that 55 of its citizens had been killed in the conflict, with 272 believed to have been lured to fight since the war started in 2022.
The same month, South Africa secured the return of 17 South Africans who were allegedly tricked into joining the war.
In December last year, South African authorities arrested five people, including a journalist, for allegedly recruiting people to join the war.
Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.
The nine arrested are expected to appear in court either later on Monday or Tuesday.

articles.title: Germany: CDU names Ilse Aigner as candidate for president
articles.summary: The steering committtee of the CDU have announced Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner as presidential candidate. This gives her a good chance of becoming the first woman to occupy the role.

image.caption: Aigner is currently the speaker of Bavaria's state parliamentImage: Alexandra Beier/AFP

blocks.text: Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) on Monday confirmed that they would be putting forward Ilse Aigner as a candidate to be Germany's next head of state.

Aigner's own CSU, the CDU's Bavarian sister party, already supports her candidacy — and the federal coalition partners the Social Democrats have also made clear they would endorse her nomination if the conservatives agree on it.
This means the 61-year-old has a good chance of taking up the largely ceremonial role when the special committee that elects a German president convenes in late January.
While Angela Merkel famously served as the country's most powerful politician for more than a decade, Germany has never had a female head of state.
Could Ilse Aigner become Germany's first female head of state?
How did Aigner come to be nominated?
Aigner's chances at the nomination had been gathering momentum for some time now, with various government politicians including Chancellor Merz saying they'd favor a female candidate.
The CSU had in particular lobbied for the 13th post-war German president to be the first one from the Bavarian party and the first woman.

Reports that Merz would suggest Aigner as a candidate to the steering committee first emerged on Friday, and were then confirmed by participants when the party leadership convened for two days of talks on Sunday.

Current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's second five-year term comes to an end next March. The special "Bundesversammlung" committee that elects a German president therefore convenes in late January to choose his successor.
The committee — comprising 1,260 people in all — is made up of federal and state lawmakers, and sometimes municipal officials and others from public life.
SPD leader and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has voiced support for her nomination.

The CDU/CSU and SPD command a majority in the committee, and it's also possible that Green party politicians might support Aigner. This means her chances of selection seem strong, at least barring unexpected developments.

blocks.caption: Frank-Walter Steinmeier's decade as president comes to an end early next year, meaning political parties are seeking a succeessorImage: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Who is Ilse Aigner?
Aigner, 61, is currently the speaker of the state parliament in Bavaria.

The youngest of four sisters and the daughter of an electrician, she worked in the family business in her early adult life before going into politics. She's a Roman Catholic, single and has no children.
Aigner began her parliamentary career in the Bavarian legislature in 1994, then moved to the Bundestag federal parliament in 1998, before returning to the Bavarian chamber in 2013.
She spent five years as federal agriculture minister under then-Chancellor Angela Merkel.
She's currently the speaker or president of the state legislature in Bavaria, a role she has held since 2018.

articles.title: EU aims to pick new ECB chief by year-end
articles.summary: Christine Lagarde's early decision to step down as head of the European Central Bank (ECB) has put the European Union on a tight schedule. The bloc expects to pick a new ECB chief by the end of…

image.caption: The successors for the ECB's top jobs would likely be negotiated among the main eurozone countriesImage: KIRILL KUDRYAVTSEV/AFP

blocks.text: The European Union (EU) wants to name the next head of the European Central Bank by the end of the year, Eurogroup chief Kyriakos Pierrakakis said Monday.
Christine Lagarde, who has headed the ECB for seven years, has announced on October 29 that she is stepping down prematurely from the position, nine months ⁠before ⁠the end of her term.
Lagarde's early decision to step down makes the schedule tight because leaders must also fill two other seats on the ECB's Executive Board ​within months.
"The ambition here is that the whole process would have completed itself by the end of the year," Pierrakakis said before a Eurogroup meeting of eurozone finance ministers.
Who pays for Europe’s economic independence?

"We understand that we need to move fast. But what has traditionally happened in ​the past is that this was a decision driven by the leaders. Today it will be primarily an information point and the discussion," he said.
Who are the candidates?
The two candidates to replace Lagarde are former Dutch Central Bank Governor Klaas Knot and the head of the Bank for International ​Settlements, Pablo ‌Hernandez de Cos from Spain.

Pierrakakis said that Dutch and Spanish ministers would present their candidates and that later on Monday he would meet with Antonio Costa, head of the European Council, which represents EU governments' heads.
The appointment process requires eurozone finance ministers to put forward a candidate, followed by a European Parliament hearing and a final decision by EU leaders.
Dutch minister says the choice needs to be 'merit based'
Spanish Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said Hernandez de Cos was the "right person for the position", referring to his long-standing experience.
"He knows the ECB inside out. He's been leading institutions such as the Bank of Spain, such as BIS as well. A steady hand, but always a profile to be able to find consensus," he told reporters.
EU wants to attract European savers to boost bloc's economy

Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen, on the other hand, said Knot was an "excellent candidate", adding: "He has a very clear understanding of the ECB mandate and he has... a lot of experience to fulfil this position."

Heinen also ​said countries should ‌not see the ECB leadership contest as ​one between northern ⁠and southern European countries, or as ⁠an "​opportunity to trade favors" on other topics such as the multi-year EU budget.
A package deal is expected

The other two seats which have to be filled are those of Isabel ‌Schnabel, the head of the ECB's market operations, who leaves on January 3, 2027, and Chief Economist Philip Lane, ​whose term ends ⁠in May 2027.
The three jobs are likely to be negotiated between the ⁠main eurozone countries — ​France, Germany, Spain and the Netherlands — as a package, Reuters news agency said, citing officials.
The expectation is that the leaders agree on a package deal on all three positions.
Can Europe's economy survive in a new world order?
"Perhaps this would facilitate things. But again, this is a decision that will be taken by the leaders at the leaders level," Pierrakakis said.
Irish Finance Minister Simon Harris, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said he hoped Lagarde's replacement would be chosen by December.
"It certainly makes sense to fill the vacancy as quickly as possible," he said. But it's also about getting it right and getting the right person. It's a really crucial appointment."

articles.title: Why Nvidia CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy matters
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has apologized for an affair with a woman the US believes was spying for China. The story could have profound implications for the world's most valuable company and the global…

image.caption: Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993Image: Joyce N. Boghosian/White House/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.
The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believes she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.
US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.
What has Nvidia and the US government said?

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.
Nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

blocks.caption: Nvidia chips are used to build and run AI applications Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: "The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company said. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information."
The company's shares fell in early trading on Monday.
While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.
"He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine."
Why it matters for Nvidia

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.
"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this."

blocks.caption: The sale of Nvidia chips to China is a major political sorepointImage: Kyodo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, says the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Jensen Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said.
"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the company is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO."
The tangled China-Nvidia web
Nvidia and Huang's attitude towards China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed their sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-licence review. Beijing has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.
Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

blocks.caption: Nvidia is at the center of the US-China rivalry in AI Image: Huang Jingwen/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials, who fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost their domestic AI sector, lead to their AI models catching up with the leading US models and could be used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.
What China hopes to gain
Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Richard Windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also casts doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.
"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he said.

blocks.caption: While China has made advances it AI, it lacks advanced chips Image: Jung Yeon-je/AFP

blocks.text: The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom, thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.
Its valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion company in October 2025.

However, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.
Edited by Nik Martin

articles.title: Deportation policy ‘might have been too tough’, says Trump, as Miller starts chief-of-staff role – US politics live

blocks.text: Key events

items: 36m agoTrump says deportation policy 'might have been too tough' ahead of Miller's first day as chief of staff

blocks.caption: Robert Mackey

blocks.text: Robert Mackey

Donald Trump said on Sunday that he “was only kidding” when he announced a day earlier that he had offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC).

Speaking to reporters on his way back the White House from his beach club in Florida, Trump explained the premise of his joke, that if the UFC boss, who is a devoted fan of the president, took over the briefing room, flanked by six fighters, reporters “wouldn’t mess around with him so much”.

“So I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea, and he is a very capable guy,” Trump added. “Of course, I was kidding. And you could see that because I put all of the great fighters as his assistants, that they’re all going to come with him … It was just a little fun.”

Earlier on Sunday, the president shared an animated AI cartoon made by one of his supporters on social media, which showed UFC fighters beating up journalists and one, Josh Hokit, repeating the racist remark about Michelle Obama he made during the UFC event at the White House on Trump’s birthday in June.

The president said that his mock announcement that White would become his spokesperson, in a social media post on Saturday, “was an example of something where I was kidding, and then people said, ‘You know, that’s actually a pretty good idea’”.

blocks.caption: Adam Gabbatt

blocks.text: Adam Gabbatt

Stephen Miller, the influential architect of Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown, is due to start as White House chief of staff today. His promotion has horrified many, handing even more power to the president’s most controversial aide.

The 41-year-old has been with Trump since the beginning of the US president’s political career – serving as a speechwriter during his 2016 presidential campaign – and has long been seen as a hardliner on the right, serving as the driving force behind first-term Trump policies such as family separation at the US-Mexico border and the travel ban on people from many Muslim-majority countries.
Here is Miller in some of his own words:
Trump says deportation policy 'might have been too tough' ahead of Miller's first day as chief of staff
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump said he thinks his administration was too aggressive on deportations and that he was open to an arrangement to allow some undocumented immigrants to remain in the US.
The president said, in his first major interview since his party lost control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, that his deportation policy was part of the reason Republicans lost.
He told CBS’s ‘60 Minutes’ in an interview that aired on Sunday:
double quotation markI think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.

The president’s comments were an unusually frank acknowledgment that one of the defining policies of his second administration had become a political liability. But they were seemingly at odds with his decision on Friday to elevate Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to White House chief of staff.
Trump said that he thinks he could reach an agreement with the new Democratic majority, adding:
double quotation markWe would work something out. And I think it’s something - I think that’s something that’s actually doable.

The president claimed that his policy “both helped and hurt”, since people gave him an “A+ for closing up the border” and “very high marks for getting the bad ones out”. But he admitted: “I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally.”

His comments come as his most controversial aide Miller was due today to start his new role as chief of staff. In a social media ‌post, Trump called Miller, 41, “one of ​my most trusted advisors” and praised the outgoing Susie Wiles for doing “an ⁠outstanding job”.

I have so many people that I have great relationships with,” Trump said in his CBS interview.

Trump will meet with Qatar’s prime minister at ⁠the White House today, according to the White House schedule, as the ⁠conflict with ⁠Iran ​drags on and diplomatic efforts to end it face significant obstacles. A US deportation flight of Iranian nationals bound for Iran by way of Pakistan was abruptly canceled Sunday morning, according to an attorney who spoke to some of the detainees slated for repatriation.
